title: AI compute and model internals (generated)
summary: From what a Claude Code session costs, through the economics of GPU capacity and falling inference prices, into how transformers, MoE, attention and post-training work, and what new architectures and open models (DeepSeek, GLM) are bringing.

concepts.title: Tracking token costs
concepts.summary: Where the Expedition starts: what a Claude Code session costs, how to see it, and Fable 5’s pricing change.
concepts.overview: The conversation opens with a practical question: how do you see what a Claude Code session costs? The answer is simpler than the reader feared. Token counts and dollar costs are read straight from the session transcripts, so tools like ccusage, the built-in `/cost` command and the status line all report the same accurate figures; the only lossy number in [claude-carbon](#c/c-claude-carbon) is its CO2 estimate (see [How can I track Claude Code token cost?](#c/c-q-track-cost)). The second thread is price itself. [Claude Fable 5](#c/c-fable-5) costs $10/$50 per million input/output tokens and left subscription plans on June 23, after which it bills through usage credits. Anthropic says it wants Fable back on subscriptions once capacity allows, and that raises the question behind the rest of the Expedition: what capacity, and what limits it? That thread leads into [compute economics](#c/c-compute-economics).

concepts.title: Compute economics
concepts.summary: Supply and demand for AI compute: what limits capacity, how fast demand grows, and where prices go.
concepts.overview: Compute economics is the hub for the question “why is capacity scarce, and will that make AI dearer?” On the supply side, the chat shows that capacity is not only a matter of GPUs. [Accelerators](#c/c-accelerators), [HBM memory](#c/c-hbm), [power and grid](#c/c-power-grid) and [electrical gear](#c/c-electrical-gear) each bind in turn, and [the bottleneck keeps moving](#c/c-binding-constraint-moves) from one to the next. On the demand side, the compute of the AI chip stock grows about 3.4× a year ([compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand)), pushed up as agents and reasoning multiply compute per query. Against that, the cost to reach a fixed capability falls far faster. The chat’s answer is a split: [frontier models stay pricey while commodity capability gets cheap](#c/c-frontier-stays-pricey), and the squeeze on premium capacity probably eases only when delayed data centers arrive in 2027–2028, if demand growth slows ([when will it cool down?](#c/c-q-cool-down)).

concepts.title: Why inference gets cheaper
concepts.summary: What is behind the falling cost of LLM inference, and how to read the headline numbers.
concepts.overview: This topic takes apart Epoch AI’s headline that the cost of inference is “halving every 2 months.” The first lesson is what the number measures: the [cost to reach a fixed capability](#c/c-inference-cost), not the cost of running one frozen model. That cost falls mostly because new, smaller models reach old benchmark bars ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)), often via [distillation](#c/c-distillation) and [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe). A frozen model does get cheaper, but through [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) and new hardware, in steps. The second lesson is that the rate was never one number: it ranges from 9× to 900× a year by milestone, falls [fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier), and shrinks to about 3× a year once hardware and competition are removed. The chat reads the smooth curve as evidence that [incremental work drives the declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines), with breakthroughs resetting the ceiling.

concepts.title: Model size & scaling
concepts.summary: How parameter counts, training compute and capability relate, and how that changed around 2023.
concepts.overview: Before 2023, capability tracked size: [parameter count](#c/c-parameter-count) grew 1000× from GPT-1 to GPT-3 and about 10× more to GPT-4 (an estimated 1.8T). Then [frontier models got smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller), and [parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled). Two forces did it. [Chinchilla scaling](#c/c-chinchilla) showed models had been too big and under-trained, shifting effort to data, and [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) split [total from active parameters](#c/c-total-vs-active), so a model like [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) can hold 671B weights yet run 37B per token. Capability now rides on [training compute](#c/c-training-compute) (still growing about 5× a year), [pre-training efficiency](#c/c-pretraining-efficiency) and [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute). This decoupling is part of why the cost of a given capability can keep falling.

concepts.title: How transformers work
concepts.summary: The parts of a transformer LLM and the techniques that plug into them: MoE, attention, KV cache.
concepts.overview: This hub collects the chat’s tour inside a model. A [transformer](#c/c-transformer) is a stack of [layers](#c/c-layers), each an [attention](#c/c-attention) step, where tokens exchange information, followed by a [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) that works on each token alone, with both added back onto a [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream). Most of the techniques discussed plug into one of those two halves. [Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) replaces the feed-forward network with many experts, of which each token uses only a few. The attention side is dominated by the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache), the memory of past keys and values that grows with context and batch size, which grouped-query and latent attention shrink. The chat’s recurring point is that both halves are being redesigned against the same limits: capacity per active parameter and cache memory.

concepts.title: Measured rates
concepts.summary: The growth and decline rates quoted in the chat, with who measured them and how.
concepts.overview: Many numbers fly through this conversation, and this hub gathers the measured ones with their sources. On demand, [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai) puts the compute of the AI chip stock at about 3.4× growth a year. On price, the cost to reach a fixed capability falls anywhere from 9× to 900× a year across all models ([all models](m-price-decline-all)), about 5–10× for frontier models once frozen list prices are controlled for ([frontier](m-price-decline-frontier)), 7–28× for open models ([open](m-price-decline-open)), and about 3× from algorithms alone ([algorithmic efficiency](m-algorithmic-efficiency-inference)), the last two from the [inference price trends paper](#c/c-price-trends-paper). Supply figures come from analysts such as [SemiAnalysis](#c/c-semianalysis) and [JLL](#c/c-jll). The chat’s rule of thumb is to [trust rates over forecasts](#c/c-trust-rates-over-forecasts): rates measured from disclosed data are sturdier than dollar forecasts from interested parties.

concepts.title: How can I track Claude Code token cost?
concepts.summary: Use ccusage, the built-in /cost command or the status line; costs come straight from transcripts.
concepts.overview: The reader wanted to track the token cost of Claude Code sessions and worried that [claude-carbon](#c/c-claude-carbon) reported cost lossily. The answer: [only the carbon is lossy](#c/c-only-carbon-lossy). Every tool reads the same `~/.claude` JSONL transcripts, so the cost figures agree. The standard choice is **ccusage** (`npx ccusage@latest`), which gives daily, monthly, per-session and per-project breakdowns and a live monitor mode. Claude Code also has a built-in `/cost` command, which on Max and Pro subscriptions shows token usage but not dollars, since those plans don’t bill per token, and a status line that can show live session cost without a plugin. claude-carbon is still fine if you also want a CO2 estimate, read as an order of magnitude.

concepts.title: claude-carbon
concepts.summary: An open tool that reads Claude Code transcripts to estimate token cost and CO2 emissions.
concepts.overview: claude-carbon is a GitHub project that reads Claude Code’s session transcripts and reports token usage, dollar cost and an estimate of CO2 emitted. The reader found it while looking for a cost tracker and was put off by caveats about lossiness. As the chat explains, those caveats concern the carbon estimate, not cost: the token and cost figures come straight from the transcripts, while the CO2 figure depends on extrapolated emission factors, cache reads counted at full rate and grid-average carbon intensity ([only the carbon is lossy](#c/c-only-carbon-lossy)). For cost alone, it is more than you need; ccusage is the usual tool ([how to track cost](#c/c-q-track-cost)).

concepts.title: Token cost is lossy
concepts.summary: The reader’s first reading of claude-carbon’s caveats: that its token cost figures are lossy.
concepts.overview: The reader’s starting assumption was that [claude-carbon](#c/c-claude-carbon) warned its token cost figures were lossy, and asked whether that would be fixed or whether a better tool existed. The chat corrected this: the lossy part is the conversion of tokens into grams of CO2, not the token or dollar counts, which come straight from the transcripts ([only the carbon is lossy](#c/c-only-carbon-lossy)). The misreading is understandable, since the caveats sit next to cost figures, but it means there is nothing to fix on the cost side.

concepts.title: Only the carbon is lossy
concepts.summary: Token and cost figures are exact; only the conversion of tokens into CO2 is an estimate.
concepts.overview: This claim corrects the reader’s [assumption that token cost is lossy](#c/c-hyp-token-cost-lossy). Tools like [claude-carbon](#c/c-claude-carbon) and ccusage read token counts and costs straight from Claude Code’s transcripts, so those numbers are accurate. The estimate comes in turning tokens into grams of CO2: emission factors for Opus and Haiku are extrapolated, cache reads are counted at full rate, and grid carbon intensity is an average. That won’t be “fixed,” because Anthropic doesn’t publish per-model energy data. The practical upshot supports the answer to [how to track cost](#c/c-q-track-cost): any transcript-based tool will do, and a CO2 number should be read as an order of magnitude.

concepts.title: Claude Fable 5
concepts.summary: Anthropic’s most powerful model, at $10/$50 per million tokens, pulled from subscriptions on June 23, 2026.
concepts.overview: Claude Fable 5 is Anthropic’s most powerful model, and the reason the reader started asking about capacity. It is priced at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens, double Opus. On June 23, 2026 it left the subscription plans: it stays available, but once normal plan limits run out it is billed through usage credits at API rates. Anthropic has said it plans to restore it as a standard subscription feature as soon as possible, gated on capacity, with no date ([will it return?](#c/c-q-fable-return)). The chat later reads Fable’s premium pricing and credit gating as a concrete case of [frontier capability staying pricey](#c/c-frontier-stays-pricey) while compute is scarce.

concepts.title: Will Fable 5 return to subscriptions?
concepts.summary: Yes, Anthropic plans to restore Fable 5 to subscriptions, but it is gated on capacity with no date.
concepts.overview: After [Fable 5](#c/c-fable-5) left subscription plans on June 23, the reader asked whether it would come back. The hint is direct: Anthropic said it plans to restore Fable 5 as a standard subscription feature as soon as possible, once capacity allows, and might extend the free window if capacity holds. There is no committed date. In the meantime Fable doesn’t vanish; it just stops being free, and continued use bills usage credits at $10/$50 per million input/output tokens once plan limits are used up. The best advice was to watch Anthropic’s announcements rather than count on a date. The word “capacity” is what sent the conversation into [what limits AI compute capacity](#c/c-q-capacity).

concepts.title: What limits AI compute capacity?
concepts.summary: Not just GPUs: chips, HBM memory, power and electrical gear all bind; Anthropic’s own limit isn’t public.
concepts.overview: The reader asked whether Fable’s capacity limit is all GPU capacity. How Anthropic sets that limit is not public, and the chat says so plainly: it could be accelerators, serving headroom, power or a commercial throttle, most likely a mix. Industry-wide, though, “it’s all GPUs” is out of date. At least four constraints bind in series: [accelerators](#c/c-accelerators), [HBM memory](#c/c-hbm), [power and the grid](#c/c-power-grid), and [electrical gear](#c/c-electrical-gear) such as transformers and switchgear. Which one binds hardest shifts over time ([the bottleneck keeps moving](#c/c-binding-constraint-moves)). The scale explains why money can’t fix it quickly: cloud capex is expected to top $600B in 2026, much of it already contracted, yet [available compute](#c/c-available-compute) still arrives on multi-year timelines.

concepts.title: The bottleneck keeps moving
concepts.summary: The binding limit on the AI buildout shifts: power, then chips, then transformers and switchgear.
concepts.overview: The chat’s main answer to [what limits capacity](#c/c-q-capacity) is that the limit moves. Through 2024 and early 2025 it was power: operators held accelerators they could not energize, and Microsoft’s Satya Nadella described chips sitting idle for lack of power. In late 2025 and early 2026 it swung back to silicon, with a SemiAnalysis-type read calling chip production “a binding constraint on the pace of the AI compute buildout” (see [SemiAnalysis](#c/c-semianalysis)). By around May 2026 the gating factor was the electrical layer: long-lead [electrical gear](#c/c-electrical-gear) decides whether a site energizes on schedule. The pattern matters more than any one reading: relieving one constraint exposes the next, which is why [available compute](#c/c-available-compute) grows more slowly than the money spent on it.

concepts.title: Accelerators (GPUs/TPUs)
concepts.summary: AI chips (GPUs, TPUs): still tight, with Nvidia taking most of the spend and Blackwell sold out.
concepts.overview: Accelerators are the chips that do the arithmetic of training and inference: Nvidia GPUs above all, plus custom silicon such as Google’s TPUs and Amazon’s Trainium. They remain one of the tight constraints on [available compute](#c/c-available-compute). In fiscal Q3 2026 Nvidia reported record data center revenue of $51.2 billion, with Jensen Huang saying [Blackwell](#c/c-blackwell) sales were off the charts and cloud GPUs sold out; Nvidia takes most accelerator spend. The chat adds a caution when reading new chips: they help on two axes that are easy to conflate, raw FLOPs for training and tokens per dollar per watt for inference. For serving a model like Fable, the inference axis matters, and it depends as much on [HBM memory](#c/c-hbm) bandwidth and capacity as on compute.

concepts.title: Blackwell
concepts.summary: Nvidia’s current volume GPU generation: sold out, and cheaper per token thanks to more memory bandwidth.
concepts.overview: Blackwell is Nvidia’s current volume generation of [accelerators](#c/c-accelerators), and it is sold out. It comes up twice in the chat. On supply, it is part of why chips were a binding constraint in late 2025 and early 2026. On cost, the same model served on Blackwell-class hardware costs less per token than on the previous generation, chiefly because of more memory bandwidth and more [HBM](#c/c-hbm) capacity, so more of the model and more concurrent requests fit per chip. That follows from [inference being memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound): bandwidth, not raw FLOPs, is usually the bottleneck. The catch is that if the new chips are sold out and HBM-constrained, the efficiency exists on paper but can’t fully relieve cost. The chat says it has little solid detail on the roadmap beyond Blackwell.

concepts.title: HBM memory
concepts.summary: High-bandwidth memory stacked beside AI chips: sold out for 2026 and a fast-growing share of AI spend.
concepts.overview: HBM (high-bandwidth memory) is the fast memory packaged next to an accelerator, and the chat calls it the underappreciated constraint. SK Hynix said all its chips were sold out for 2026, and Samsung had customers for its 2026 HBM output. SemiAnalysis estimates memory could reach about 30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from about 8% in 2023 and 2024, and HBM now uses about 23% of DRAM wafer capacity, up from single digits two years earlier, driving a wider memory shortage. HBM matters so much because [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound): serving speed depends on how fast weights and the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) move from HBM to the chip, so HBM bandwidth and capacity gate [available compute](#c/c-available-compute) as much as the chips do.

concepts.title: Power & grid
concepts.summary: Power access and grid interconnection, which are pushing much of 2026’s planned AI capacity to 2028.
concepts.overview: Power was the binding constraint through 2024 and early 2025, when operators held chips they could not energize, and it is still what slips timelines. Chip manufacturing, power access, land and grid connections are tightening at once. Grid interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks are projected to push 30–50% of planned 2026 AI data center capacity to 2028, and one estimate says about half of planned U.S. data centers for 2026 will be delayed or cancelled. Deeper fixes are slow: most of the projected U.S. nuclear capacity increase comes after 2035, as small modular reactors become viable. These delays are why the chat puts physical supply relief for [available compute](#c/c-available-compute) in 2027–2028 ([when will the squeeze cool down?](#c/c-q-cool-down)).

concepts.title: Electrical gear
concepts.summary: High-voltage transformers and switchgear, the newest chokepoint, with lead times of up to 36–48 months.
concepts.overview: By around May 2026, the constraint on new AI data centers had moved to the “boring” electrical layer: high-voltage transformers and medium-voltage switchgear, the long-lead equipment that decides whether a finished site can be energized on schedule. Lead times for high-voltage transformers have stretched from 12–18 months to as long as 36–48 months in some cases. This is the latest step in [the moving bottleneck](#c/c-binding-constraint-moves), and one reason the chat argues the squeeze on premium capacity can’t be bought away quickly: with demand growing about 3.4× a year and gear on multi-year lead times, scarce frontier capacity gets priced up or rationed ([will the squeeze push costs up?](#c/c-q-squeeze)).

concepts.title: Available AI compute
concepts.summary: How much AI compute capacity is online, and how fast it can grow given chips, power and gear.

attributes.method: McKinsey: ~70 GW to ~220 GW of global supply within five years

concepts.overview: Available AI compute is the supply side of [compute economics](#c/c-compute-economics): the data center capacity actually energized and serving. It is growing fast but not fast enough. McKinsey sees global data center supply rising from about 70 GW to about 220 GW within five years, roughly 75% of that growth from AI. JLL expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity between 2026 and 2030. Cloud capex should top $600B in 2026 (+36%), about $450B of it on AI infrastructure. Yet each of [accelerators](#c/c-accelerators), [HBM](#c/c-hbm), [power](#c/c-power-grid) and [electrical gear](#c/c-electrical-gear) limits how fast that money turns into capacity. Because 30–50% of planned 2026 capacity may slip to 2028, the chat places real relief in 2027–2028 ([when will it cool down?](#c/c-q-cool-down)).
concepts.article:
## What counts as “available” compute?

Available compute is capacity that is built, powered and serving, not chips ordered or data centers announced. The gap between the two is the story of 2026. Money is not the constraint: major cloud companies are expected to spend over $600 billion on capex in 2026, a 36% rise from 2025, with about $450 billion going to AI infrastructure. The sources describe this demand as “funded, contracted, and under construction” rather than speculative. The problem is converting spend into energized racks, which needs [accelerators](#c/c-accelerators), [HBM memory](#c/c-hbm), [power and grid connections](#c/c-power-grid) and [electrical gear](#c/c-electrical-gear), all at once.

## How fast is it growing?

Two longer-horizon numbers anchor the chat. McKinsey’s figure is that global data center supply could grow from roughly 70 GW today to about 220 GW within five years, with around 75% of that growth driven by AI. JLL expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity to come online between 2026 and 2030, with the sector growing at about a 14% compound annual rate and the buildout needing up to $3 trillion by 2030.

Both are analyst forecasts, and the chat treats them as softer than measured rates: several of the supply figures trace back to a few analyst shops re-reported across many outlets, so the percentages are directional estimates ([trust rates over forecasts](#c/c-trust-rates-over-forecasts)).

## Why is it arriving late?

Because the constraints are physical and bind in series ([the bottleneck keeps moving](#c/c-binding-constraint-moves)). Grid interconnection queues and construction bottlenecks are projected to push 30–50% of planned 2026 AI data center capacity to 2028. HBM is sold out for 2026, and high-voltage transformer lead times have stretched to 36–48 months. As a result, component demand that was expected to peak in 2026 will instead be spread through 2027 and 2028 as delayed projects come online. Deeper power fixes, notably nuclear, are mostly a story for after 2035.

## What does it mean for prices?

Supply is the half of the squeeze that is easiest to date. Set against [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand) growing about 3.4× a year, supply that is gated by multi-year lead times means scarce frontier capacity gets priced up or rationed in the near term; Fable 5’s pricing and credit gating are read as an example ([will the squeeze push costs up?](#c/c-q-squeeze)). The chat’s hedged view is that the squeeze on premium capacity eases when the delayed 2026 projects land in 2027–2028, but only if frontier demand growth slows at the same time ([when will it cool down?](#c/c-q-cool-down)). More supply also [lowers the cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost), though efficiency gains there move far faster than new capacity.

concepts.title: Compute demand
concepts.summary: Demand for AI compute: the AI chip stock’s compute grows about 3.4× a year, doubling every 7 months.

attributes.method: Stock of AI chip compute from revenue data, disclosures and analyst reports

concepts.overview: Compute demand is the other half of [compute economics](#c/c-compute-economics). The number the chat anchors on comes from [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai): the total computing power of the stock of AI chips grows about 3.4× a year, doubling roughly every 7 months since 2022, far faster than Moore’s Law’s two-year doubling. What bends the curve upward is that [agents multiply per-query compute](#c/c-agents-multiply-compute): reasoning and agentic systems use vastly more compute per request, stacked on top of user growth. Meanwhile [inference is overtaking training](#c/c-inference-overtakes-training) as the main workload, which makes demand stickier. [Jensen Huang](#c/c-jensen-huang) now sees at least $1T of demand through 2027, though he sells the chips. Cheaper tokens don’t cool this down; by the [Jevons paradox](#c/c-jevons-paradox) they raise it.
concepts.article:
## How fast is demand growing?

The most careful measure in the chat is Epoch AI’s: the total computing power of the stock of AI chips is growing about 3.4× per year, doubling roughly every 7 months since 2022. Epoch builds it from revenue data, financial disclosures and analyst reports. For scale, the chat compares it to Moore’s Law, which doubles about every two years. Sustained over years, a 7-month doubling is an extraordinary rate.

Strictly, this measures the compute being installed, which is used as a proxy for demand: chips get bought because someone expects to use them.

## Why is the curve bending up?

Because the compute per request is rising, not just the number of requests. Nvidia’s framing from GTC is that computing demand rose roughly a million times over two years, the product of two multipliers: compute per inference session up about 10,000× as models moved from simple chatbots to reasoning and agents, and usage up about 100× ([agents multiply per-query compute](#c/c-agents-multiply-compute)). The exact multipliers are Nvidia’s, but the mechanism is the chat’s key point: reasoning models and agents consume far more compute per query, and that stacks on user growth.

The mix of work is shifting too. AI was about a quarter of data center workloads in 2025, mostly training; JLL expects inference to overtake training in 2027 and AI to reach about half of all workloads by 2030 ([inference overtakes training](#c/c-inference-overtakes-training)). Inference demand grows with adoption and recurs, whereas training a model is a one-time or periodic spend, so demand becomes stickier.

## What do the dollar forecasts say?

Jensen Huang’s high-confidence demand figure went from $500 billion through 2026 to at least $1 trillion through 2027, with the remark “we are going to be short.” The chat flags him as an interested party, since Nvidia sells the chips, though the direction is corroborated elsewhere. Its general rule is that measured rates like 3.4× a year are more trustworthy than dollar forecasts ([trust rates over forecasts](#c/c-trust-rates-over-forecasts)).

## Doesn’t cheaper inference reduce demand?

No, and this is the central tension of the Expedition. The [cost to reach a fixed capability](#c/c-inference-cost) falls roughly 100× a year in the headline figure, far faster than demand grows. But people buy the frontier, not a fixed capability, and the frontier costs more per query every year. Efficiency gains get used up by capability growth rather than passed on as lower bills: the [Jevons paradox](#c/c-jevons-paradox). The result is a widening split in which [frontier capability stays pricey while commodity capability gets cheap](#c/c-frontier-stays-pricey).

concepts.title: Agents multiply per-query compute
concepts.summary: Nvidia’s framing: reasoning and agents raised compute per session ~10,000×, times ~100× more usage.

attributes.method: ~1,000,000× over two years: compute per session ×10,000, usage ×100

concepts.overview: This is Nvidia’s explanation, from GTC, of why [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand) is bending upward rather than growing steadily. Over two years, it says, computing demand rose roughly a million times, the product of two multipliers: compute per inference session rose about 10,000× as models moved from simple chatbots to reasoning and agentic systems, and usage itself grew about 100×. The figures come from an interested party, but the mechanism is the chat’s key insight: a reasoning model or an agent burns far more compute per request than a chatbot did, and that growth stacks on top of user growth. It is also why the frontier keeps getting more expensive per query even as the cost of a fixed capability collapses.

concepts.title: Inference overtakes training
concepts.summary: Inference is expected to overtake training as the main AI data center load around 2027.
concepts.overview: According to [JLL](#c/c-jll), AI made up about a quarter of data center workloads in 2025, with training driving most of the demand. Inference is expected to overtake training in 2027, and by 2030 AI could be half of all workloads with inference the main driver. The shift matters for the shape of [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand): training a model is a one-time or periodic investment, while inference grows with adoption and recurs every day, so inference demand is stickier and compounds with usage. JLL also flags the fragility: this “inference supercycle” depends on inference applications that don’t yet exist at scale being adopted quickly.

concepts.title: Will the squeeze push costs up?
concepts.summary: Yes for frontier tiers in the near term; no for any given capability, whose cost keeps collapsing.
concepts.overview: The reader asked whether the gap between demand and supply must drive costs up further. The chat, flagging that it is reasoning rather than reporting, answers: yes for the frontier and premium tier in the near term, no for a given capability over time. Supply can’t keep pace in the short run: 30–50% of planned 2026 capacity may slip to 2028, HBM is sold out and transformers take 36–48 months, while [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand) grows about 3.4× a year. The scarce resource, frontier inference capacity, gets priced up or rationed; [Fable 5](#c/c-fable-5)’s $10/$50 pricing and credit gating look like an instance. But the cost of a fixed capability halves about every two months, so today’s frontier becomes next year’s cheap tier. Hence [frontier pricey, commodity cheap](#c/c-frontier-stays-pricey).

concepts.title: Frontier pricey, commodity cheap
concepts.summary: A widening spread: newest models stay expensive while older capability levels keep collapsing in price.
concepts.overview: This is the chat’s resolution of two exponentials running against each other: [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand) growing about 3.4× a year, and the [cost to reach a fixed capability](#c/c-inference-cost) falling about 100× a year. Both are real, and they apply to different things. The newest frontier models are scarce and keep getting more expensive per query as reasoning and agents consume more compute, so they stay pricey or get pricier; [Fable 5](#c/c-fable-5) is the example at hand. The trailing capability tier keeps collapsing in price as smaller models catch up to it. The [Jevons paradox](#c/c-jevons-paradox) explains why your bill doesn’t fall: savings are spent on more capability. So “AI got cheaper” and “the frontier got more expensive” can both be true indefinitely.

concepts.title: Jevons paradox
concepts.summary: When a resource gets cheaper to use, total use rises; cheaper tokens mean more tokens, not smaller bills.
concepts.overview: The Jevons paradox is the observation that making a resource more efficient to use can raise total consumption rather than cut it. It is named after the economist William Stanley Jevons, who noticed in the 19th century that more efficient steam engines increased Britain’s coal use. The chat applies it to inference: making tokens cheaper increases the total tokens consumed rather than reducing spending, because people buy the frontier, and reasoning and agents consume the savings. That is why the ~100×-a-year fall in the [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost) doesn’t show up as a 100× smaller bill, and why cheaper inference pushes [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand) up. It underpins the [frontier pricey, commodity cheap](#c/c-frontier-stays-pricey) split.

concepts.title: When will the squeeze cool down?
concepts.summary: Nobody knows; supply relief is a 2027–2028 story, and cooling also needs demand growth to slow.
concepts.overview: The chat calls this the most uncertain question and distrusts anyone who claims to know. It lays out conditions instead of a date. Supply relief is physical and slow: nearly 100 GW of new capacity is expected between 2026 and 2030, and delayed 2026 projects landing in 2027–2028 is when [available compute](#c/c-available-compute) meaningfully loosens. Demand is the bigger swing factor. Cooling needs demand growth to slow as easy gains saturate, the inference applications the bull case assumes to fail to appear, or disappointing returns to cut capex. A Stanford teaching model, explicitly a toy rather than a forecast, sketches scenarios: an “AI winter” if demand growth slows to about 100% a year, an energy breakthrough shifting the bottleneck to memory bandwidth, or balanced improvement compressing margins. The hedged best guess: premium capacity eases in 2027–2028 only if frontier demand slows.

concepts.title: Trust rates over forecasts
concepts.summary: Measured growth rates are the most trustworthy numbers; dollar forecasts and timing calls are the softest.
concepts.overview: This is the chat’s rule for weighing its own numbers. Rates measured from disclosed data, such as [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai)’s 3.4× a year for compute and the two-month halving of the cost to reach a capability, are the sturdiest. Dollar forecasts and timing calls are the softest, and most come from parties with a position: chipmakers like Nvidia ([Jensen Huang](#c/c-jensen-huang)’s $1T figure), real-estate analysts, infrastructure investors. Many supply figures also trace back to a few analyst shops, such as [SemiAnalysis](#c/c-semianalysis), McKinsey and Bloomberg Intelligence, re-reported across many outlets, so agreement among outlets is less independent than it looks. Epoch and academic sources such as RAND and Brookings are the most neutral. Cross-source agreement on direction is more trustworthy than any single number, including the chat’s own timing guesses.

concepts.title: Epoch AI
concepts.summary: A research group tracking AI trends in compute, prices, model size and training; the chat’s most neutral source.
concepts.overview: Epoch AI is an independent research group that measures trends in AI, and it is the source the chat leans on most and trusts most. It supplies the demand figure (the AI chip stock’s compute growing about 3.4× a year), the [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost) (halving about every two months, but 9× to 900× a year depending on the milestone), [training compute](#c/c-training-compute) growing about 5× a year, [pre-training efficiency](#c/c-pretraining-efficiency) improving about 3× a year, the finding that [scale drove two-thirds of gains](#c/c-scale-two-thirds), and the estimates behind [frontier models getting smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller). The chat rates it the most neutral source against interest-conflicted forecasters, while noting its headline cost figure is widely misread and that its size estimates for closed models are informed guesses.
concepts.article:
## What is Epoch AI?

Epoch AI is a research organization that collects data on how AI is developing: how much compute goes into training, how large models are, how fast prices fall and how much hardware is installed. It publishes datasets, trend pages and short analyses. In this conversation it is the backbone of nearly every measured rate.

## Which of its numbers does the chat use?

- **Compute demand**: the total computing power of the AI chip stock grows about 3.4× a year, doubling roughly every 7 months since 2022, built from revenue data, disclosures and analyst reports ([compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand)).
- **Inference cost**: the cost to run an LLM at a fixed level of performance halves roughly every 2 months, about two orders of magnitude a year ([cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost)).
- **The spread of that rate**: 9× to 900× a year depending on the performance milestone, with the fastest drops in the most recent year, so it is less clear they will persist ([price decline, all models](m-price-decline-all)).
- **Model size**: parameter counts grew 1000× from GPT-1 to GPT-3 and about 10× more to GPT-4; in 2023 the trend reversed, with GPT-4o at about 200B and Claude 3.5 Sonnet at about 400B ([frontier models got smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller)).
- **Training**: training compute for frontier language models grows about 5× a year since 2020, doubling every ~5.2 months; pre-training compute efficiency improves about 3× a year; and about two-thirds of language-model gains over the last decade came from scale.
- **A forecast**: in late 2024, about an 80% chance most next-generation models would be larger than GPT-4, and about a 60% chance frontier sizes grow less than 10× over three years.

## Why does the chat trust it most?

Because it measures rather than sells. Most other forecasts in the chat come from chipmakers, real-estate analysts or investors, while Epoch, along with academic sources such as RAND and Brookings, has no position in the outcome. Its rates are measured from disclosed data, which the chat ranks as the most trustworthy kind of number ([trust rates over forecasts](#c/c-trust-rates-over-forecasts)).

## Where do its numbers need care?

Three cautions come up. First, the inference-cost headline is “one of the most widely misread statistics in the space”: it holds the capability fixed, not the model, so it does not mean a given model gets 100× cheaper ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)). Second, it rests on benchmarks, which Epoch itself says don’t fully measure usefulness, and on list prices, which proprietary vendors rarely cut for old models, inflating the extreme figures. Third, its parameter counts for closed models such as Claude 3.5 Sonnet are estimates, not disclosed figures; Anthropic has never published a parameter count.

concepts.title: SemiAnalysis
concepts.summary: A semiconductor analyst firm behind many re-reported figures on chip supply and memory spending.
concepts.overview: SemiAnalysis is a semiconductor and AI-infrastructure research firm whose estimates show up, often secondhand, all over the chat’s supply picture. A SemiAnalysis-type read describes chip production as a “binding constraint on the pace of the AI compute buildout” in late 2025 and early 2026, part of the case that [the bottleneck keeps moving](#c/c-binding-constraint-moves). It also estimates memory could account for about 30% of hyperscaler AI spending in 2026, up from about 8% in 2023 and 2024 (see [HBM](#c/c-hbm)). The chat’s caution is that many figures trace back to a handful of shops like this one, re-reported across outlets, so they should be read as directional analyst estimates rather than hard facts ([trust rates over forecasts](#c/c-trust-rates-over-forecasts)).

concepts.title: JLL
concepts.summary: A real-estate analyst whose data center outlook covers the shift to inference and new capacity to 2030.
concepts.overview: JLL is a commercial real-estate firm whose data center outlook supplies several of the chat’s medium-term figures. It reports that AI was about a quarter of data center workloads in 2025, mostly training, and expects [inference to overtake training](#c/c-inference-overtakes-training) in 2027, with AI near half of workloads by 2030. On supply it expects nearly 100 GW of new capacity between 2026 and 2030, a sector growing at about 14% a year, and a buildout needing up to $3 trillion by 2030 ([available compute](#c/c-available-compute)). JLL also names the fragility in the bull case: the inference supercycle depends on applications that don’t yet exist at scale. The chat counts it among analysts with a position in the outcome, not a neutral measurer.

concepts.title: Jensen Huang
concepts.summary: Nvidia’s CEO, who raised his AI demand estimate to at least $1T through 2027: “we are going to be short.”
concepts.overview: Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s CEO, is the chat’s loudest voice on demand. His high-confidence demand figure rose from $500 billion through 2026 to at least $1 trillion through 2027, with the line “we are going to be short.” He also said Blackwell sales were off the charts and cloud GPUs sold out, and Nvidia’s GTC framing of a million-fold rise in computing demand underlies [agents multiply per-query compute](#c/c-agents-multiply-compute). The chat treats him as an interested party, since he sells the chips, and ranks his dollar figures among the most interest-conflicted numbers in the conversation ([trust rates over forecasts](#c/c-trust-rates-over-forecasts)), even though the direction of his claims about [compute demand](#c/c-compute-demand) is corroborated elsewhere.

concepts.title: Cost to reach a capability
concepts.summary: The cost to run an LLM at a fixed benchmark level: halving about every 2 months, but varying widely.

attributes.method: Epoch headline: cost at a fixed performance level halving ~every 2 months

concepts.overview: This is the measurement behind the claim that “AI inference is getting cheaper.” [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai) reports that the cost to run an LLM at a fixed level of performance has been halving roughly every two months, about 100× a year. The crucial detail is what stays fixed: the capability, not the model ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)). The number mostly tracks new, smaller models reaching old benchmark bars, through [distillation](#c/c-distillation), [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) and algorithmic progress, while [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) and hardware make a frozen model cheaper more slowly. It is also not one rate: it ranges from 9× to 900× a year by milestone, and falls to about 3× a year once hardware and competition are removed. And since it rests on benchmarks, it is really the cost to reach a benchmark score, an imperfect proxy for usefulness.
concepts.article:
## What does it measure?

Epoch AI’s figure is “the cost to inference an LLM at a fixed level of performance.” Pick a capability bar, such as a benchmark score, and ask what the cheapest model that clears it costs to run; then watch that cost over time. Measured this way, the cost has been halving roughly every two months, a fall of about two orders of magnitude a year.

The fixed thing is the capability, not the model. The model that clears a bar in 2026 is usually a different, smaller and more efficient one than the model that cleared it in 2025. A task that needed GPT-4-class compute in 2023 might be handled by something Haiku-sized today at a small fraction of the cost ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)).

## What drives it down?

Mostly capability-bar chasing: new, smaller models reaching old quality levels, often by [distillation](#c/c-distillation) from a bigger model or by architectures like [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) that decouple size from running cost ([parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled)). On top of that, a frozen set of weights also gets cheaper through [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization), such as batching, [quantization](#c/c-quantization), [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention) and [KV-cache](#c/c-kv-cache) work, and through new hardware like [Blackwell](#c/c-blackwell). Those effects are real but far more modest, and they come in steps rather than along a smooth curve ([does a given model get cheaper?](#c/c-q-sonnet-cheaper)).

## Is it one number?

No. The rate varies from 9× to 900× a year depending on the milestone. It falls fastest at the high-capability end (31× a year in the top GPQA-Diamond bin against 1.7× in the lowest), because new bars have the most room for cheap catch-up ([prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier)). The extreme figures come from counting all models at current list prices, which proprietary vendors rarely cut for old models, and they are concentrated in the last year. Controlling for that, the [inference price trends paper](#c/c-price-trends-paper) finds about 5–10× a year for frontier models, 7–28× for open models, and about 3× from algorithms alone. The chat’s ladder, from real technology progress to headline: ~3×, ~5–12×, ~10–30×, up to 100–900× ([is the rate constant?](#c/c-q-epoch-constant)).

## Why doesn’t my bill fall 100× a year?

For three reasons. People buy the frontier, not a fixed capability, and the frontier gets more expensive per query as reasoning and agents consume more compute, so savings are spent on capability ([Jevons paradox](#c/c-jevons-paradox)). The price you pay is a business decision only loosely tied to serving cost: API prices often hold flat over a model’s life and then drop in a step when a successor launches. And the figure measures an idealized cost-to-capability, not either the cost to serve or the price charged.

## How good a proxy is it?

Only as good as the benchmarks. Epoch is candid that benchmarks don’t comprehensively measure usefulness: they miss capabilities beyond knowledge and reasoning, and things like output speed. So “cost to reach capability X” is really “cost to reach benchmark score X,” a decent but imperfect stand-in for what users care about.

concepts.title: Does a given model get cheaper to run?
concepts.summary: Not 100× a year: a frozen model gets cheaper through serving tricks and hardware, in steps.
concepts.overview: The reader asked whether Epoch’s falling inference cost means a particular version of Sonnet keeps getting that much cheaper to run. No. The 100×-a-year figure is dominated by new, smaller models reaching old capability bars ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)). A frozen set of weights does get cheaper, through different and smaller mechanisms: [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) on the same weights, the biggest lever, and new hardware generations with more memory bandwidth. Providers also quietly swap in a [distilled](#c/c-distillation) or replacement model, which can look like the model got cheaper. These come as step changes, not a smooth curve. And the API price is a separate business decision, loosely coupled to cost: often flat through a model’s life, then dropping in a step when a successor launches. Anthropic’s internal serving costs aren’t public, so there is no real number for any Sonnet.

concepts.title: A frozen model gets 100× cheaper
concepts.summary: The reader’s first reading of Epoch’s figure: that one specific model gets 100× cheaper a year.
concepts.overview: On first hearing that inference cost halves every two months, the reader asked whether that means a specific build, such as a given version of Sonnet, gets that much cheaper to run. It is the natural reading, and the chat calls the Epoch number one of the most widely misread statistics in the space. The metric holds capability fixed, not the model: the cheapest model that clears a bar keeps getting cheaper, usually because a new, smaller model replaced the old one ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)). A frozen model gets cheaper too, but far more slowly and in steps ([does a given model get cheaper?](#c/c-q-sonnet-cheaper)).

concepts.title: Fixed capability, not fixed model
concepts.summary: Epoch’s cost metric holds the capability bar fixed, not the model; cheaper successors do most of the work.
concepts.overview: This is the key to reading the [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost). The fixed thing in Epoch’s metric is a capability, such as a benchmark score or a class of coding problems, not a model. So the claim is that the cheapest model able to clear a given bar keeps getting much cheaper, and that model is usually a different, smaller, more efficient successor. A task that needed GPT-4-class compute in 2023 might now be done by something Haiku-sized for a fraction of the cost. It corrects the reader’s [assumption that a frozen model gets 100× cheaper](#c/c-hyp-frozen-model-cheaper), and it explains why [distillation](#c/c-distillation) and model replacement dominate the curve while [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) contributes more modestly.
concepts.article:
## What is held fixed?

Epoch’s metric is “the cost to inference an LLM **at a fixed level of performance**.” The fixed level is a capability: a benchmark score (the chat’s example is “MMLU 80%”) or the ability to solve a class of coding problems. For each such bar, Epoch asks what the cheapest model that reaches it costs to run, and how that changes over time. The model is free to change, and it does.

## What does that imply?

The cheapest model that hits a given bar in 2026 is a different, smaller, more efficient model than the one that hit it in 2025. The capability holds still; the model delivering it shrinks and cheapens. That is where the headline 100×-a-year comes from: it measures the falling cost of *re-reaching old capability bars*, not the falling price of any shipped product. The chat’s concrete example is a task that needed GPT-4-class compute in 2023 being handled by something Haiku-sized today at a tiny fraction of the cost.

## Then what makes a specific model cheaper?

Different and smaller forces. The biggest is [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) on the same weights: batching, [quantization](#c/c-quantization), [speculative decoding](#c/c-speculative-decoding), [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention)-style kernels and [KV-cache](#c/c-kv-cache) work. Next are hardware generations with more memory bandwidth and HBM. These come in lumps, not along a smooth exponential.

Between the two interpretations sits [distillation](#c/c-distillation) and model replacement. Providers don’t serve the same giant model forever; they distill it into a smaller student or replace it with a new architecture that hits the same quality more cheaply. To a user it can look as though “the model got cheaper,” but the artifact was swapped, and that swap is largely what the Epoch curve captures.

## Why does the distinction matter?

Because it changes what you should expect from your bills. The spectacular rate is about capability bars, not about any model you use, and the price you are charged is a separate business decision that often holds flat and then steps down when a successor launches ([does a given model get cheaper?](#c/c-q-sonnet-cheaper)). The same framing also explains a later surprise: the fastest declines come at high-capability bars, where cheap catch-up has not yet happened ([prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier)).

concepts.title: Serving optimization
concepts.summary: Software that serves the same weights more cheaply: batching, quantization, speculative decoding, better kernels.
concepts.overview: Serving optimization is everything that makes a trained model cheaper to run without changing its weights, and the chat calls it the biggest lever for a frozen model. It includes continuous or dynamic batching to keep accelerators busy, [quantization](#c/c-quantization) to lower-precision numbers, [speculative decoding](#c/c-speculative-decoding), better attention kernels such as [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention), and KV-cache techniques like [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention), [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization) and [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching). Most of these attack the same root problem: [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound), so they move less data or move it less often. They stack in a modern serving stack and explain most of how a deployed model gets cheaper over its life, as opposed to techniques like grouped-query attention that must be trained in ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)).
concepts.article:
## What is it?

Serving optimization is inference software work on the same weights. The model doesn’t change; how it is run does. The chat names it as the real answer to “does Sonnet get cheaper to run?”: yes, mostly this way. These techniques can cut serving cost meaningfully over a model’s life, though at a far more modest pace than the headline cost curve, and in steps.

## What are the main techniques?

- **Continuous or dynamic batching** keeps the accelerator saturated by folding many requests into each step.
- **[Quantization](#c/c-quantization)** runs the model at lower precision (FP8, INT8, INT4), often with negligible quality loss.
- **[Speculative decoding](#c/c-speculative-decoding)** lets a small draft model propose tokens that the big model checks in parallel.
- **[FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention)** and similar kernels compute attention without writing the full score matrix to slow memory.
- **KV-cache techniques**: [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention) removes wasted cache memory, [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization) stores the cache at lower precision, and [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching) reuses the cache of shared prompts.

## Why do they work?

Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound). The bottleneck is usually moving data between the GPU’s big, slow HBM and its small, fast on-chip SRAM, not arithmetic; the compute units sit idle waiting. Almost every optimization is a way to move less data or move it less often. The [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache), which grows with sequence length and batch size, is the object most of them fight over.

## How do they fit together?

They stack rather than compete. A modern serving stack typically runs a model with grouped-query attention, using FlashAttention kernels, under PagedAttention memory management, with prefix caching and often KV quantization on top, plus continuous batching. Each attacks a different facet: kernel efficiency, fragmentation, cache precision and redundant recomputation.

The chat draws one line through the list ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)). FlashAttention, PagedAttention, KV quantization and prefix caching work on frozen weights, so they can make an already-deployed model cheaper. [Grouped-query](#c/c-gqa), [multi-query](#c/c-mqa) and [latent attention](#c/c-mla) shrink the cache at the source but must be trained in. Which combination any proprietary provider runs is not published, so the general picture is solid but provider-specific attributions are guesses.

concepts.title: Quantization
concepts.summary: Running a model at lower numerical precision (FP8, INT8, INT4) to cut memory and serving cost.
concepts.overview: Quantization stores and computes a model’s numbers at lower precision, such as FP8, INT8 or INT4 instead of 16-bit, often with negligible quality loss. Smaller numbers mean less memory and less data to move, which matters because [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound). It is one of the main [serving optimizations](#c/c-serving-optimization) that make a frozen model cheaper to run, and the same idea applied to the cache gives [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization). It can also go deeper than serving: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) trains natively in FP8 and ships only FP8 weights, with a script to convert them to BF16. The chat lists more aggressive sub-8-bit training and inference as a direction it cannot yet confirm in flagship models.

concepts.title: Speculative decoding
concepts.summary: A small draft model proposes several tokens and the big model checks them in parallel.
concepts.overview: Generating text one token at a time leaves a large model underused: each step does little arithmetic but must stream all the weights from memory. Speculative decoding exploits that. A small, fast draft model proposes the next few tokens, and the big model verifies them all in one parallel pass, keeping the ones it agrees with. When the draft is usually right, the big model produces several tokens per pass instead of one. It is one of the [serving optimizations](#c/c-serving-optimization) that make a frozen model cheaper without touching its weights. The chat notes a link to architecture: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3)’s multi-token prediction heads, trained to predict further ahead, double as a speculative-decoding accelerator at inference.

concepts.title: FlashAttention
concepts.summary: An attention kernel that computes attention block by block in fast on-chip memory, never writing the full score matrix.
concepts.overview: FlashAttention is the best-known attention kernel optimization. Naive attention computes the full matrix of scores between every pair of tokens, writes it to slow HBM, reads it back for the softmax, writes again and reads again to weight the values. Because [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound), that traffic dominates. FlashAttention tiles the work into blocks that fit in fast SRAM and fuses scores, softmax and value-weighting into one pass, using an “online” softmax that normalizes correctly block by block. The output is mathematically identical, but memory grows linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically, and it runs faster. Since it changes nothing about the weights, it is a pure [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) that makes an already-trained model cheaper ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)). Versions 2 and 3 followed.
concepts.article:
## What problem does it solve?

[Attention](#c/c-attention) compares every token’s query with every other token’s key. A naive implementation computes the full attention-score matrix for the sequence, writes it to the GPU’s HBM, reads it back to apply softmax, writes the result, and reads it again to multiply by the values. For a long sequence that intermediate matrix is enormous, and the round trips to HBM dominate the time while the arithmetic units wait. This is the general rule that [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound), in its sharpest form.

## How does it work?

Two ideas: tiling and fusion. FlashAttention processes attention in small blocks that fit in the GPU’s fast on-chip SRAM, and computes scores, softmax and value-weighting for each block in one fused pass, without ever writing the full score matrix to HBM.

The tricky part is softmax, which normally needs every score before it can normalize. FlashAttention uses a running, or “online,” softmax: it keeps a running maximum and running sum as blocks arrive and rescales earlier partial results, so the final output is correctly normalized even though it never saw all the scores at once.

## What does it buy?

The output is mathematically identical to standard attention, but memory traffic falls sharply, so it is both faster and uses far less memory. Memory now grows linearly with sequence length rather than quadratically. Later versions refined it: FlashAttention-2 improved how work is split across GPU threads, and FlashAttention-3 was tuned for features of Hopper-class hardware.

## Why does it matter for cost?

FlashAttention changes nothing about a model’s weights or outputs. It is a pure serving win that can be applied to an already-trained model, which makes it a textbook case of how a frozen model gets cheaper over its life ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)). It usually runs alongside [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention), prefix caching and KV quantization in a modern serving stack. The chat classes it with the efficiency techniques that are quality-neutral by design: it makes attention cheaper, not the model smarter.

concepts.title: KV cache
concepts.summary: The stored keys and values of earlier tokens, kept per layer; the biggest memory cost of inference.
concepts.overview: When a model generates text, each new token attends to every earlier token. Those earlier tokens’ keys and values don’t change once computed, so instead of recomputing them at every step the model caches them: the KV cache. It exists per [layer](#c/c-layers), grows linearly with sequence length and batch size, and for long contexts can outgrow the model weights in memory. That makes it the central object of inference optimization, since [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound). Some techniques shrink it at the source by using fewer K/V heads ([grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa), [multi-query attention](#c/c-mqa)) or compressing it ([multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla)); others manage it better at serving time ([PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention), [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization), [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching)). Because only keys and values are cached, [K/V heads set the cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob).
concepts.article:
## What is it?

An LLM generates autoregressively: one token at a time, each new token attending to all the previous ones through [attention](#c/c-attention). Attention needs every earlier token’s key and value vectors. Those don’t change once computed, so rather than recompute them at each step, the model stores them. That store is the KV cache.

Only keys and values are cached. The query for the current token is used once and discarded, because no future step needs past queries. That asymmetry is why the number of K/V heads, not query heads, sets the cache size ([K/V heads set cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob)).

## Why is it so large?

It grows linearly with sequence length and with batch size, and every [layer](#c/c-layers) keeps its own, since each layer’s heads produce their own keys and values; a 60-layer model caches 60 layers’ worth. For long contexts it can dwarf the model weights in memory. It is the single biggest memory consumer during inference, which is why the chat says nearly every inference optimization is ultimately a fight over the KV cache.

## How do models shrink it at the source?

By changing the architecture, which must be done at training time. [Multi-query attention](#c/c-mqa) has all query heads share a single K/V head, cutting the cache by roughly the number of heads at some cost to quality. [Grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa) is the compromise that won: query heads split into groups, each sharing one K/V head; 32 query heads in 8 groups gives a 4× smaller cache with little quality loss. [Multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla), DeepSeek’s approach, compresses keys and values into a small shared latent; in DeepSeek-V3 it is 512-dimensional, about 32× smaller than full K/V.

Research also lets adjacent layers share one KV cache instead of each storing its own, reusing cached activations rather than weights.

## How do servers manage it better?

Three [serving optimizations](#c/c-serving-optimization) work on frozen weights. [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention) (from vLLM) stores the cache in fixed-size pages tracked by a table, like operating-system virtual memory, removing reserved-but-empty memory so more requests fit per GPU. [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization) stores keys and values in 8 bits or fewer instead of 16. [Prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching) computes the cache for a shared prefix, such as a system prompt, once and reuses it; it is the mechanism behind API prompt-caching discounts.

## Where is this heading?

The newer designs attack the cache from another side: attending to fewer past tokens. DeepSeek-V3.2’s sparse attention picks a small subset of earlier tokens to attend to, and hybrid models like [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) keep full attention in only one layer in four. The chat sums up the whole attention side of model design as a fight to minimize KV-cache pressure.

concepts.title: Inference is memory-bound
concepts.summary: Inference is limited by moving data between slow HBM and fast on-chip memory, not by arithmetic.
concepts.overview: The counterintuitive fact behind most inference optimizations is that the bottleneck is usually not arithmetic but data movement: shuttling weights and activations between the GPU’s large but slow memory ([HBM](#c/c-hbm)) and its small, fast on-chip SRAM. Attention in particular reads and writes large matrices, and the compute units sit idle waiting. So almost every optimization is a way to move less data or move it less often. That explains why [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention) avoids writing the score matrix to HBM, why the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) is the object everyone fights over, and why new chips like [Blackwell](#c/c-blackwell) serve models more cheaply mainly through more memory bandwidth and capacity rather than more FLOPs.
concepts.article:
## What does “memory-bound” mean?

A GPU has two kinds of memory that matter here: big but slow HBM, where weights and the KV cache live, and small but fast on-chip SRAM, where arithmetic actually happens. A workload is memory-bound when its speed is set by how fast data can move between the two, not by how fast the chip can calculate. For transformer inference that is usually the case: the arithmetic units sit idle waiting for data.

## Why is inference like this?

Attention is the extreme case. A naive implementation computes a large score matrix, writes it to HBM, reads it back for softmax, writes it again and reads it again, so HBM round trips dominate the time. On top of that, the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) that attention reads grows with sequence length and batch size and can outgrow the weights themselves.

## Why does batching help?

When a model generates one token at a time for one request, each step must stream the weights it uses through the chip but does comparatively little arithmetic per byte moved. Serving many requests together lets each weight read do more work, which is why continuous batching, keeping the accelerator busy with many requests at once, is one of the basic serving optimizations.

## How does it shape optimization?

Almost every optimization in the chat is a scheme to move less data or move it less often. [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention) keeps attention in SRAM. [Quantization](#c/c-quantization) and [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization) shrink the bytes. [GQA](#c/c-gqa), [MQA](#c/c-mqa) and [MLA](#c/c-mla) shrink the cache. [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention) and [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching) avoid waste and recomputation. Seen this way, the list of [serving optimizations](#c/c-serving-optimization) is one idea applied many times.

## What does it mean for hardware?

That memory bandwidth, not raw FLOPs, is usually the thing to watch. The same model served on [Blackwell](#c/c-blackwell)-class hardware costs less per token mainly because of more bandwidth and more [HBM](#c/c-hbm) capacity, which fits more of the model and more concurrent requests per chip. It is also why HBM supply is such a tight constraint on AI capacity: for serving, the inference-efficiency axis is gated as much by HBM as by compute.

concepts.title: Distillation
concepts.summary: Training a smaller “student” model on a stronger model’s outputs to reach its quality more cheaply.
concepts.overview: Distillation trains a smaller student model to imitate a stronger teacher. With a closed teacher, whose weights and probabilities you can’t see, that means [supervised fine-tuning](#c/c-sft) on the teacher’s generated outputs. The technique appears in three places in the chat. It is a main reason the [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost) falls: providers distill big models into cheaper ones that reach old quality bars, and the price-trends authors suggest it helps explain why [prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier). It is a common post-training ingredient, sometimes transferring reasoning more effectively than RL. And it is the subject of a correction: the chat’s claim that distillation from closed models explains a chunk of open models’ reasoning gains overreached; it clearly works and was widespread, but its share is unmeasured.
concepts.article:
## What is it?

Distillation trains a smaller “student” model to approximate a larger or more capable “teacher.” With open models the student can learn from the teacher’s full output probabilities; with closed models it can’t, since weights, hidden states and output distributions are hidden, so distillation means generating a large set of the teacher’s outputs and fine-tuning on them. In practice it is supervised fine-tuning on a stronger model’s responses, which the chat calls “a souped-up SFT.”

## How does it make inference cheaper?

It is the bridge between a frozen model getting cheaper and the headline cost curve. Providers don’t keep serving the same giant model forever; they distill it into a smaller student that approximates it, or replace it with a new model that reaches the same quality more cheaply. To a user it can look as if “the model got cheaper,” but the artifact was swapped, and this is largely what Epoch’s [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost) captures ([fixed capability, not fixed model](#c/c-capability-not-model)).

The authors of the [price trends paper](#c/c-price-trends-paper) suggest greater use of distillation, along with mixture of experts, may explain why costs fall fastest for high-capability bars: distilling a fresh, expensive frontier model into something smaller is a big one-time win with no equivalent left for an old, already-cheap model.

## Where does it fit in post-training?

It is often part of the recipe. Many strong open models get much of their post-training quality by distilling from a larger or more capable teacher. One RLVR study contrasted the two methods: RL mostly made the model better at sampling answers it could already produce, while distillation could transfer genuinely new reasoning patterns from a stronger teacher, sometimes more effectively than RL.

## How much of open models’ progress is distillation from closed models?

The reader challenged the chat’s earlier remark that “a chunk of apparent reasoning gains may be distillation,” and the chat split it into three claims:

1. **Distilling closed models works**: well established. OpenAI sells model distillation as a product. TinyGSM used 12.3M synthetic math problems from GPT-3.5-turbo to take a 125M-parameter model to 63.1% on grade-school math.
2. **It was widespread in open models**: strongly supported, especially in 2023–2024. Alpaca was Llama fine-tuned on about 52K instructions generated by an OpenAI model; Open Orca and ShareGPT data came from GPT-4 and ChatGPT outputs.
3. **It explains a chunk of reasoning gains specifically**: an overreach. The evidence shows distillation *can* transfer reasoning, not *how much* of any model’s reasoning came from it. The flagship open reasoning result, DeepSeek-R1, cuts the other way: RL on the base model produced the reasoning, and distillation then spread R1’s own reasoning to smaller models.

No reliable “X% is distillation” figure exists, because labs rarely disclose post-training data and using frontier outputs is often contractually prohibited, so the evidence is often circumstantial.

concepts.title: Is the cost-decline rate constant?
concepts.summary: It was never one number: 9× to 900× a year by milestone, with defensible estimates fairly stable.
concepts.overview: The reader asked whether Epoch’s cost-decline rate is holding steady. The answer reframes the question: there is no single rate. The decline ranges from 9× to 900× a year depending on which capability milestone you measure, so it is a family of lines, not one line speeding up or slowing down. The extreme figures come from counting all models at current list prices ([all models](m-price-decline-all)), are concentrated in the last year, and may not persist. The defensible estimates are tamer and fairly stable: about 5–10× a year for frontier models ([frontier](m-price-decline-frontier)), 7–28× for open models ([open](m-price-decline-open)), and about 3× from algorithms alone. The reader’s guess that the decline slows at the top turned out backwards ([prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier)).

concepts.title: Frontier bars are slower to catch
concepts.summary: The reader’s guess that higher benchmark bars take cheap models longer to reach, so declines slow at the top.
concepts.overview: The reader reasoned that as benchmark scores rise, cheaper models should take longer and longer to catch up, so the cost decline should slow at the high end. The chat calls it a sharp hypothesis that should hold under some assumptions, then reports that the data show the opposite: [prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier), 31× a year in the top GPQA-Diamond bin against 1.7× in the lowest. New bars have the most room for cheap catch-up. The reader’s intuition does survive in another form, though: the fastest drops are recent, and it is unclear whether they will persist, which is the closest thing in the data to “this should get harder.”

concepts.title: Prices fall fastest at the frontier
concepts.summary: Costs fall fastest for high-capability bars: 31× a year in the top GPQA-Diamond bin vs 1.7× in the lowest.
concepts.overview: This finding corrects the reader’s guess that [frontier bars are slower to catch](#c/c-hyp-frontier-slower). In the [inference price trends paper](#c/c-price-trends-paper), models in the highest GPQA-Diamond bin fell in price by 31× a year, while those in the lowest bin fell by only 1.7×; other studies show the same pattern. The reason is headroom. A newly reached high bar is at first cleared only by one expensive model, so the first cheaper model to match it is a huge multiplier, while low bars were cleared years ago and their cost is already wrung out. The authors suggest different mechanisms act at the top, such as [distillation](#c/c-distillation) and [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe). The caveat: those top-end rates are recent and may not persist.

concepts.title: Inference price trends paper
concepts.summary: A 2025 arXiv paper (2511.23455) on price per benchmark level, split by frontier, open and algorithmic trends.
concepts.overview: This paper, arXiv 2511.23455, studies how the price of reaching a given benchmark level changes over time and, unlike the headline figures, controls for confounds. It finds that for frontier models the price for a given performance level falls about 5–10× a year ([frontier](m-price-decline-frontier)), and that isolating algorithmic efficiency, by dividing out hardware price declines and using open models to control for competition, leaves about 3× a year ([algorithmic efficiency](m-algorithmic-efficiency-inference)). Split by capability bin, it shows [prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier): 31× a year in the top GPQA-Diamond bin against 1.7× in the lowest, which the authors tentatively attribute to distillation and mixture of experts. The chat treats it as the most careful account of what is real technology progress.

concepts.title: Price decline, all models
concepts.summary: 9×–900× a year across milestones for all models at list prices, inflated because old list prices rarely fall.

attributes.method: All models incl. proprietary, current list prices

concepts.overview: This is the widest and most quoted version of the inference price decline. Measured across all models, proprietary ones included, at their current list prices, the cost to reach a given performance milestone falls anywhere from 9× to 900× a year depending on the milestone, and the fastest drops came in the most recent year, so it is unclear they will last ([Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai)). The chat puts it at the top of its ladder of numbers as the most headline-grabbing and most confounded. Proprietary vendors rarely cut the price of older models, so when a cheap new model launches, the old model’s frozen list price exaggerates the apparent fall. Controlling for that gives the tamer [frontier](m-price-decline-frontier) figure.

concepts.title: Price decline, frontier
concepts.summary: About 5–10× a year for frontier models once frozen list prices are controlled for.

attributes.method: Frontier models, controlling for frozen list prices

concepts.overview: Once the frozen-list-price confound is stripped out, the [inference price trends paper](#c/c-price-trends-paper) finds the price for a given benchmark level falling about 5–10× a year for frontier models. The chat calls this range, together with nearby estimates it summarizes as 5–12×, the most defensible “real” figure for price-for-performance, and notes these middle estimates have been fairly stable over time, unlike the extreme [all-models figures](m-price-decline-all). It sits between pure [algorithmic efficiency](m-algorithmic-efficiency-inference) at about 3× a year and the [open-model trend](m-price-decline-open) at 7–28×.

concepts.title: Price decline, open models
concepts.summary: 7–28× a year for open-weight models (geometric mean about 11.8×), fairly uniform across quality levels.
concepts.overview: Open-weight models give a cleaner read on price decline, because they are not subject to the strategic list-price games of proprietary vendors, who tend to leave an old model’s price frozen. Their price for a given performance level falls a fairly consistent 7–28× a year, with a geometric mean of about 11.8×, and the rate is roughly uniform across quality levels. That uniformity contrasts with the steep top-versus-bottom gap seen when proprietary models are included ([prices fall fastest at the frontier](#c/c-fastest-at-frontier)). In the chat’s ladder of numbers it sits at about 10–30× a year, above the [frontier](m-price-decline-frontier) estimate and well below the [all-models](m-price-decline-all) headline.

concepts.title: Inference algorithmic efficiency
concepts.summary: About 3× a year of pure algorithmic efficiency in inference, once hardware and competition are divided out.

attributes.method: Algorithmic only; hardware and competition removed

concepts.overview: This is the most conservative number in the price-decline family, and the one closest to “real underlying technology progress.” The [inference price trends paper](#c/c-price-trends-paper) starts from the price for a given benchmark level, divides out hardware price declines, and controls for competition using open models, leaving about 3× a year of improvement from algorithms alone. The chat puts it at the bottom of its ladder, below the [frontier](m-price-decline-frontier) figure of 5–12× and far below the [all-models](m-price-decline-all) headline. It later uses the smoothness of this ~3× curve as evidence that [incremental work drives cost declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines): many small wins, not a few big jumps. Mixture of experts is only one ingredient within it, alongside data, distillation, quantization and attention work.

concepts.title: How fast are parameter counts growing?
concepts.summary: Totals climb into the trillions via MoE while active parameters stay low; closed frontier sizes are undisclosed.
concepts.overview: The reader asked how fast parameter counts are rising and how that relates to capability. The honest answer has two parts. For the closed frontier, counts are mostly undisclosed, so trends rest on estimates; [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai)’s late-2024 forecast put about 80% odds on most next-generation models being larger than GPT-4, and about 60% on frontier sizes growing less than 10× over three years, slower than the GPT-3-to-GPT-4 jump. For open models, totals have resumed climbing into the hundreds of billions and low trillions through [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe), while active parameters stay far lower ([total vs active](#c/c-total-vs-active)). Behind this sits the 2023 reversal when [frontier models got smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller), and the broader point that [parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled). The chat discounts splashier claims, such as a 25-trillion-parameter teacher model, as unsourced.

concepts.title: Parameter count
concepts.summary: The number of weights in a model: once the main lever on capability, now a loose guide.
concepts.overview: A model’s parameter count is the number of learned weights it has. Through the GPT era it grew exponentially and tracked capability: 1000× from GPT-1’s 117 million to GPT-3’s 175 billion in two years, then about 10× more to GPT-4, estimated at 1.8 trillion. Had that continued, models would be near 10 trillion today. Instead [frontier models got smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller) in 2023, and since then [parameters have decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled).
