[Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) also makes the phrase ambiguous: [total vs active parameters](#c/c-total-vs-active) now diverge, so you have to ask which count is meant. Frontier counts are mostly undisclosed; Anthropic, OpenAI since GPT-4, and Google publish none.

concepts.title: Frontier models got smaller
concepts.summary: In 2023 frontier models reversed course and got smaller than GPT-4, by Epoch AI’s estimates.
concepts.overview: Before 2023, frontier language models grew steadily bigger. Then, according to [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai), the trend reversed. Models that followed GPT-4 (estimated at about 1.8 trillion parameters) were smaller: the original GPT-4o at around 200 billion and Claude 3.5 Sonnet at around 400 billion, probably an order of magnitude below GPT-4. The chat flags those figures hard: they are Epoch’s estimates, not disclosed numbers, and Anthropic has never published a Claude parameter count. The reversal followed from [Chinchilla scaling](#c/c-chinchilla), which moved effort toward more data on smaller models, and from [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe). It is key evidence that [parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled), since benchmark scores kept rising while size fell.

concepts.title: Parameters decoupled from capability
concepts.summary: Since about 2023, parameter count says little about capability, which rides on compute, data and algorithms.
concepts.overview: Up to about 2023, bigger meant better, and parameter count was the main lever on capability. Since then the two have come apart: benchmark scores kept climbing while frontier parameter counts arguably fell and then grew only modestly. [Chinchilla scaling](#c/c-chinchilla) showed models had been too big for their data, and [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) split [total from active parameters](#c/c-total-vs-active). Capability now rides on [training compute](#c/c-training-compute), still growing about 5× a year, on data, on [pre-training efficiency](#c/c-pretraining-efficiency), and on [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute). The decoupling matters for cost: if capability still needed proportionally more active parameters, the [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost) could not fall the way it has.
concepts.article:
## What changed?

Before 2023 the story was a simple exponential: parameters grew 1000× from GPT-1 to GPT-3 and about 10× more to GPT-4, and capability rose with them. After GPT-4, [frontier models got smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller), yet benchmark scores kept climbing rapidly. Since then, knowing a model’s parameter count tells you fairly little about where it lands on a benchmark. Size went from the main lever to one of several, and not the dominant one.

## What broke the link?

Two forces. [Chinchilla scaling](#c/c-chinchilla), the 2022 finding that for a fixed compute budget the field had built models too big and trained them on too little data, pushed developers toward roughly 20 tokens per parameter and toward curating large, high-quality datasets. Capability that would have come from more parameters came instead from more and better data on a smaller model.

[Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) made “parameter count” ambiguous. In a dense model every parameter fires on every token; in an MoE model only a few experts do. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 671B total parameters but only 37B active per token, so it has the capacity of its total and the running cost of its active count ([total vs active](#c/c-total-vs-active)).

## What drives capability now?

About two-thirds of language-model improvements over the last decade came from scale, but scale meant [training compute](#c/c-training-compute), not parameter count ([scale drove two-thirds of gains](#c/c-scale-two-thirds)). Training compute still grows about 5× a year; you can pour that into a modest-sized model by training it on far more data and for longer. [Pre-training efficiency](#c/c-pretraining-efficiency) improves about 3× a year, giving more capability per parameter. And a growing share of capability comes from [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute), letting the model think longer at inference, an axis entirely independent of size.

## Why does it matter for cost?

This decoupling is why inference can keep getting cheaper for a given capability. If capability still required proportionally more active parameters, serving cost could not fall the way Epoch’s price data shows. MoE and the parameter-capability split are a big part of the machinery behind the 5–12×-a-year decline in cost for a given performance ([cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost)).

concepts.title: Chinchilla scaling
concepts.summary: The 2022 finding that models were too big for their data; about 20 training tokens per parameter.
concepts.overview: Chinchilla is the name of a 2022 DeepMind study and model that changed how compute is spent. It found that for a fixed compute budget, the field had been building models too large and training them on too little data. The resulting rule of thumb, roughly 20 training tokens per parameter, pushed developers away from simply building bigger models and toward curating massive, high-quality datasets. Much capability that would have come from extra parameters came instead from more and better data on a smaller model. The chat names it as one of the two forces, with [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe), behind the 2023 reversal in which [frontier models got smaller](#c/c-models-got-smaller), and so behind [parameters decoupling from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled).

concepts.title: Mixture of experts
concepts.summary: An architecture where each token uses only a few “expert” sub-networks, so size and per-token cost come apart.
concepts.overview: Mixture of experts (MoE) replaces a transformer layer’s [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) with many parallel [experts](#c/c-experts), and a small learned [router](#c/c-router) sends each token to only a few of them. The model can hold a very large total number of parameters while each token only pays for the active few: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 671B total but 37B active ([total vs active](#c/c-total-vs-active)). That makes MoE central to why [parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled) and a likely factor in the falling [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost). The idea dates to 1991, became practical in deep nets in 2017, and became the open-model default in 2024–2025. Making it work took years of incremental fixes such as [load balancing](#c/c-load-balancing) and [shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts).
concepts.article:
## Where do the experts live?

A transformer layer has two parts: [attention](#c/c-attention), where tokens look at each other, and a [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) that processes each token on its own. MoE replaces only the feed-forward network. Attention stays dense and shared, and every token uses all of it. So “8 experts” or “256 experts” means the FFN block has been split into that many parallel sub-networks. An [expert](#c/c-experts) is just one of those weight blocks, not a specialist in a topic.

## How are experts chosen?

A tiny learned [router](#c/c-router), essentially one linear layer, scores every expert for each token. A softmax turns the scores into weights, the top-k experts (usually 1 or 2 in classic designs; DeepSeek-V3 uses 8) process the token, and their outputs are combined by those weights. The choice is made fresh for every token at every MoE layer: a 60-layer model makes 60 routing decisions per token, and the next token gets its own. Neighbouring words like “the” and “mitochondria” may route to entirely different experts ([how does MoE pick experts?](#c/c-q-moe-how)).

## What does it buy, and what does it cost?

In a dense model, per-token compute scales with the full parameter count. MoE lets total parameters, and so total capacity, grow while per-token compute stays pinned to the active subset: a bigger model’s capacity at a smaller model’s running cost. The trade is memory: all experts must be stored in expensive HBM even though most sit idle for any given token, and routing adds engineering overhead, especially when experts are spread across GPUs and tokens must be shipped to wherever their chosen expert lives.

## Where did it come from?

The idea is old. It began with the 1991 paper [Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts](#c/c-moe-1991) by Jacobs, Hinton, Jordan and Nowlan. The version that matters for LLMs, sparse and gated inside deep nets, came from Shazeer and colleagues at Google in 2017 ([sparsely-gated MoE layer](#c/c-sparse-gated-moe)), reaching 137 billion parameters. [GShard](#c/c-gshard) put it into the Transformer in 2020, and [Switch Transformer](#c/c-switch-transformer) simplified routing to one expert per token in 2021. From 2024, with [Mixtral](#c/c-mixtral) and DeepSeek-V3, it became the dominant open architecture.

The breakthrough itself delivered little value at first. What made MoE trainable and servable was a long tail of incremental fixes: [load-balancing](#c/c-load-balancing) losses, expert-capacity limits, routing stability, top-1 routing, [shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts) and systems work to shard experts across GPUs. The chat uses this as its main example that [incremental work drives cost declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines).

## Did MoE cause the cost drop?

Not provably. Epoch’s price data starts around April 2024, long after MoE was invented; its spread through open models overlaps the window, but it is one ingredient in the ~3×-a-year algorithmic slice alongside data, distillation, quantization and attention work ([did MoE drive the cost drop?](#c/c-q-moe-cost-drop)). The price-trends authors do suggest MoE, with distillation, may help explain why costs fall fastest at high capability. The chat calls MoE a hybrid: primarily a capacity-per-active-parameter play that buys quality per unit of inference cost.

## How do today’s open models differ?

All converged on MoE but split on two choices. Granularity: DeepSeek uses many small experts (256 routed at a width of 2048), while [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) uses few large ones and alternates MoE with dense layers. Shared experts: DeepSeek-V3, [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) and GLM-4.5 keep an always-on shared expert, while [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) dropped it, one of the unsettled questions in MoE design.

concepts.title: Total vs active parameters
concepts.summary: With MoE, total parameters (capacity, memory) and active parameters per token (cost) diverge.
concepts.overview: In a dense model every parameter is used for every token, so one number describes both size and cost. [Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) splits it in two. Total parameters set the model’s capacity and how much memory it needs; active parameters per token set the compute each token costs. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 671B total but 37B active; [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) has 1T total but 32B active. A model can look huge and run cheap at the same time. That makes “how fast are parameter counts growing?” a question with two answers: open-model totals are climbing into the trillions while active counts stay low ([parameter count](#c/c-parameter-count)). The catch is memory: all parameters still sit in expensive HBM even when idle.
concepts.article:
## Why are there two numbers?

In a dense transformer, every parameter fires on every token, so cost scales with size. In a [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) model, each token passes through only a few [experts](#c/c-experts) at each layer. The total parameter count counts every expert; the active count counts only what a single token actually uses. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) is the standard illustration: 671B total, 37B active per token.

## What does each number tell you?

Total parameters roughly measure capacity: the model has the memorization capacity of its total count. They also set the memory bill, since all 671B of DeepSeek-V3’s parameters sit in HBM even though most are idle for any token. Active parameters set the per-token cost and roughly track the work done per token. The chat’s summary: the total count buys capacity; the active count sets cost.

## How does this change the size trend?

“How fast is parameter count growing?” now has two answers. Totals can keep climbing while active parameters stay flat or grow much more slowly. For open models that publish counts, totals have resumed climbing into the hundreds of billions and low trillions, while active parameters stay far lower. [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) pushes the ratio furthest among the models discussed: 1 trillion total, 32B active, across 384 experts. [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) Maverick has 400B total and 17B active.

## Why does it matter?

It is one of the two forces behind [parameters decoupling from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled), and part of why the [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost) keeps falling: a model can gain capacity without a proportional rise in serving compute. It also means headline parameter counts need a second question before they can be compared: total or active?

concepts.title: DeepSeek-V3
concepts.summary: DeepSeek’s open MoE model: 671B total, 37B active, 61 layers, 256 experts, MLA attention, shipped in FP8.

attributes.signature: MLA (KV cache squeezed to a 512-dim latent), many small experts (256 × 2,048 wide) plus a shared one, aux-loss-free balancing, multi-token prediction, native FP8. V3.2 adds DeepSeek Sparse Attention on top.

concepts.overview: DeepSeek-V3 is the most thoroughly documented open frontier model in the chat, and its reference example for how a modern LLM is built. It is a [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) with 671B total and 37B active parameters ([total vs active](#c/c-total-vs-active)). Its public config gives the exact shape: 61 layers (3 dense, 58 MoE), hidden size 7168, 256 routed experts with 8 active plus 1 [shared expert](#c/c-shared-experts), 128 attention heads, a 129,280-token vocabulary, and a 160K context stretched from 4K with YaRN. Its distinctive techniques are [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla), which compresses the KV cache into a 512-dimensional latent, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing, and multi-token prediction; it trains natively in FP8. Its weights and inference code are open, but not its training data. It led to [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32).
concepts.article:
## What is its shape?

Straight from its public `config.json`:

- **Layers**: 61 (`num_hidden_layers`), the first 3 dense (`first_k_dense_replace: 3`) and the remaining 58 MoE.
- **Hidden size**: 7168, the width of the residual stream; every token is a 7168-number vector at every layer boundary.
- **Dense FFN width**: 18432 in the 3 dense layers, about 2.6× the hidden size.
- **Expert FFN width**: 2048 (`moe_intermediate_size`), much slimmer than the hidden size.
- **Experts**: 256 routed, 8 active per token, plus 1 shared, the “9 active” some articles cite.
- **Attention heads**: 128, with `num_key_value_heads` also 128, because MLA’s compression is expressed in other fields.
- **Vocabulary**: 129,280.
- **Context**: 163,840 (160K), reached via YaRN RoPE scaling from an original 4,096.

Total parameters are 671B, of which 37B are active per token.

## Why are its experts so small?

In a dense transformer the FFN’s middle width is usually several times the hidden size. DeepSeek-V3’s experts have a middle width of 2048, smaller than the 7168 hidden size. That is deliberate: many small, fine-grained experts give the router finer choices than a few fat ones. A token reaching an MoE layer is sent to 8 of 256 experts; each does 7168 → 2048 → 7168 with its own weights, and their outputs plus the shared expert’s are summed back into the residual stream. [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) takes the opposite approach, with few large experts.

## What techniques set it apart?

**[Multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla)** projects keys and values into a shared low-rank latent that is cached and expanded per head on the fly. The config shows `kv_lora_rank: 512` against 16,384 for full K/V (128 heads × 128), so the cache is about 32× smaller. Position rides in a separate 64-dimensional slice (“decoupled RoPE”) because RoPE doesn’t survive the compression cleanly.

**Auxiliary-loss-free load balancing** adjusts per-expert bias terms to spread the load instead of adding a [load-balancing](#c/c-load-balancing) loss that can hurt quality; the config’s `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` names it.

**Multi-token prediction** trains the model to predict several future tokens in a causal chain, giving a stronger training signal; the extra heads double as a [speculative-decoding](#c/c-speculative-decoding) accelerator.

**FP8**: DeepSeek trains natively in FP8 and ships only FP8 weights, with a script to convert to BF16 ([quantization](#c/c-quantization)).

## How open is it?

More than most. The weights are on Hugging Face, the inference code is in DeepSeek’s GitHub repository, the architecture has a native implementation in Hugging Face `transformers`, and DeepSeek released pieces of its training infrastructure, such as the DualPipe pipeline-parallelism algorithm and an expert-parallel load balancer. What it did not release is a turnkey script to reproduce the model from scratch, and above all the training data, which essentially no major lab publishes.

## What came next?

The line ran V3 → V3.1 → V3.1-Terminus → V3.2-Exp → V3.2. The backbone of MoE plus MLA barely changed over about a year; the one architectural addition was DeepSeek Sparse Attention, and the capability gains came from scaled-up reinforcement-learning post-training ([DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32)).

concepts.title: Training compute
concepts.summary: Compute used to train frontier language models: growing about 5× a year since 2020, per Epoch AI.
concepts.overview: Training compute is the total arithmetic spent training a model, and in the chat it is the kind of scale that really drives capability. [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai) finds training compute for frontier language models has grown about 5× a year since 2020, doubling roughly every 5.2 months. About two-thirds of language-model gains over the last decade came from scale in this sense ([scale drove two-thirds of gains](#c/c-scale-two-thirds)), not from parameter count. The two have come apart: you can pour 5× more compute into a model each year without making it 5× bigger, by training a modest-sized model on far more data and for longer, following [Chinchilla scaling](#c/c-chinchilla). That is one pillar of [parameters decoupling from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled).

concepts.title: Pre-training efficiency
concepts.summary: Pre-training compute efficiency improves about 3× a year, giving more capability per parameter.
concepts.overview: Pre-training efficiency measures how much less compute it takes, year over year, to reach the same capability in pre-training, thanks to better algorithms, architectures and data. [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai) estimates it improves roughly 3× a year. In the chat it is one of the three things capability now rides on, alongside [training compute](#c/c-training-compute) and [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute), once [parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled): algorithmic progress gets more capability per parameter each year. It has a counterpart on the serving side, where about 3× a year of the inference price decline is attributed to [algorithmic efficiency](m-algorithmic-efficiency-inference) alone.

concepts.title: Scale drove two-thirds of gains
concepts.summary: About two-thirds of language-model gains over the last decade came from scale, meaning training compute.
concepts.overview: [Epoch AI](#c/c-epoch-ai) estimates that about two-thirds of the improvements in language-model performance over the last decade came from increases in model scale. The chat stresses what “scale” means here: [training compute](#c/c-training-compute), not parameter count. Before about 2023 the two moved together, so the distinction hardly mattered; since then they have come apart, with training compute still rising about 5× a year while parameter counts stalled or fell ([parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled)). The remaining third comes from algorithmic and data improvements, and the newest capability axis, [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute), sits outside this historical accounting.

concepts.title: Test-time compute
concepts.summary: Capability gained by letting a model think longer at inference, independent of its size.
concepts.overview: Test-time compute is capability that comes from spending more computation when the model answers, by letting it reason in a long chain of thought before responding, rather than from being bigger or better trained. The chat calls it an axis entirely independent of parameter count, and one reason [parameters decoupled from capability](#c/c-params-decoupled). It has two sides. It is the current capability frontier: the big quality gains of 2025, such as DeepSeek-V3.2’s, came from reinforcement-learning post-training that teaches models to use thinking time productively. And it is expensive: reasoning and agents raised compute per session enormously ([agents multiply per-query compute](#c/c-agents-multiply-compute)), which is why the frontier stays pricey. The chat also treats it as the latest breakthrough that keeps the cost curve from flattening ([increments drive declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines)).
concepts.article:
## What is it?

Test-time compute is computation spent at inference, at “test time,” rather than during training. In practice it means reasoning models that “think” longer, producing an extended chain of reasoning before their final answer. A growing share of capability now comes from this rather than from the model being bigger. The chat calls it a capability axis completely orthogonal to parameter count.

## How does a model learn to use it?

Mostly through reinforcement learning after pre-training. Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which scores answers in domains like math and code by whether they are actually correct, encourages long chains of thought, and behaviours like self-reflection emerge on their own. The chat describes this as the mechanism behind the test-time-compute paradigm: RL teaches the model to use its thinking time productively. DeepSeek-V3.2’s jump to GPT-5-comparable results came from exactly this kind of scaled-up post-training, not from architecture ([DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32)).

## Why does it make the frontier expensive?

Because it trades compute per request for capability. Nvidia’s framing is that compute per inference session rose about 10,000× as models moved from chatbots to reasoning and agents ([agents multiply per-query compute](#c/c-agents-multiply-compute)). That is why falling cost per token doesn’t translate into cheaper frontier use: the frontier consumes more tokens per query each year ([frontier pricey, commodity cheap](#c/c-frontier-stays-pricey)).

## Is it a breakthrough or a tweak?

The chat names it as the current breakthrough. Its view is that sustained cost declines come mostly from incremental work, with occasional paradigm shifts such as MoE, the Transformer and now test-time compute resetting the ceiling so the incremental curve doesn’t flatten ([increments drive declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines)). It also notes the caveat: if reasoning scaling dominates the next phase, that is more paradigm shift than tweak, and past patterns are a weak guide.

concepts.title: How does MoE pick experts?
concepts.summary: A small learned router scores every expert for each token and the top few run, fresh at every layer.
concepts.overview: The reader asked how MoE knows which parameters to activate and whether it keeps switching. It doesn’t “know” in any semantic sense. A tiny learned [router](#c/c-router), essentially one linear layer, scores every [expert](#c/c-experts) for the current token by a dot product with each expert’s learned routing vector; a softmax turns scores into weights; the top-k experts (usually 1 or 2 in classic designs) process the token; and their outputs are blended by those weights. And yes, it switches constantly: the decision is made fresh for every token at every MoE layer, so a 60-layer model makes 60 routing decisions per token, and neighbouring words can go to entirely different experts. Keeping the router from collapsing onto a few favourites needs [load balancing](#c/c-load-balancing).

concepts.title: Feed-forward network
concepts.summary: The per-token half of a transformer layer, with no cross-token mixing; the part MoE splits into experts.
concepts.overview: Each transformer [layer](#c/c-layers) has two halves. [Attention](#c/c-attention) is where tokens exchange information; the feed-forward network (FFN, or MLP block) then processes each token’s vector on its own, with no cross-token interaction. It expands the vector to a wider intermediate size, applies a nonlinearity, and projects back down. Much of a model’s “stored knowledge” computation is thought to happen here, and it holds a large share of the parameters. It is the part [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) replaces: MoE splits the FFN into many parallel [experts](#c/c-experts) and routes each token to a few, leaving attention untouched. In DeepSeek-V3, dense layers use an 18432-wide FFN while each expert uses a slim 2048.
concepts.article:
## What does it do?

Inside each transformer block, attention comes first and mixes information across tokens; then the feed-forward network processes each token’s vector independently. It is the only other main component of the layer, and it is where a lot of the “stored knowledge” computation happens. Like attention, it is wrapped in a residual connection and normalization, so its output is added to the running representation as an adjustment rather than replacing it ([residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream)).

## What is its shape?

An FFN expands, then contracts. It projects the token vector up to a larger intermediate width, applies a nonlinearity, and projects back down to the hidden size. In a dense transformer the intermediate width is usually several times the hidden size; the chat gives 4× as a typical ratio. DeepSeek-V3’s three dense layers use an intermediate size of 18432, about 2.6× its 7168 hidden size.

## How does MoE change it?

[Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) replaces the FFN, and only the FFN, with many parallel copies, the [experts](#c/c-experts), and a [router](#c/c-router) that sends each token to a few of them. Attention stays dense and shared. MoE experts are often deliberately small: each of DeepSeek-V3’s 256 experts has an intermediate width of just 2048, narrower than the hidden size, so a token goes 7168 → 2048 → 7168 through each of its 8 chosen experts. Since only the chosen experts run, total parameters can grow while per-token compute stays fixed.

## Why split the design space this way?

The chat frames modern model design around two bottlenecks, one per half of the layer. On the FFN side the fight is over capacity per active parameter, won so far by MoE, with open models split on expert size and shared experts. On the attention side it is over KV-cache memory. The two optimizations compound: DeepSeek-V3.2’s sparse attention speeds up the attention half while MoE handles the FFN half.

concepts.title: Experts
concepts.summary: In MoE, one of many parallel feed-forward weight blocks; experts rarely specialize in human topics.
concepts.overview: An expert is one of the N parallel [feed-forward](#c/c-ffn) weight blocks in a [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) layer: 8 in early designs, 256 in DeepSeek-V3, 384 in Kimi K2. Attention stays dense; only the FFN is split. All experts sit in HBM, but for any token only the few picked by the [router](#c/c-router) do any work. The name misleads. Experts are not specialists in French or chemistry: when researchers inspect trained models, experts mostly specialize in low-level syntactic or positional patterns, such as punctuation or number-like tokens, not topics a human would recognise. Designs vary in how many and how large they are (many small in DeepSeek, few large in Llama 4) and whether some are [shared](#c/c-shared-experts) by every token.
concepts.article:
## What is an expert, physically?

Just one of N parallel feed-forward weight blocks. When a model is said to have “8 experts” or “256 experts,” its FFN block has been split into that many sub-networks, each with its own weights; the attention machinery is untouched. For each token, the [router](#c/c-router) picks a few experts, and only those do arithmetic. All the experts still have to be stored in HBM, even though most sit idle for any given token.

## What do experts specialize in?

Not what the name suggests. The appealing picture of a “chemistry expert” activated for a chemistry question is mostly false. When researchers inspect trained routers, experts tend to specialize in low-level, often syntactic or positional patterns: certain token types, punctuation, number-like tokens, particular structural roles. Some specialization is real, but it is alien to how a human would carve up knowledge. The chat’s summary: routing distributes computational sub-patterns rather than dispatching to topic specialists. That also fits the per-token routing: adjacent words in one sentence can go to entirely different experts.

## How big and how many?

Designs split here. DeepSeek-V3 uses many small, fine-grained experts: 256 routed experts, each with an intermediate width of only 2048, with 8 chosen per token. [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) uses fewer, larger experts, with 2 active at a width of 8,192. Many small experts give the router finer-grained choices. [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) goes to 384 experts.

## What keeps them all useful?

Without intervention, training collapses onto a few favourite experts and leaves the rest dead. [Load balancing](#c/c-load-balancing), through an auxiliary loss, capacity caps or DeepSeek’s bias-adjustment method, keeps tokens spread across experts. [Shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts), which every token uses, take on general-purpose processing so routed experts don’t each relearn the basics.

concepts.title: Router
concepts.summary: A tiny learned layer that scores every expert for each token and sends it to the top few.
concepts.overview: The router, or gate, is the small network in front of a [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) layer that decides which [experts](#c/c-experts) process each token. It is essentially one learned linear layer: it takes the token’s vector and produces a score for every expert, a dot product between the token and each expert’s learned routing vector. A softmax turns the scores into weights, the top-k experts run, and their outputs are combined by those weights. There is no semantic “knowing” involved. The decision is remade for every token at every MoE layer, so a 60-layer model routes each token 60 times. Left alone, routing collapses onto a few favourite experts, which is why [load balancing](#c/c-load-balancing) shapes how routers are trained.
concepts.article:
## How does it score experts?

For each incoming token vector, the router produces a list of numbers, one per expert, saying how well each expert matches this token right now. Each score is a dot product between the token’s representation and that expert’s learned routing vector. A softmax turns the scores into weights; the top-k highest-scoring experts get the token; and their outputs are combined, weighted by the router’s scores. In classic designs k is 1 or 2; DeepSeek-V3 picks 8 of 256.

## How often does it decide?

Constantly. Routing happens fresh for every token, independently, at every MoE layer. A 60-layer model makes 60 routing decisions for one token as it flows up the stack, and the next token gets its own 60, probably landing on different experts. It is not “this prompt is about cooking, load the cooking experts”: the active set churns token by token and layer by layer.

## What can go wrong?

Collapse. If the router picks freely, a few experts get picked slightly more early on, train more, get better, and get picked even more, until a couple of experts do all the work. Classic MoE training adds an auxiliary [load-balancing](#c/c-load-balancing) loss and an expert-capacity cap to prevent this. DeepSeek-V3 instead nudges per-expert bias terms to balance load while keeping the actual choice based on token-expert affinity; its config uses a sigmoid scoring function and a method named `noaux_tc`, for “no auxiliary loss.”

## What do closed models do?

Unknown in detail. The token-choice top-k routing described here is the standard picture for the open architectures that publish details, such as Mixtral and DeepSeek. Closed frontier models are broadly understood to be MoE, but their routing schemes are not disclosed.

concepts.title: Load balancing
concepts.summary: Techniques that keep MoE routing spread across experts so training doesn’t collapse onto a few.
concepts.overview: Left to itself, a [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) [router](#c/c-router) collapses: a few experts get picked slightly more early on, train more, get better and get picked even more, leaving most experts dead and most parameters wasted. Load balancing prevents that. Classic MoE adds an auxiliary loss that penalizes lopsided routing, plus an expert-capacity cap: a ceiling on tokens per expert per batch, with overflow tokens dropped (passed through without FFN processing) or rerouted. The tension is to balance enough to use all the experts without destroying the useful specialization the router is learning. DeepSeek-V3 goes auxiliary-loss-free, adjusting per-expert bias terms instead, to avoid the quality cost of the extra loss. The chat counts load balancing among the incremental fixes that turned MoE from an idea into a working architecture ([increments drive declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines)).

concepts.title: Shared experts
concepts.summary: A few always-on MoE experts every token uses, so routed experts need not relearn the basics.
concepts.overview: Shared experts are one or more [experts](#c/c-experts) that every token passes through, alongside the few chosen by the router. They capture common, general-purpose processing, so the routed experts can focus on the variable, specialized part instead of each redundantly relearning the basics. DeepSeek popularized the idea; [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 1 shared expert on top of 8 routed ones, which is where the “9 active experts” figure comes from. [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) and GLM-4.5 kept it, but [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) dropped it, making Qwen3 a live test of whether it is needed. The chat calls it one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design.

concepts.title: Mixtral
concepts.summary: Mistral’s open MoE model family, which helped make sparse MoE the dominant open architecture from 2024.
concepts.overview: Mixtral is the open-weight [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) family from the French lab Mistral. In the chat it marks a turning point in MoE’s history: the technique, invented decades earlier and developed at Google, became the dominant open architecture from 2024, with Mixtral and DeepSeek-V3 running at high sparsity, activating only a few experts per token out of a large pool. That spread overlaps the window of Epoch’s price data, which is why the reader asked whether MoE drove the cost drop ([did MoE drive the cost drop?](#c/c-q-moe-cost-drop)). The chat also cites Mixtral as one of the open architectures whose published details match the standard top-k routing picture.

concepts.title: Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts
concepts.summary: The 1991 paper by Jacobs, Hinton, Jordan and Nowlan that introduced the mixture-of-experts idea.
concepts.overview: “Adaptive Mixtures of Local Experts,” published in 1991 by Robert Jacobs, Geoffrey Hinton, Michael Jordan and Steven Nowlan, is where the [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) idea begins: several expert networks, with a gating network learning which expert should handle each input. The chat uses it to correct the impression that MoE is a recent breakthrough. The core idea is more than three decades old, and the version that matters for LLMs came much later with the [sparsely-gated MoE layer](#c/c-sparse-gated-moe) of 2017. That long gap is central to the chat’s argument that ideas reset the ceiling while years of incremental engineering deliver the value ([increments drive declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines)).

concepts.title: Sparsely-gated MoE layer
concepts.summary: Shazeer et al.’s 2017 Google paper that made sparse, gated MoE work inside deep networks, up to 137B parameters.
concepts.overview: In 2017, Noam Shazeer and colleagues at Google published “Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer.” It is the version of [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) that matters for modern LLMs: a sparse, gated MoE layer dropped into a deep network, activating only a subset of experts per input, which allowed models of up to 137 billion parameters. It appeared the same year as the [Transformer](#c/c-transformer) itself. It built on the [1991 idea](#c/c-moe-1991) and led to [GShard](#c/c-gshard), which put MoE into the Transformer. The chat’s point about its date: it predates Epoch’s inference price data by years, so the cost curve can’t show MoE’s arrival.

concepts.title: GShard
concepts.summary: Google’s 2020 work that put mixture of experts into the Transformer, scaling past 600B parameters.
concepts.overview: GShard, from Google in 2020, is the step where [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) was folded into the [Transformer](#c/c-transformer) specifically, scaling past 600 billion parameters. It sits in the chain from the [sparsely-gated MoE layer](#c/c-sparse-gated-moe) of 2017 to the [Switch Transformer](#c/c-switch-transformer) of 2021, which simplified routing further. Like the other milestones, it came well before Epoch’s price data begins around April 2024, so it can’t be matched to a step in the cost curve.

concepts.title: Switch Transformer
concepts.summary: A 2021 MoE design that routed each token to a single expert, pushing toward trillion-parameter models.
concepts.overview: Switch Transformer, from 2021, simplified [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) routing to a single expert per token (top-1), which pushed toward trillion-parameter models. It followed [GShard](#c/c-gshard) and is part of the lineage that led to the open MoE models of 2024–2025, such as [Mixtral](#c/c-mixtral) and [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3). The chat lists the top-1 simplification among the incremental fixes, alongside load balancing, capacity limits and shared experts, that turned MoE from a clever idea into the architecture behind most frontier models, and names Switch Transformer as the first in a decade of routing improvements such as Hash routing and StableMoE.

concepts.title: Did MoE drive the cost drop?
concepts.summary: Not provably: MoE predates Epoch’s price data, and it is one of many ingredients in the algorithmic slice.
concepts.overview: The reader asked when MoE appeared and whether it lined up with a drop in Epoch’s cost curve. The history answers the first part: the idea dates to [1991](#c/c-moe-1991), the deep-network version to [2017](#c/c-sparse-gated-moe), and Transformer versions to 2020–2021. Epoch’s inference price data only starts around April 2024, so it can’t show MoE’s arrival. What the window does capture is MoE spreading to become the dominant open architecture, with [Mixtral](#c/c-mixtral) and DeepSeek-V3. Even so, the chat won’t call MoE the cause: the decline combines hardware, competition and about 3× a year of [algorithmic efficiency](m-algorithmic-efficiency-inference), and MoE is only one ingredient of that slice, alongside data, distillation, quantization and attention work. The larger lesson is that [incremental work drives the declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines).

concepts.title: Increments drive cost declines
concepts.summary: Steady cost declines come mostly from many small improvements, with occasional breakthroughs resetting the ceiling.
concepts.overview: The reader asked whether future price cuts will come from breakthroughs like MoE or from incremental tweaking. The chat’s answer, which it labels its own interpretation rather than Epoch’s claim, is that the framing is a false binary. [Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) was both: the idea landed in 1991 and 2017, but its value came from a long tail of fixes such as [load balancing](#c/c-load-balancing), capacity limits, top-1 routing and [shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts). Breakthroughs reset the ceiling; years of engineering then grind cost toward it. The evidence is the shape of the curve: the ~3×-a-year [algorithmic efficiency](m-algorithmic-efficiency-inference) decline is smooth, not a staircase. Breakthroughs, now [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute), keep the curve from flattening. Whether that holds going forward is uncertain.

concepts.title: Transformer
concepts.summary: The 2017 architecture behind every current frontier LLM: stacked layers of attention and feed-forward blocks.
concepts.overview: The Transformer, introduced in 2017, is the architecture every current frontier LLM is built on, in its decoder-only form. It is a stack of [layers](#c/c-layers), each an [attention](#c/c-attention) step, where tokens exchange information, followed by a [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) that processes each token alone, both added back onto a running [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream). A token starts as an embedding, is refined layer by layer, and only the final layer’s output becomes a prediction ([one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction)). The original had 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers; modern open models run 30 to 80 or more. Most of the techniques in this Expedition, from [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) to KV-cache compression, are modifications of one half of this block.
concepts.article:
## What is it made of?

A decoder-only transformer turns each token into an embedding vector, passes it up through a stack of [layers](#c/c-layers), and at the top turns the final vector into a probability distribution over the next token via one last projection, the “unembedding.” Each layer, or transformer block, has two sub-parts in sequence:

- **[Attention](#c/c-attention)**: the multi-head query/key/value lookup, the only place tokens exchange information.
- **[Feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn)**: processes each token’s vector on its own; where much “stored knowledge” computation happens.

Both are wrapped in residual connections and normalization, so each layer adds an adjustment to a running representation, the [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream), rather than replacing it.

## How does information flow?

Sequentially. Layer 1 turns raw embeddings into slightly context-aware vectors; layer 2 makes them more context-aware; and so on up the stack. Every layer has its own separately learned attention heads and FFN, so depth is a stack of different transformations, not one repeated. Early layers tend to capture local, surface patterns; later ones more abstract, longer-range structure. Only the final layer’s output is read off as a prediction ([one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction)). Each layer also keeps its own [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) during generation.

## How big are they?

The original 2017 Transformer used 6 layers in its encoder and 6 in its decoder. GPT-2 and BERT ran about 12 to 48. Modern open models land around 30 to 80 or more: about 30 for the 7–8B class, 60 to 100+ for larger ones. Models grow both wider and deeper, with width often scaling faster; depth has diminishing returns and is traded against width and, in MoE models, expert count ([how many layers?](#c/c-q-layer-count)). Closed models don’t disclose their shapes, but the structure holds across them.

## What has changed since 2017?

Mostly the parts, not the plan. On the FFN side, [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) splits the block into many experts. On the attention side, [grouped-query](#c/c-gqa) and [latent attention](#c/c-mla) shrink the KV cache, and sparse and linear attention cut its cost on long contexts. The chat notes the Transformer shares its birth year with the sparsely-gated MoE layer, and counts both among the breakthroughs that reset the ceiling for years of incremental work ([increments drive declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines)).

concepts.title: PagedAttention
concepts.summary: vLLM’s idea of storing the KV cache in fixed-size pages, like OS virtual memory, to eliminate wasted memory.
concepts.overview: PagedAttention, the core idea of the vLLM serving system, attacks waste in the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) rather than its raw size. Traditionally each request reserved one large contiguous block of memory sized for the longest possible output; most requests never filled it, so much memory sat reserved but empty. PagedAttention borrows the operating system’s virtual-memory trick: split the cache into fixed-size pages that can live anywhere, tracked by a lookup table. That nearly eliminates the waste, fits many more concurrent requests per GPU, and so lowers cost per token. It also makes sharing cheap: requests with the same prefix can point to the same pages, which helps [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching). It works on frozen weights, so it is a pure [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization).

concepts.title: Grouped-query attention
concepts.summary: Groups of query heads share one key/value head, shrinking the KV cache with little quality loss.
concepts.overview: Grouped-query attention (GQA) shrinks the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) at its source. In standard multi-head attention every query head has its own key and value head, so the cache stores K and V for all of them. GQA keeps all the query heads but splits them into groups, each sharing one K/V head: 32 query heads in 8 groups means 8 K/V sets instead of 32, a 4× smaller cache. It is the compromise between full multi-head attention and [multi-query attention](#c/c-mqa), which shares a single K/V head and loses more quality. The trick works because [K/V heads set the cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob) while query heads aren’t cached. GQA is now near-universal, used by [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) and [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3), but must be trained in.
concepts.article:
## What problem does it solve?

The [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) is the biggest memory cost of inference. In standard multi-head attention there are N query heads, N key heads and N value heads in matched sets, and the cache stores K and V for all N, at every layer, for every past token. Queries aren’t cached, since each is used once and discarded; only keys and values stick around for future tokens. So the cache size is set by the number of K/V heads ([K/V heads set cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob)).

## How does it work?

Keep all N query heads but split them into a handful of groups, and let each group share one key head and one value head. With 32 query heads in 8 groups of 4, you store 8 K/V sets instead of 32, a 4× cache reduction. Every query still asks its own question, but queries in a group look up against the same keys and values.

The extreme version is [multi-query attention](#c/c-mqa): all N query heads share a single K/V head, cutting the cache by roughly N× but denting quality. GQA sits in the middle, giving the queries more variety to look up against than MQA while keeping most of its memory savings.

## Why did it win?

Because it shrinks the KV cache substantially with minimal quality loss, it has become near-universal in modern models. Among the open models discussed, [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) and [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) use it as the safe default. In a Llama 4 config you would see `num_key_value_heads` much smaller than `num_attention_heads`. The chat also calls it an example of a small architectural “tweak” that mostly serves inference efficiency.

## How does it compare with MLA?

[Multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla), used by DeepSeek and Kimi K2, compresses keys and values into a small shared latent rather than sharing heads. It saves more cache memory than GQA but pays a compute cost to compress and decompress. The chat summarizes the attention side of open-model design as GQA (simple, default) versus MLA (more compression, more complexity), with sparse and linear attention emerging.

## Can it be added to an existing model?

Not as a serving trick. Unlike FlashAttention or PagedAttention, GQA changes the model’s structure, so the model must be trained that way ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)). It explains why newer models are cheaper to serve, not why a deployed model gets cheaper over its life. Like the other attention-efficiency techniques, the chat classes it as quality-neutral by design: it cuts cost rather than making the model smarter.

concepts.title: Multi-query attention
concepts.summary: All query heads share a single key/value head, cutting the KV cache by about the number of heads.
concepts.overview: Multi-query attention (MQA) is the extreme way to shrink the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache). It keeps all N query heads, so every head still asks its own question, but collapses keys and values to a single shared head. Since only keys and values are cached ([K/V heads set cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob)), the cache shrinks by roughly N×. The cost is expressiveness: forcing every query to look up against one shared set of keys and values can hurt quality. That trade-off is why [grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa), which shares one K/V head per group of queries, won out as the compromise. Like GQA, MQA must be trained in; it can’t be applied to an existing model at serving time.

concepts.title: Multi-head latent attention
concepts.summary: DeepSeek’s attention that caches a small compressed latent instead of full keys and values.
concepts.overview: Multi-head latent attention (MLA) is DeepSeek’s more aggressive way to shrink the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache). Instead of sharing K/V heads as [grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa) does, it projects keys and values into a shared low-rank latent vector, caches only that, and reconstructs head-specific keys and values on the fly with light projections. In [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) the latent is 512-dimensional against 16,384 for full K/V, about 32× smaller. It saves more memory than GQA while trying to keep more of multi-head attention’s expressiveness, at the price of compress-and-expand compute. Position needs special handling: RoPE doesn’t survive the compression, so a small “decoupled RoPE” slice carries it separately. [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) adopted MLA; it must be trained in.
concepts.article:
## How does it work?

Standard attention caches a full key and value vector for every head, at every layer, for every past token. MLA instead projects keys and values into a shared low-rank latent space and caches only the compact latent. When attention runs, lightweight projections expand the latent back into the head-specific keys and values each head needs. Where [GQA](#c/c-gqa) saves memory by having fewer K/V heads, MLA keeps every head but compresses what is stored.

## How much does it save?

DeepSeek-V3’s config shows it in one number. `kv_lora_rank: 512` is the latent the keys and values are squeezed into for the cache. Uncompressed, 128 heads × 128 dimensions per head would be 16,384. So the cached latent is about 32× smaller than naive full K/V. Queries get their own low-rank compression too (`q_lora_rank: 1536`), though queries aren’t cached.

The config also lists `num_key_value_heads: 128`, equal to the query heads, which looks like plain multi-head attention; that is because MLA’s compression lives in other fields rather than in fewer K/V heads.

## What is decoupled RoPE?

RoPE encodes position by rotating query and key vectors, and that rotation doesn’t play well with the low-rank compression. MLA’s fix is to carry position separately. Each head’s query-key dimension is split into a 128-dimensional content part (`qk_nope_head_dim`) and a 64-dimensional positional part (`qk_rope_head_dim`). Position rides in its own slice so it survives the compression cleanly.

## What does it cost?

Compute and complexity. Compressing and expanding keys and values adds work at every attention step, which is why the chat calls it “more compression, more complexity” against GQA’s “simple, default.” It is also newer and less universally adopted than GQA, so the chat held it a little more loosely. Like GQA it must be baked in during training rather than applied to a finished model ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)), and it is an efficiency technique meant to preserve quality, not add it.

## Who uses it?

DeepSeek’s V3 line, where V3.2 added sparse attention on top of it, and [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2), which borrowed it from DeepSeek. [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) uses MLA in its few full-attention layers. [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) and [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) stayed with GQA.

concepts.title: KV-cache quantization
concepts.summary: Storing cached keys and values at 8 bits or fewer instead of 16, halving cache memory or more.
concepts.overview: The [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) doesn’t have to be stored at full precision. KV-cache quantization stores keys and values in 8-bit or lower formats instead of 16-bit, halving the cache or better, so a server can fit longer contexts or more concurrent requests. As with weight [quantization](#c/c-quantization), there is a trade-off between quality and size, and keys tend to be more sensitive than values, so some schemes quantize them differently. It works on a frozen model, making it one of the [serving optimizations](#c/c-serving-optimization) that let a deployed model get cheaper without retraining ([serving tricks vs baked-in](#c/c-serving-vs-training)).

concepts.title: Prefix caching
concepts.summary: Computing the KV cache for a shared prompt prefix once and reusing it; the basis of prompt-caching discounts.
concepts.overview: Many requests start the same way: a long system prompt, a shared document, a few-shot preamble. Prefix caching computes the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) for that shared prefix once and reuses it across requests instead of recomputing it every time. It is the serving-side mechanism behind the prompt-caching discounts on APIs, such as the 90%-off cached-input pricing that came up in the first Fable search. [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention) makes it cheap to implement, since requests can point at the same physical cache pages. Like the other cache techniques that work on frozen weights, it is a [serving optimization](#c/c-serving-optimization) that can lower cost for an existing model.

concepts.title: Serving tricks vs baked-in
concepts.summary: Some efficiency tricks work on frozen weights; others, like GQA and MLA, must be trained in.
concepts.overview: The chat splits the attention and cache optimizations into two groups, and the split answers the reader’s earlier question about whether a given model gets cheaper. [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention), [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention), [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization) and [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching) work on frozen weights: they can be applied to a model already deployed, so they explain how it gets cheaper over its life ([does a given model get cheaper?](#c/c-q-sonnet-cheaper)). [Grouped-query](#c/c-gqa), [multi-query](#c/c-mqa) and [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla) change the architecture and must be baked in at training time, so they make new models cheaper, not old ones. In practice the two groups stack: a modern serving stack runs a GQA model with FlashAttention kernels, PagedAttention memory management, prefix caching, often KV quantization, and continuous batching.

concepts.title: Attention
concepts.summary: The step where tokens exchange information: each token’s query is matched against others’ keys to blend their values.
concepts.overview: Attention is the only step in a transformer [layer](#c/c-layers) where tokens exchange information; the [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) then works on each token alone. Each token produces a [query, key and value](#c/c-qkv); its query is compared with every other token’s key, the match scores become weights via a softmax, and the token takes in a weighted blend of their values. Many [heads](#c/c-heads) run in parallel, each learning a different relationship. Attention is also where inference gets expensive: the past keys and values are stored in the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache), and moving it and the score matrix around is why [inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound). Much of the Expedition’s optimization story, from [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention) to [GQA](#c/c-gqa) and [MLA](#c/c-mla), is about making attention cheaper.
concepts.article:
## What does attention do?

Each token produces three vectors: a query, a key and a value. The token uses its query to look up relevant information from every other token’s key, then pulls in those tokens’ values, weighted by how well query and key matched. Concretely, the query is compared with all keys by dot product, a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the result is a weighted blend of the values. The chat’s analogy is a soft database lookup: query = what I’m looking for, key = what I advertise, value = what I hand over ([query, key, value](#c/c-qkv)).

## Where does it sit in the model?

Every transformer block has two sub-parts: attention first, then the [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn). Attention is the only place tokens exchange information, where context mixing happens; the FFN processes each token independently. [Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) replaces the FFN but leaves attention dense and shared. Each [layer](#c/c-layers) has its own independently learned attention [heads](#c/c-heads).

Attention on its own is order-blind: it treats the input as a bag of tokens, so position has to be added, which modern models do by rotating queries and keys (RoPE).

## Why is it expensive?

Two reasons. Every new token must attend to all earlier tokens, so their keys and values are stored in the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache), which grows with context length and batch size and becomes the biggest memory cost of inference. And a naive implementation builds a full score matrix and shuttles it to and from slow HBM several times, so attention is limited by data movement, not arithmetic ([inference is memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound)). Its cost also grows with the square of sequence length, which is what makes long contexts costly.

## How is it being made cheaper?

Along several lines:

- **Better kernels**: [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention) computes attention in fast on-chip memory without writing the score matrix out.
- **Fewer or compressed K/V**: [GQA](#c/c-gqa), [MQA](#c/c-mqa) and [MLA](#c/c-mla) shrink the cache at the source.
- **Smarter cache management**: [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention), [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization) and [prefix caching](#c/c-prefix-caching).
- **Attending to fewer tokens**: DeepSeek-V3.2’s sparse attention selects a small subset of earlier tokens, cutting cost from quadratic to roughly linear in sequence length.
- **Replacing most of it**: hybrid models like [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) keep full attention in one layer in four and use cheaper linear attention elsewhere.

The chat stresses that these are efficiency plays, designed to keep quality the same while cutting cost.

concepts.title: Query, key, value
concepts.summary: The three vectors each token makes for attention: query (what I seek), key (what I offer), value (what I give).
concepts.overview: In [attention](#c/c-attention), each token produces three vectors from its current representation, via learned projections. The **query** is what the token is looking for (“I’m a verb, looking for my subject”). The **key** advertises what it offers (“I’m a noun, I could be a subject”). The **value** is the content it hands over if matched. Each token’s query is compared with every other token’s key by dot product, a softmax turns the scores into weights, and the token receives a weighted blend of values: a soft database lookup. A [head](#c/c-heads) is one complete set of these projections. Only keys and values are stored for later tokens, which is why the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) is named after them and why [K/V heads set its size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob).
concepts.article:
## What are the three vectors?

Each token’s representation is turned, by three learned projections, into:

- a **query (Q)**: what this token is looking for;
- a **key (K)**: what this token advertises about itself;
- a **value (V)**: the content this token contributes if another token attends to it.

The chat’s example: a verb’s query says “I’m looking for my subject”; a noun’s key says “I could be a subject”; the noun’s value is what the verb takes in once they match.

## How do they combine?

Like a soft database lookup. The current token’s query is compared against every other token’s key with a dot product, giving a match score for each. A softmax turns the scores into weights that sum to one. The output is the weighted blend of the values. Unlike a real database, nothing is looked up exactly: every value contributes a little, in proportion to how well its key matched.

## Why are only keys and values cached?

Because of how generation works. The current token’s query is used once, right now, and then discarded; no future step needs it. But past keys and values must stay available so future tokens can attend to them. So the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) stores keys and values only, and its size depends on the number of K/V heads rather than query heads. That asymmetry is what [GQA](#c/c-gqa) and [MQA](#c/c-mqa) exploit ([K/V heads set cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob)).

## How does position get in?

Q and K on their own carry no sense of order. RoPE, the method nearly every current model uses, rotates each query and key by an angle that depends on the token’s position, so their dot product ends up depending on how far apart the two tokens are. That is why position handling touches the Q and K vectors specifically, and why MLA needs a separate positional slice when it compresses keys.

concepts.title: Heads (Q · K · V)
concepts.summary: One head is a complete query-key-value lookup with its own projections; layers run dozens in parallel.
concepts.overview: A head is one complete instance of the [query-key-value](#c/c-qkv) lookup, with its own learned projections that turn each token into its particular Q, K and V. One head can learn only one kind of relationship, so transformers run many in parallel in every layer: multi-head attention. Each might track something different, such as subject-verb agreement, pronoun reference or nearby punctuation, though real heads are messier than those tidy labels. Their outputs are concatenated and combined. “Query heads” are just the Q parts of these heads. In standard attention, query and K/V heads come in matched sets; the trick behind [GQA](#c/c-gqa) and [MQA](#c/c-mqa) is to keep many query heads while cutting K/V heads, because [K/V heads set cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob). Every [layer](#c/c-layers) has its own separate heads.
concepts.article:
## What is a head?

One complete query-key-value lookup. A head has its own learned projections that turn each token’s representation into its own Q, K and V, then runs the match-and-blend of [attention](#c/c-attention) with them. The phrase “query heads” refers to the query component of each head, its Q projection.

## Why have many?

Because one head can only learn one kind of relationship to look for. Multi-head attention runs many heads in parallel in every layer, each with independent projections, so each learns to attend to a different pattern. Loosely, one might track subject-verb agreement, another which pronoun refers to which noun, another nearby punctuation or positional structure. Those descriptions are illustrative; real heads are often messier and less interpretable, but the principle that heads specialize in different relationships is sound. Their outputs are concatenated and combined, giving the layer many views of token relationships at once. DeepSeek-V3 has 128 heads per layer.

## Do layers share heads?

No. Every [layer](#c/c-layers) has its own completely separate, independently learned set of heads, with their own Q, K and V weights. Layer 1’s heads and layer 7’s share nothing. That is part of why depth adds capability: layer 3’s heads might link low-level syntax while layer 20’s track discourse-level relationships. It also means each layer keeps its own KV cache.

## Why do query and K/V heads differ in cost?

In standard multi-head attention there are as many query heads as key and value heads, in matched sets. But only keys and values are cached, so the number of K/V heads sets the memory cost, while the number of query heads is mostly a compute and expressiveness knob. [MQA](#c/c-mqa) keeps all query heads and collapses to one K/V head; [GQA](#c/c-gqa) shares one K/V head per group of query heads. You can have many query heads (cheap, not cached) and deliberately few K/V heads (expensive, cached) ([K/V heads set cache size](#c/c-kv-heads-memory-knob)). Exact head counts in closed models aren’t disclosed.

concepts.title: K/V heads set cache size
concepts.summary: Only keys and values are cached, so the number of K/V heads, not query heads, sets cache size.
concepts.overview: This is the insight that makes [GQA](#c/c-gqa) and [MQA](#c/c-mqa) click. During generation, the current token’s query is used once and thrown away, but past keys and values must be kept so future tokens can attend to them. So the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) grows with the number of key/value heads, not query heads. That separates two knobs that standard multi-head attention ties together. Query heads are the expressiveness knob: many different questions, cheap because they aren’t cached. K/V heads are the memory knob: expensive because they are. GQA and MQA turn the memory knob down while leaving the query heads alone.

concepts.title: Layers
concepts.summary: Transformer blocks stacked in sequence, each refining every token’s vector and passing it up.
concepts.overview: A transformer is a stack of layers, or blocks, applied in sequence. Each layer takes every token’s vector, runs [attention](#c/c-attention) (where tokens exchange information) and then a [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn), adds the result back to the [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream), and hands a more context-aware vector to the next layer. Every layer has its own independently learned [heads](#c/c-heads), FFN and [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache). Early layers tend to catch local, surface patterns and later ones more abstract structure. Layers don’t each predict a token; there is [one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction). Modern open models use about 30 to 80 or more layers ([how many?](#c/c-q-layer-count)), though [many layers do little](#c/c-layer-redundancy) and some research [shares weights across layers](#c/c-parameter-sharing).
concepts.article:
## How do layers work together?

As a pipeline, not a committee. A token starts as an embedding vector. Layer 1 transforms it into a slightly context-aware vector of the same size; layer 2 transforms that further; and so on up the stack. Only after the last layer does the vector go through a final projection into next-token probabilities. The chat’s image is an assembly line where each station refines one workpiece and only the last station reads off the answer, rather than 12 voters each guessing and averaging ([one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction)).

## What is inside a layer?

Two sub-parts in sequence. [Attention](#c/c-attention) is the multi-head query-key-value lookup and the only place tokens exchange information. The [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) then processes each token on its own; it is what [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) replaces. Both are wrapped with residual connections and normalization, so each layer adds an adjustment to the running representation, the [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream), rather than replacing it.

## Does each layer have its own heads?

Yes, unambiguously. Every layer has its own separately learned attention [heads](#c/c-heads) with their own Q, K and V weights, and its own FFN. That is why depth adds capability rather than repetition: each layer is free to specialize at its level of abstraction, with early layers catching local syntax and later ones discourse-level or semantic structure. The per-layer independence runs all the way through: each layer keeps its own [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache), and in an MoE model makes its own routing decision, so a 60-layer model routes each token 60 times.

## Do layers ever share or repeat?

In frontier models, as far as is publicly known, no. But research has probed the default. [Cross-layer parameter sharing](#c/c-parameter-sharing), as in ALBERT, ties weights across layers to save memory at the cost of expressiveness; [looped depth](#c/c-looped-depth) runs one block repeatedly; some work lets adjacent layers share a KV cache. Separately, trained models drift toward redundancy on their own: [many layers do little](#c/c-layer-redundancy), and a meaningful fraction can be pruned with modest loss.

## How many are there?

The 2017 Transformer had 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers; GPT-2 and BERT ran about 12 to 48; modern open models about 30 to 80 or more, with 7–8B models near 30 and larger ones reaching 60 to 100+. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 61. Depth has diminishing returns, so architects trade it against width and expert count by experiment ([how many layers?](#c/c-q-layer-count)).

concepts.title: Each layer predicts a token
concepts.summary: The reader’s guess that every layer predicts the next token and the guesses are blended.
concepts.overview: Hearing that models have many [layers](#c/c-layers), the reader guessed that each layer predicts the next token and the predictions are blended. The chat calls it a very common and very natural misconception, and corrects it: layers are sequential, not parallel, and only the last one connects to a prediction ([one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction)). Intermediate layers produce representations, not guesses. What does accumulate is information: each layer adds its refinement to the [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream) as the vector rises.

concepts.title: One prediction, at the top
concepts.summary: Layers refine a representation in sequence; only the final layer’s output becomes a next-token prediction.
concepts.overview: This corrects the idea that [each layer predicts a token](#c/c-hyp-layers-predict). A token enters as an embedding and flows up the stack; each [layer](#c/c-layers) transforms it into a more contextualized vector of the same size and passes it on. Only after the final layer is the vector run through one last projection, the unembedding, into vocabulary-sized logits and then next-token probabilities. So there is exactly one prediction, made at the top; intermediate layers produce representations, not guesses. The [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream) is why the picture of gradual refinement fits: each layer nudges a shared vector. There is one nuance: techniques like the “logit lens” and “early exit” apply the final projection to intermediate layers to read out a rough early guess, but that is a diagnostic or optimization trick, not normal operation.

concepts.title: Residual stream
concepts.summary: The running vector each layer adds its output to, so layers make adjustments rather than replace.
concepts.overview: In a transformer, each sub-layer’s output is added back to its input (with normalization) rather than replacing it. The running sum that flows up the stack is called the residual stream: every [layer](#c/c-layers)’s attention and feed-forward steps read from it and write an adjustment into it. That is why the model is best pictured as gradual refinement, with [one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction), rather than layers each starting over. The stream’s width is the model’s hidden size, 7168 numbers per token in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3). The structure also has consequences: together with normalization it helps prevent representation collapse, and it explains how a layer can end up doing almost nothing, since a near-zero adjustment just passes the vector through ([many layers do little](#c/c-layer-redundancy)).
concepts.article:
## What is it?

Both sub-parts of a transformer block, [attention](#c/c-attention) and the [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn), are wrapped in residual connections: the input is added back to the output, with normalization. So each layer doesn’t produce a fresh representation; it makes an adjustment to the running one. The vector that flows up the stack, collecting these adjustments, is called the residual stream.

## How wide is it?

Its width is the model’s hidden size, also called `d_model`. In [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) it is 7168: at every layer boundary, every token is a vector of 7168 numbers. It is the model’s central dimension. The embedding table outputs vectors of this size, attention reads and writes vectors of this size, MoE experts project out of and back into it, and the final unembedding projects from it to the vocabulary. A wider stream lets each token carry more information, but cost scales with it.

## Why does it matter for how layers behave?

It makes the “refinement” picture literal: each layer nudges a shared representation rather than starting over, and the prediction is read once from the top ([one prediction, at the top](#c/c-one-prediction)).

It also shapes how layers fail. A layer whose adjustment is close to zero simply passes the vector through, nearly an identity. Research finds many middle and later layers in large models end up like this, which is why a meaningful fraction can be pruned with modest loss ([many layers do little](#c/c-layer-redundancy)). In the other direction, the residual structure and normalization are part of what prevents representation collapse, where successive layers stop differentiating and the representation degenerates.

## Why is it a design win?

Beyond this chat, residual connections are the standard explanation for why very deep networks can be trained at all: because the input passes straight through, learning signals can flow back through many layers without fading. That is what makes 60- or 100-layer stacks practical.

concepts.title: Cross-layer parameter sharing
concepts.summary: Tying weights across layers to shrink the parameter count; saves memory, not compute, and costs expressiveness.
concepts.overview: In a standard transformer every [layer](#c/c-layers) has its own weights. Cross-layer parameter sharing, or weight tying, reuses weights across layers to shrink the parameter count. The cleanest example is ALBERT (2019), a BERT variant that used one set of layer weights for every layer. The catch is instructive: it cuts parameters but not compute, since the same layer still runs N times, so it saves memory, not inference FLOPs. There is a spectrum: sharing in groups, sharing only some sub-components, or cycling, with [looped depth](#c/c-looped-depth) at one end. Forced similarity costs expressiveness, so an independent stack generally wins for a fixed compute budget. As far as is publicly known, leading frontier models don’t use it; it lives mostly in efficiency research and smaller models.

concepts.title: Looped depth
concepts.summary: Treating a model as one block applied repeatedly, sometimes a variable number of times.
concepts.overview: Looped depth, or recurrence in depth, takes [parameter sharing](#c/c-parameter-sharing) to its end point: instead of a stack of different layers, the model is one block applied over and over, sometimes a variable number of times per input. That blurs the line between a deep stack and a shallow stack run in a loop. The Universal Transformer was an early take on the idea. Like other forms of sharing, it saves parameters rather than compute. The chat places it within efficiency research rather than current frontier practice, where fully independent layers remain the norm.

concepts.title: Many layers do little
concepts.summary: In large trained models many middle and late layers are near-identity and can be pruned with modest loss.
concepts.overview: Research probing trained transformers finds that many [layers](#c/c-layers), especially in the middle and later parts of deep models, do surprisingly little: their transformations are close to identity, passing the [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream) through almost unchanged. A meaningful fraction can be pruned or merged with modest quality loss. The chat frames this as the emergent form of layers being “too similar”: wasted parameters and compute, which is why layer-pruning and depth-efficiency research exists. It is one reason depth has diminishing returns ([how many layers?](#c/c-q-layer-count)). The chat rates it directionally well supported but uncertain in the specifics: how much can be pruned varies a lot by model, task and measurement.

concepts.title: How many layers do models use?
concepts.summary: From 6+6 in 2017 to 30–80+ in modern open models; depth is traded against width and expert count.
concepts.overview: The original 2017 [Transformer](#c/c-transformer) used 6 encoder and 6 decoder layers. GPT-2 and BERT ran about 12 to 48. Modern open models land roughly between 30 and 80 or more: around 30 for the 7–8B class, and 60 to 100+ as models reach tens of billions of parameters and beyond; [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 61. Bigger models grow both wider and deeper, with width often scaling faster. Depth has diminishing returns: doubling layers doesn’t double capability, and past a point [many layers do little](#c/c-layer-redundancy) and training gets harder. So architects tune a three-way trade-off between depth, width and, in MoE models, expert count, by experiment rather than formula. Closed models like Claude, GPT-4 and Gemini don’t disclose their layer counts.

concepts.title: Open frontier models
concepts.summary: The open-weight models discussed (DeepSeek, Llama 4, Qwen3, Kimi, GLM): their shapes and techniques.
concepts.overview: This hub gathers the open-weight frontier models the chat compares. 2025 was the year [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) became the open-weight default, and designs then fanned out along two axes ([how do they compare?](#c/c-q-open-model-shapes)). [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) and its successor [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32) use many small experts and compressed [latent attention](#c/c-mla); [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) is the conservative reference with few large experts and [GQA](#c/c-gqa); [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) dropped the shared expert; [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) pushes sparsity to 1T total and 32B active; [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) tests hybrid linear attention. Techniques like [NoPE](#c/c-nope) and sparse attention point ahead. A recurring caution: exact specs are most reliable for models with real technical reports and public configs.

concepts.title: Training & reasoning
concepts.summary: How models are trained after pre-training, especially reinforcement learning for reasoning, and what moves quality.
concepts.overview: This hub covers the training side of the Expedition, which the chat argues is now where most quality gains come from.
