Its evidence is the DeepSeek line: over a year the architecture barely changed, and [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32)’s jump to GPT-5-comparable results came from scaled-up reinforcement-learning post-training. The central development is reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards, which scores math and code answers by whether they are actually correct and in doing so teaches models to reason at length, the engine behind [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute). It is made affordable by the GRPO algorithm and patched by a wave of variants. The field disputes whether this RL creates new reasoning or sharpens what the base model already had, and [distillation](#c/c-distillation) from stronger models is part of most recipes.

concepts.title: How do the open models compare?
concepts.summary: All converged on MoE but split on expert size, shared experts, and GQA versus MLA attention.
concepts.overview: The reader asked how many layers, experts and heads the current open frontier models have and what makes each distinct. The chat’s throughline: design has organized around two bottlenecks. On the feed-forward side, everyone converged on [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) but split on granularity, with many small experts in [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) versus few large ones in [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4), and on [shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts), kept by DeepSeek and [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2) but dropped by [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3). On the attention side the split is [GQA](#c/c-gqa) (Qwen3, Llama 4) versus [MLA](#c/c-mla) (DeepSeek, Kimi K2), with sparse and linear attention emerging. Both fights aim to maximize capacity per active parameter and minimize KV-cache pressure. The chat declined to give exact layer and head counts from secondhand roundups; reliable numbers come from model configs, as it later did for DeepSeek-V3.

concepts.title: DeepSeek-V3.2
concepts.summary: The latest step in DeepSeek’s V3 line: one architectural change, sparse attention, plus much more RL post-training.
concepts.overview: DeepSeek-V3.2 caps a line that ran V3 → V3.1 → V3.1-Terminus → V3.2-Exp → V3.2, which DeepSeek ran almost as a controlled experiment. The only architectural change from V3.1-Terminus is DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA): a cheap “lightning indexer” scores earlier tokens, and attention runs only over the selected few, cutting attention cost from quadratic to roughly linear in sequence length. DSA was meant to keep quality level, not raise it, and it did, with roughly 2–3× faster long-text processing, 30–40% less memory at 128K context, and an API price cut of over 50%. The capability jump came from elsewhere: a scalable reinforcement-learning framework and more post-training compute brought V3.2 to GPT-5-comparable results, and the V3.2-Speciale variant reached gold-medal level at IMO and IOI 2025. Those comparisons are DeepSeek’s own reported results. The backbone of [MoE](#c/c-moe) and [MLA](#c/c-mla) from [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) is unchanged.

concepts.title: Llama 4
concepts.summary: Meta’s first MoE generation (April 2025): conservative design with few large experts and GQA.

attributes.signature: The conservative MoE: few, large experts (2 active, 8,192 wide), MoE alternating with dense layers, plain GQA.

concepts.overview: Llama 4 is Meta’s first [mixture-of-experts](#c/c-moe) generation, released in April 2025. Maverick has 400B total and 17B active parameters, 128 experts, a 1M-token context, and about 22 trillion training tokens; Scout, the smaller sibling, has 109B parameters and a 10M-token context. Its MoE philosophy differs from [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3)’s: fewer but larger experts (2 active, 8,192 wide, versus DeepSeek’s many 2,048-wide ones), and MoE alternating with dense blocks every other layer rather than in nearly every block. On attention it uses [grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa), the industry default. The chat calls it the conservative, classic-MoE reference point against DeepSeek’s more aggressive design, and rates its specs among the most reliable, since Meta published a technical report.

concepts.title: Qwen3
concepts.summary: Alibaba’s open model family, top of its size classes; uses GQA and dropped the shared expert.

attributes.signature: Dropped the shared expert that DeepSeek, Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 keep; GQA; tops its size classes.

concepts.overview: Qwen3, from Alibaba’s Qwen team, is widely regarded as the top open-weight family in its size classes. It uses [grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa). Its notable [MoE](#c/c-moe) choice is a subtraction: DeepSeek-V3, Kimi K2 and GLM-4.5 all keep an always-on [shared expert](#c/c-shared-experts), but Qwen3 dropped it. That makes Qwen3 a live experiment in whether the shared expert is necessary, one of the genuinely unsettled questions in MoE design. The chat notes that its internal numbers come partly from third-party comparison write-ups, so specific layer and head counts should be checked against the model card.

concepts.title: Kimi K2
concepts.summary: Moonshot AI’s scale standout: 1T total and 32B active parameters across 384 experts, with MLA.

attributes.signature: Pushes sparsity furthest (1T total, 32B active); borrows MLA from DeepSeek and keeps the shared expert.

concepts.overview: Kimi K2, from Moonshot AI, is the scale standout among the open models discussed: 1 trillion total parameters but only 32 billion active, across 384 experts. That pushes the gap between [total and active parameters](#c/c-total-vs-active) further than almost anyone. It borrows [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla) from the DeepSeek lineage rather than using GQA, and keeps the [shared expert](#c/c-shared-experts). The chat flags that these specs come partly from comparison roundups rather than a first-party report it could verify, so the figures are well attested but secondhand. Moonshot’s smaller [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) explores hybrid attention, and whether the next flagship adopts it is an open question.

concepts.title: Kimi Linear
concepts.summary: A 48B Moonshot model using full attention in only 1 of 4 layers and linear attention in the rest.
concepts.overview: Kimi Linear is a 48B model from Moonshot AI that tests the most forward-looking attention idea in the chat: hybrid linear attention. Only one layer in four uses full attention, with [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla) and no positional encoding ([NoPE](#c/c-nope)); the other three use a cheaper linear “Delta Attention.” It shows competitive quality at significantly higher throughput. The open question is scale: sub-quadratic and hybrid attention works at small-to-mid scale, and whether Moonshot uses it in its upcoming K3 flagship is described as a decisive data point for whether linear attention is production-ready at the frontier.

concepts.title: NoPE
concepts.summary: Dropping explicit positional encoding and letting the causal mask convey order; helps extend context.
concepts.overview: Attention on its own doesn’t know token order, so models usually add position explicitly, today mostly with RoPE rotations. NoPE (“no positional embeddings”) counterintuitively drops that in some layers and relies on the causal mask alone, which lets each token see only earlier tokens, to convey order. SmolLM3 uses periodic NoPE layers alongside GQA, and [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) uses no positional encoding at all in its full-attention blocks, leaving position to its other layers. The chat notes it helps when extending to very long contexts. It appears only in smaller or periodic-layer form, not yet as standard in a major flagship, so the chat lists it among the positional-encoding rethinks still to land.

concepts.title: Linear attention
concepts.summary: Swapping most full-attention layers for cheaper linear variants, keeping a few full-attention layers for quality.
concepts.overview: Linear attention replaces the quadratic all-pairs comparison of standard [attention](#c/c-attention) with a cheaper mechanism whose cost grows linearly with sequence length. In practice nobody goes all the way: the working design is a hybrid that keeps a minority of full-attention layers and makes the rest linear. [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) is the reference case, using full attention (with [MLA](#c/c-mla)) in only one layer in four and a linear "Delta Attention" elsewhere, with competitive quality at much higher throughput. It is one of two routes to cheap long context; the other is [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/c-dsa), which keeps full attention but runs it over a selected subset of tokens. Whether a flagship model adopts linear attention is, per the Sources, one of the decisive open questions for the next generation, the same bet that [hybrids](#c/c-hybrids-win) of attention and state-space layers are making.
concepts.article:
## What problem does it solve?

Standard [attention](#c/c-attention) compares every token with every earlier token, so its cost grows with the square of the sequence length, and the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) it needs grows with every token generated. For long documents and long agent traces this becomes the dominant cost. Linear attention is one of several "sub-quadratic" families that try to break that curve, alongside state-space mixing of the kind used by [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) and trainable sparsity like [DSA](#c/c-dsa).

## How is it used in real models?

No production design the Sources describe goes fully linear. The pattern is to keep only a fraction of layers as full attention and make the rest linear. [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) uses full attention (with [MLA](#c/c-mla)) in 1 of every 4 layers and a linear "Delta Attention" in the rest, and reports competitive quality at significantly higher throughput. It also drops explicit positional encoding in its full-attention blocks ([NoPE](#c/c-nope)), which helps when extending to very long contexts.

Kimi Linear is a smaller (48B) model, so it shows the idea works at mid scale, not at the flagship frontier.

## Why do the full-attention layers stay?

A linear or recurrent mechanism compresses the past into a fixed-size summary, and a [fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets): it is weaker at precisely recalling an arbitrary earlier token. Keeping a minority of full-attention layers restores that recall while most of the network stays cheap. The Mamba-hybrid literature reached the same answer, with Jamba's ablations settling on [about one attention layer in six](#c/c-attention-ratio).

## What is still unsettled?

Sub-quadratic attention works at small-to-mid scale; whether it holds quality at frontier scale is the unresolved bet. The Sources name Kimi's upcoming K3 flagship as a decisive data point for linear attention's production viability. It sits on the list of [what hasn't landed in open flagships yet](#c/c-q-bleeding-edge), and, like the other efficiency techniques, its goal is to [preserve quality while cutting cost](#c/c-architecture-is-efficiency) rather than to make the model smarter.

concepts.title: DeepSeek Sparse Attention
concepts.summary: DeepSeek's trainable sparse attention: a cheap indexer picks relevant earlier tokens, and full attention runs only over those.
concepts.overview: DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) was the only architectural change between DeepSeek V3.1-Terminus and [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32). It works in two stages: a deliberately cheap, low-precision "lightning indexer" scores every preceding token against the current query, then ordinary [attention](#c/c-attention) runs only over the top k selected tokens. That cuts attention from O(L²) to O(Lk). DeepSeek held the rest of the recipe fixed to isolate its effect and measured parity quality, with roughly 2–3× faster long-text processing and 30–40% less memory at 128K context, enough to support a 50%+ API price cut. It is the cleanest example of the claim that [architecture is mostly efficiency](#c/c-architecture-is-efficiency), and it spread fast: [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) adopted it within months. Its main rival for cheap long context is [linear attention](#c/c-linear-attention).
concepts.article:
## How does it work?

DSA sits on top of DeepSeek's existing [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla). For each new token it runs a two-stage path. First, a "lightning indexer" computes an index score between the current query token and each preceding token. The indexer is built to be cheap: it runs in low precision with few heads. Second, full attention runs only over the k tokens the indexer selected, instead of over the whole context.

Because the expensive step now touches k tokens rather than all L, attention cost drops from quadratic, O(L²), to O(Lk), which is linear in context length for a fixed k. Since sparse attention optimizes the attention layers while [MoE](#c/c-moe) optimizes the FFN layers, the two savings compound.

## Did it make the model better?

No, and that was the point. DeepSeek ran the V3 → V3.2 line as a controlled experiment: V3.2-Exp added DSA to V3.1-Terminus through continued training, with the training recipe held fixed so DSA's effect could be isolated. The stated goal was not to improve on V3.1-Terminus but to minimize the degradation that sparsity causes. The result was virtually identical output quality with large long-context efficiency gains: roughly 2–3× faster long-text processing and about 30–40% lower memory at 128K context, which enabled an API price cut of more than 50%.

That makes DSA the purest example in the conversation of an efficiency play. The capability jump in V3.2 came from elsewhere, from [scaled RL post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training).

## Has anyone else adopted it?

At first DSA was new (late 2025) and specific to DeepSeek; V3.2 described fine-grained sparse attention at this scale as a first. One source already noted GLM adopting it. That was confirmed by [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5), whose architecture is registered as `glm_moe_dsa` and whose report credits DSA with letting it scale to 744B parameters and 28.5T training tokens without compromising long-context understanding. The Sources read this as evidence that [techniques spread fast](#c/c-techniques-spread-fast). Whether trainable sparsity becomes as universal as [grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa) did is still open, and it is listed among the [bleeding-edge ideas](#c/c-q-bleeding-edge).

## How does it compare with linear attention?

Both attack the quadratic cost of long context, from different directions. DSA keeps exact attention but applies it to a learned subset of tokens; [linear attention](#c/c-linear-attention) replaces most attention layers with a cheaper mechanism that summarizes the past. Neither is yet a settled winner across model families.

concepts.title: Aux-loss-free load balancing
concepts.summary: DeepSeek's way to balance expert load by nudging per-expert biases instead of adding an auxiliary loss.
concepts.overview: In a [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) model the [router](#c/c-router) tends to overuse a few [experts](#c/c-experts), so training normally adds an auxiliary loss that penalizes imbalance; that extra loss can degrade quality. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) avoids it: it adjusts a per-expert bias term to steer load toward underused experts, while the actual gating still follows pure token-to-expert affinity. The config shows it directly, with `topk_method: "noaux_tc"` ("no auxiliary loss") and `scoring_func: "sigmoid"`. It is DeepSeek's answer to the general [load balancing](#c/c-load-balancing) problem, and one of three distinctive techniques in V3 alongside [MLA](#c/c-mla) and [multi-token prediction](#c/c-mtp).

concepts.title: Multi-token prediction
concepts.summary: A training objective that predicts several future tokens in sequence; the extra heads can also draft for speculative decoding.
concepts.overview: Multi-token prediction trains a model to predict not only the next token but several beyond it. In [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) the predictions form a causal chain rather than being made in parallel: the model predicts a later token using the ones before it. Its first purpose is a stronger training signal. Its second is practical: the extra prediction heads double as a draft model for [speculative decoding](#c/c-speculative-decoding) at inference. The DeepSeek config sets its depth with `num_nextn_predict_layers: 1`. Today it is an auxiliary objective; whether it should become the main objective is an open research question, listed among [novel architecture directions](#c/c-q-novel-architectures) that are credible but unproven at frontier scale.

concepts.title: Fine-grained experts
concepts.summary: Using many small experts rather than a few large ones, giving the router finer choices per token.
concepts.overview: Fine-grained experts are a [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) design in which each [expert](#c/c-experts) is deliberately small and many are active at once. [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) has 256 routed experts, each with an [intermediate size](#c/c-intermediate-size) of only 2048, narrower than its 7168 [hidden size](#c/c-hidden-size); a token goes to 8 of them plus one [shared expert](#c/c-shared-experts), each doing 7168→2048→7168, and the outputs are summed back into the residual stream. That is backwards from a normal dense FFN, which expands to several times the hidden size, and it is the whole point: many small experts give the [router](#c/c-router) finer-grained combinations. [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) took the opposite philosophy, with fewer, larger experts (2 active at 8192 wide). Expert granularity is one of the main axes on which open designs split.

concepts.title: Two bottlenecks shape design
concepts.summary: Open-model design organizes around two fronts, the FFN and attention, both fighting for capacity and cache.
concepts.overview: Looking across the current [open frontier models](#c/c-open-models), the design choices sort onto two bottlenecks. On the FFN side everyone converged on [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) but split on granularity ([fine-grained experts](#c/c-fine-grained-experts) as in DeepSeek versus few large ones as in [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4)) and on whether to keep [shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts). On the attention side the split is [grouped-query attention](#c/c-gqa) (simple, default: [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3), Llama 4) versus [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla) (more compression, more complexity: DeepSeek, [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2)), with [sparse](#c/c-dsa) and [linear attention](#c/c-linear-attention) as the frontier. Both axes fight the same war: maximize capacity per active parameter and minimize [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) pressure, which follows from inference being [memory-bound](#c/c-memory-bound).

concepts.title: Hidden size
concepts.summary: The width of the residual stream: the length of the vector representing each token between layers.
concepts.overview: Hidden size, often called `d_model`, is the central dimension of a transformer: every token, at every layer boundary, is a vector of this length flowing up the [residual stream](#c/c-residual-stream). In [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) it is 7168 (the user's question had it as 716, a dropped digit the assistant corrected). The embedding table outputs vectors of this size, [attention](#c/c-attention) reads and writes them, and the final unembedding projects from it to the vocabulary. A wider hidden size lets each token carry more information, but cost scales with it. It is the reference against which the [FFN intermediate size](#c/c-intermediate-size) is measured: dense FFNs expand beyond it, while [fine-grained experts](#c/c-fine-grained-experts) are narrower than it.

concepts.title: FFN intermediate size
concepts.summary: The inner width an FFN expands to before projecting back down to the hidden size.
concepts.overview: A [feed-forward network](#c/c-ffn) expands each token vector to a larger intermediate width, applies a nonlinearity, then projects it back to the [hidden size](#c/c-hidden-size). The intermediate size is that middle width, a temporary scratch space inside one FFN. In a dense transformer it is usually several times the hidden size: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3)'s three dense layers use `intermediate_size: 18432`, about 2.6× its 7168 hidden size. Its experts use `moe_intermediate_size: 2048`, smaller than the hidden size, which is what makes them [fine-grained experts](#c/c-fine-grained-experts). The number the user asked about, "expert intermediate dimension 2048," is this per-expert width.

concepts.title: Open weights, not open training
concepts.summary: Open models publish weights and inference code, some training pieces, but never the data or a reproducible pipeline.
concepts.overview: "Open" in open models usually means open weights. For [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) the weights are on Hugging Face, the inference code is public, the architecture is fully specified (Hugging Face `transformers` implements it natively), and DeepSeek even released training infrastructure such as DualPipe (pipeline parallelism overlapping computation and communication) and an expert-parallel load balancer. What is missing is the training data and the full pre-training orchestration, so from-scratch reproduction is not possible. The same holds for [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4), [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) and [Kimi K2](#c/c-kimi-k2). The reasons for keeping data secret are now as much legal (copyright and consent scrutiny) as competitive, which is why fully open [open-data corpora](#c/c-open-data-corpora) and [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) are the main windows into [training data](#c/c-training-data).

concepts.title: RoPE
concepts.summary: Rotary position embedding: encodes position by rotating query and key vectors, so attention sees relative distance.
concepts.overview: [Attention](#c/c-attention) is order-blind on its own, so a model must inject position somehow. RoPE, the method nearly every current model uses, does it by rotating rather than adding: it splits each [query and key](#c/c-qkv) vector into coordinate pairs and rotates each pair by an angle proportional to the token's position, with different pairs spinning at different frequencies. Because attention compares queries and keys by dot product, rotating both makes the score depend on the difference of their angles, that is, on how far apart the tokens are. Relative position falls out of the geometry. RoPE's weakness is that angles beyond the trained length are unseen territory, which is the problem [YaRN](#c/c-yarn) solves; it also complicates [MLA](#c/c-mla)'s cache compression, which DeepSeek handles with a "decoupled RoPE".
concepts.article:
## Why does a transformer need it?

Attention treats its input as a bag of tokens: nothing in the query–key comparison says which token came first. Without some positional signal, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" would look the same. Earlier approaches added a position vector to each token; RoPE instead encodes position geometrically, and it has become the method nearly every current model uses.

## How does the rotation work?

Take a token's query and key vectors and split each into pairs of coordinates. Treat each pair as a point in a 2D plane and rotate it by an angle proportional to the token's position: position 1 is rotated a little, position 50 more, position 1000 more still. Different pairs rotate at different frequencies. High-frequency pairs spin fast and make fine local distinctions; low-frequency pairs spin slowly and track long-range position.

The payoff is in the dot product. When both query and key are rotated by amounts proportional to their positions, their dot product depends on the difference of the angles, that is, on the distance between the two tokens, not on where they sit in the sequence. So RoPE gives the model relative position information for free. In DeepSeek's config, `rope_theta: 10000` is the base that sets how the frequencies are spread.

## Where does it break down?

RoPE works within the range of positions seen in training. If a model was trained on sequences up to 4096 tokens (DeepSeek-V3's `original_max_position_embeddings: 4096`), the slow-frequency pairs have never been rotated past the angles position 4096 produces. At position 8000 they land at unseen angles, the model extrapolates, and quality falls off a cliff. Stretching the context therefore needs a correction such as Position Interpolation or its frequency-aware refinement, [YaRN](#c/c-yarn).

## How does it interact with other techniques?

RoPE does not combine cleanly with [multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla)'s compression of keys and values, so DeepSeek uses a "decoupled RoPE": each head's query/key splits into a 128-dimensional content part and a separate 64-dimensional positional part (`qk_rope_head_dim: 64`) that carries position alongside the compressed latent. Some newer models go the other way and drop explicit positional encoding in some layers altogether ([NoPE](#c/c-nope)), relying on the causal mask to convey order. RoPE's own rapid adoption after publication is cited as a precedent for how quickly [techniques spread](#c/c-techniques-spread-fast).

concepts.title: YaRN
concepts.summary: A RoPE context-extension method that stretches long-range frequencies while leaving local ones intact.
concepts.overview: YaRN ("Yet another RoPE extensioN") lets a model trained on short sequences handle much longer ones without retraining from scratch. Plain [RoPE](#c/c-rope) fails beyond its trained length because slow-rotating frequencies reach unseen angles. The earlier fix, Position Interpolation, squeezed every position uniformly and blurred fine local distinctions. YaRN is frequency-dependent: it leaves fast (local) frequencies alone, interpolates slow (long-range) ones, blends the band in between, and adds an attention-temperature correction (`mscale`). [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) uses it textbook-style, training at 4096 tokens and stretching 40× to about 160K with a short fine-tune. The saving is large because long-context pre-training is brutally expensive, but a stretched window is generally weaker at its far end than natively trained context. How [GLM-5.2](#c/c-q-glm52-adds) reached 1M tokens is unpublished.
concepts.article:
## What problem does it solve?

[RoPE](#c/c-rope) encodes position by rotating query and key coordinate pairs at a range of frequencies. It works within the positions seen in training. A model trained on 4096-token sequences has never seen the rotation angles that position 8000 produces on its slow-frequency pairs, so it extrapolates into unseen territory and quality collapses. Context extension asks how to take a model trained at 4096 and make it handle something like 160K without pre-training at that length, which is very expensive because attention cost grows with sequence length.

## What did Position Interpolation get wrong?

The first fix, Position Interpolation (PI), squeezes positions back into the trained range: for 8× the context, divide every position by 8, so position 8000 is treated as 1000. It works with a little fine-tuning, but it compresses all frequencies uniformly. That crowds the high-frequency pairs that encode fine local distinctions, so the model gets worse at telling nearby tokens apart even as it gains range. YaRN keeps PI's idea for the frequencies that need it and drops it where it does harm.

## How does YaRN work?

YaRN treats frequencies differently:

- **High-frequency pairs** encode short-range relationships. Nearby tokens stay nearby however long the document gets, so YaRN leaves these largely alone, preserving local precision.
- **Low-frequency pairs** encode long-range position and are the ones that run out of range. YaRN interpolates these, as PI does, so the long-range signal stays within the trained domain.
- **A middle band** gets a smooth blend between the two rather than a hard switch.

Stretching context also slightly distorts the sharpness of attention scores, so YaRN scales the attention logits by a small temperature correction. It belongs to the "NTK-aware" family of methods and is its most refined commonly used member.

## What does it look like in DeepSeek-V3?

DeepSeek-V3's `rope_scaling` block is a textbook YaRN setup: `type: "yarn"`; `factor: 40`, the extension multiplier; `original_max_position_embeddings: 4096`, the pre-extension training length; `beta_fast: 32` and `beta_slow: 1`, which set the boundaries between left-alone and interpolated frequencies; and `mscale` fields, the temperature correction. 4096 × 40 gives the config's `max_position_embeddings: 163840`, about 160K.

## What does it cost?

YaRN needs only a short fine-tuning pass on a small amount of long-context data, and sometimes works reasonably with none, so training short and extending is a large practical saving, another case of getting capability without proportionally more compute. It is not a free lunch: a model stretched 40× is generally not as good across its full window as one genuinely trained at that length, and effective use of the far end is often weaker than the headline number suggests. That is one reason context-length claims across models are not always comparable. YaRN is also classed as an [efficiency technique](#c/c-architecture-is-efficiency), not a quality one.

concepts.title: What changed across DeepSeek versions?
concepts.summary: Across V3 to V3.2 only DSA changed architecturally; the capability jump came from scaled RL post-training.
concepts.overview: DeepSeek ran the V3 line almost as a controlled experiment. V3.1 improved on the [V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) checkpoint, V3.1-Terminus improved slightly on V3.1, V3.2-Exp added [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/c-dsa) through continued training, and [V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32) kept exactly that architecture. So the backbone ([MoE](#c/c-moe) plus [MLA](#c/c-mla)) barely changed in about a year, and DSA's aim was efficiency at parity quality. The capability jump came from a scalable RL framework and scaled-up post-training compute, which DeepSeek reports brought V3.2 to GPT-5-comparable performance, with the V3.2-Speciale variant reaching gold-medal level at the 2025 IMO and IOI; those comparisons are DeepSeek's own. The arc supports two claims: [architecture is mostly efficiency](#c/c-architecture-is-efficiency) and [quality gains moved to post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training).

concepts.title: Architecture is mostly efficiency
concepts.summary: Most architecture innovations make similar quality cheaper rather than making models smarter.
concepts.overview: Sort the techniques in this Expedition by what they buy and most land on the efficiency side. [MLA](#c/c-mla), [DSA](#c/c-dsa), sparse and [linear attention](#c/c-linear-attention), [GQA](#c/c-gqa) and MQA, [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization), [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention), [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention) and [YaRN](#c/c-yarn) are all engineered to preserve quality while cutting memory or compute; DSA is the purest example, since DeepSeek measured parity on purpose. [Mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) is the in-between case: it buys capacity per active parameter, so quality per unit of inference cost. Better data remains a major quality lever, but it is not architecture. The practical reading is that these techniques drive the fall in [inference cost](#c/c-inference-cost), while the capability gains of 2025 came from [post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training).
concepts.article:
## What does the claim say?

Most of the architectural innovations discussed in this conversation are efficiency plays, not quality plays. They let you deliver similar quality more cheaply, or fit more model and context into the same hardware; by themselves they do not make the model smarter.

## Which techniques are efficiency plays?

The Sources list them explicitly as primarily efficiency, quality-neutral by design:

- [Multi-head latent attention](#c/c-mla): compresses the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache).
- [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/c-dsa) and sparse or [linear attention](#c/c-linear-attention): cheaper long context.
- [Grouped-query](#c/c-gqa) and [multi-query attention](#c/c-mqa): smaller cache.
- [KV-cache quantization](#c/c-kv-quantization).
- [FlashAttention](#c/c-flashattention) and [PagedAttention](#c/c-pagedattention).
- [YaRN](#c/c-yarn) context extension.

Each is designed to preserve quality while cutting cost. DSA is the cleanest demonstration: DeepSeek held the training recipe fixed and measured virtually identical output quality with large long-context savings.

## Where does mixture of experts fit?

[MoE](#c/c-moe) is the hybrid case. It is primarily a capacity-per-active-parameter play: a model can hold far more total parameters than it activates for each token. That buys quality per unit of inference cost rather than being purely efficiency or purely quality.

## If not architecture, what moved quality?

In DeepSeek's V3.2 line the thing that pushed capability was not an attention trick but post-training: a scalable RL framework and more post-training compute. Better and more training data also remains a major quality lever throughout, though it is not architecture. Hence the companion claim that [quality gains moved to post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training), and the picture of architecture in a consolidating phase, converging on MoE plus compressed or sparse attention.

## Why does it matter for cost?

If architecture mostly delivers the same quality more cheaply, it is a large part of why the cost of reaching a fixed capability keeps falling (see [cost to reach a capability](#c/c-inference-cost)), through many small gains rather than one breakthrough, the pattern the Sources call [increments drive cost declines](#c/c-increments-drive-declines).

concepts.title: Quality gains moved to post-training
concepts.summary: In 2025 the big capability jumps came from scaled RL post-training and test-time compute, not architecture.
concepts.overview: The notable quality improvements of 2025 did not come from rearranging attention or FFN blocks. They came from scaling RL-based [post-training](#c/c-post-training) and [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute). DeepSeek's V3 → V3.2 arc is the clean case: one architectural change aimed at efficiency, while scaled RL post-training delivered the capability jump. [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) tells the same story, with its novel engineering in the slime RL pipeline rather than in the transformer. The Sources call this migration, from architecture to the training recipe, the most notable development of the period, and it is the flip side of [architecture is mostly efficiency](#c/c-architecture-is-efficiency).
concepts.article:
## What is the claim?

Architectural innovations have mostly been efficiency multipliers. The notable quality improvements of the last year came from scaling post-training reinforcement learning and test-time compute. The action moved from the architecture to the training recipe; the Sources judge that migration itself to be the most notable development of the period.

## What is the evidence?

[DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32) is the clearest case. Its only architectural change from V3.1-Terminus was [DSA](#c/c-dsa), designed for parity quality. What pushed capability was a scalable RL framework and scaled-up post-training compute, which DeepSeek reports brought V3.2 to performance comparable with GPT-5, and its high-compute V3.2-Speciale variant to gold-medal level at the 2025 IMO and IOI. Those comparisons come from DeepSeek's own materials, so they should be read as reported rather than independently settled (see [vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)).

[GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) repeats the pattern: its report's emphasis is [slime](#c/c-slime), an asynchronous RL infrastructure for large-scale agent training, not a new transformer design.

## What does the RL actually do?

The machinery behind the jump is [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr), usually with [GRPO](#c/c-grpo). Optimizing for verifiably correct answers over long chains of thought teaches the model to use inference-time thinking productively, which is how [reasoning emerges from RL](#c/c-reasoning-emerges). The competition-math and coding gold medals are the natural showcase because those are the verifiable domains where RLVR is strongest.

## What does this mean for architecture?

Over roughly a year, DeepSeek's backbone ([MoE](#c/c-moe) plus [MLA](#c/c-mla)) barely changed. The Sources describe architecture as consolidating, converging on MoE with compressed or sparse attention, while a steady drumbeat of incremental efficiency techniques continues and new intuitions migrate to training and reasoning.

concepts.title: What hasn't landed in open flagships yet?
concepts.summary: Linear attention at flagship scale, trainable sparse attention elsewhere, shared-expert choices and NoPE have not yet become standard.
concepts.overview: The Sources flag this answer as speculative, written from a January 2026 cutoff plus a few searches. Four directions were visible in research but not standard in a flagship open release. First, [linear or hybrid attention](#c/c-linear-attention) at flagship scale: [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) works at 48B, and Kimi's K3 is the decisive test. Second, trainable sparse attention beyond DeepSeek: [DSA](#c/c-dsa) is brand new, with GLM possibly adopting it (which [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) later confirmed). Third, whether to keep [shared experts](#c/c-shared-experts), since [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) dropped them while DeepSeek and Kimi kept them. Fourth, [NoPE](#c/c-nope). A looser tail, meant as "things to go check" rather than claims: sub-8-bit training and inference, [multi-token prediction](#c/c-mtp) as the main objective, and attention–FFN disaggregated serving.

concepts.title: Post-training
concepts.summary: Everything after pre-training that turns a raw base model into a useful, aligned assistant.
concepts.overview: Pre-training builds capability; post-training elicits and directs it and adds alignment. It starts from a [base model](#c/c-base-model) that has vast latent knowledge but no orientation toward helping, and runs a sequence of stages: [supervised fine-tuning](#c/c-sft) on demonstrations, learning a [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) from comparisons, then reinforcement learning, either [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf) against learned preferences or [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) against verifiers. [DPO](#c/c-dpo) and distillation are common variations. It uses a small fraction of the total compute, yet shapes most of the behavior, safety and personality you experience, and in 2025 it became the main source of capability gains ([quality moved to post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training)). The overall arc runs [from imitation to evaluation](#c/c-imitation-to-evaluation).
concepts.article:
## Why is it needed?

[Pre-training](#c/c-pre-training) produces a [base model](#c/c-base-model): a raw next-token predictor. Ask it a question and it might continue with more questions, because in its training data questions are often followed by similar questions. It has enormous latent knowledge but no orientation toward being helpful, following instructions or conversing. Post-training is everything done afterwards to turn it into a useful, aligned, instruction-following assistant. It uses a small fraction of the total compute, but it is where much of the behavior you interact with gets shaped.

## What are the stages?

The classic recipe has three stages.

1. **[Supervised fine-tuning](#c/c-sft)** (instruction tuning): continue next-token training on curated prompt–response demonstrations. This teaches the assistant format and does most of the work of making the model behave like an assistant at all, but it can only imitate what it is shown.
2. **[Reward modeling](#c/c-reward-model)**: collect comparisons (which of two responses is better, judged by humans or increasingly by AI) and learn from them, usually as a separate model that scores responses.
3. **Reinforcement learning**: generate responses, score them, and update the model toward higher-scoring ones. [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf) scores with a learned model of human preference; [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr), the reasoning-model development, scores with a deterministic verifier.

Stage 3 is what lets the model exceed the quality of its demonstrations, provided the reward signal is good.

## Is it really that tidy?

No. The stages blur and repeat: labs interleave SFT and RL over several rounds, and a fuzzy *mid-training* or continued pre-training phase (for example heavy math and code) sits between the two phases. [DPO](#c/c-dpo) skips the separate reward model and optimizes directly on preference pairs, a lighter Stage 2+3. [Distillation](#c/c-distillation), training on a stronger model's outputs, is often part of the recipe and is essentially a souped-up SFT. Exact recipes are proprietary and vary a lot.

## Which parameters change?

By default, all of them, but gently: [full fine-tuning](#c/c-full-fine-tuning) with a learning rate often an order of magnitude or more below pre-training, over far fewer tokens, to avoid [catastrophic forgetting](#c/c-catastrophic-forgetting). Parameter-efficient methods such as [LoRA](#c/c-lora) train only small adapters. Frontier labs are generally understood to use full fine-tuning for large-scale RL; people adapting open models overwhelmingly use LoRA (see [does post-training change all parameters?](#c/c-q-full-or-subset)).

## Why does it matter so much now?

Safety and alignment behavior (refusals, honesty, tone) is shaped mostly here, which is why two models with similar base capabilities can feel very different. And in 2025 the big capability jumps came from scaling RL post-training rather than from architecture ([quality moved to post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training)). The data behind it is its own discipline: [post-training data](#c/c-post-training-data) and the question of whether [specialists beat a generalist](#c/c-q-specialists).

concepts.title: RLVR
concepts.summary: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards: train against automatic right-or-wrong checks instead of a learned reward model.
concepts.overview: RLVR is the dominant [post-training](#c/c-post-training) paradigm for reasoning models. Where [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf) optimizes against a [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) learned from human preferences, a noisy and gameable proxy, RLVR uses deterministic verifiers that check ground truth: run the code against tests, compare the math answer to the known solution. That is why it works first in math and code. [DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1) was the landmark demonstration, showing that [reasoning emerges from RL](#c/c-reasoning-emerges); [GRPO](#c/c-grpo) made it affordable. It has characteristic failure modes ([length bias](#c/c-length-bias), [exploration collapse](#c/c-exploration-collapse), [reward hacking](#c/c-reward-hacking)) and a live dispute over whether it [sharpens rather than expands](#c/c-rlvr-sharpens) ability. The open problem is extending it beyond checkable domains.
concepts.article:
## How does it differ from RLHF?

Both are Stage 3 of [post-training](#c/c-post-training): the model generates responses, something scores them, and the model is updated toward higher scores. They differ in where the score comes from. [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf) uses a [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) trained on human preferences, which is good for subjective qualities like tone and helpfulness but is a noisy proxy the model can learn to satisfy without being right. RLVR replaces it with a deterministic verifier giving binary feedback on whether the answer is actually correct. A verifier checks ground truth rather than approximating it, so it is much less gameable.

## Why math and code first?

Those are the domains where correctness can be checked mechanically: run the code against tests, verify the math answer against a known solution. The reward is "did it get the right answer," not "did a human like it." The data is correspondingly different: verifiable problems plus the checking machinery, curated toward medium difficulty and ordered by a curriculum (see [RL data & curriculum](#c/c-rl-data-curriculum)). The competition-math and coding gold medals claimed for DeepSeek-V3.2-Speciale are the natural showcase for exactly this reason.

## What did it unlock?

[DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1) showed that RLVR can elicit sophisticated reasoning, including an "aha moment" in which self-reflection emerged spontaneously. Researchers consistently report that RL incentivizes extended chain-of-thought with emergent self-reflection and branching. Nobody taught the model to say "wait, let me reconsider"; it fell out of optimizing for correct answers over long reasoning chains. This is how RLVR teaches a model to use [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute) productively (see [reasoning emerges from RL](#c/c-reasoning-emerges)). The algorithm that made it practical is [GRPO](#c/c-grpo).

## What goes wrong?

Three recurring failure modes drive the flurry of [GRPO variants](#c/c-grpo-variants):

- [Length bias](#c/c-length-bias): chains get longer without getting better.
- [Exploration collapse](#c/c-exploration-collapse): if every sampled attempt is wrong there is no learning signal.
- [Reward hacking](#c/c-reward-hacking): satisfying the verifier without genuine reasoning.

## Does it create new ability?

This is contested. One careful study found that across PPO, GRPO and others, RLVR raises the probability of correct samples but reduces the set of problems the model can solve at all: it concentrates ability the base model already had, while distillation from a stronger teacher can transfer genuinely new reasoning patterns. The same work found current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and remain far from optimal. The Sources weigh this as a serious critique rather than settled fact; other work reports broader gains (see [RLVR sharpens, doesn't expand](#c/c-rlvr-sharpens)).

## What is the open frontier?

Extending verifiable rewards beyond cleanly checkable domains. "Write a good essay," "give sound legal analysis" or "be a helpful agent over 50 tool calls" have no ground-truth verifier. Candidate approaches include learned verifiers, rubric-based rewards and process rewards that score reasoning steps rather than only final answers. It is unresolved and moving fast, as is [agentic RL](#c/c-agentic-rl).

concepts.title: RLHF
concepts.summary: Reinforcement learning from human feedback: optimize the model against a reward model learned from human preferences.
concepts.overview: RLHF is the classic Stage 3 of [post-training](#c/c-post-training). Humans (or increasingly AI) compare pairs of responses, a [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) is trained on those preferences, and the language model is then optimized with RL, traditionally [PPO](#c/c-ppo), to produce responses the reward model scores highly. It is well suited to subjective qualities such as helpfulness, tone and harmlessness, where no mechanical checker exists. Its weakness is that the reward model is a learned, noisy proxy the policy can learn to satisfy without actually being better, a form of [reward hacking](#c/c-reward-hacking). [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) swaps that proxy for a deterministic verifier where correctness is checkable, and [DPO](#c/c-dpo) skips the separate reward model altogether.

concepts.title: DeepSeek-R1
concepts.summary: DeepSeek's reasoning model, the landmark demonstration that RL with verifiable rewards can produce reasoning.
concepts.overview: DeepSeek-R1 is the case study for [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr). Its headline finding was emergent behavior: during RL training on correct answers, the model spontaneously developed self-reflection, the so-called "aha moment", without being taught to reconsider its work (see [reasoning emerges from RL](#c/c-reasoning-emerges)). That made it central to the distillation debate. Its reasoning came largely from RLVR on the base model rather than from copying closed frontier models; DeepSeek then distilled R1's reasoning into smaller models of its own, which the Sources frame as [RL, not copying, built R1](#c/c-rl-built-r1). Like [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3), its weights are open, with DualPipe among the training infrastructure DeepSeek released.

concepts.title: Reasoning emerges from RL
concepts.summary: Optimizing only for correct answers makes long chain-of-thought, self-reflection and branching appear untaught.
concepts.overview: A striking result of [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr): reward a model only for reaching correct answers over long reasoning chains, and extended chain-of-thought, self-reflection and branching emerge during training without being demonstrated. [DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1)'s "aha moment", where the model began reconsidering its own steps, is the landmark example, and researchers report the pattern consistently. This is the mechanism behind the [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute) paradigm: RLVR teaches the model to use inference-time thinking productively. It is challenged by the finding that [RLVR sharpens rather than expands](#c/c-rlvr-sharpens) what the base model could already do, so how "new" the emerged reasoning is remains disputed.

concepts.title: GRPO
concepts.summary: Group Relative Policy Optimization: RL that scores each attempt against its group's average, with no critic network.
concepts.overview: GRPO is the algorithm that made [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) affordable, and it became the de facto choice for reasoning training. It comes from DeepSeek's earlier math work. [PPO](#c/c-ppo), the RLHF workhorse, runs a separate critic (value) network alongside the model, roughly doubling memory and compute. GRPO drops the critic: for each problem it samples a group of attempts (say 16), scores them all with the verifier, and uses the group's average reward as the baseline, reinforcing better-than-average attempts and suppressing worse ones. That cost cut is much of why reasoning training spread so fast across labs. Its structure also creates [exploration collapse](#c/c-exploration-collapse) when every attempt fails, and a wave of [GRPO variants](#c/c-grpo-variants) followed to fix its failure modes.
concepts.article:
## What problem does it solve?

Reinforcement learning on a language model needs a baseline: to know whether an attempt was good, you compare its reward with what was expected. [PPO](#c/c-ppo), the standard algorithm in [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf), gets that expectation from a separate critic or value network that runs alongside the model and estimates how good each step is. That roughly doubles the memory and compute of training, which is painful at the scale of large language models.

## How does it work?

GRPO eliminates the critic. For one problem it samples several reasoning traces, for example 16 attempts, scores each with the verifier, and judges every attempt relative to the group average. Attempts better than average are reinforced; worse ones are suppressed. The group itself supplies the baseline that PPO needed a whole network for.

It pairs naturally with [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr): a verifier can score many attempts cheaply and objectively, and a group of attempts on the same problem gives a meaningful comparison.

## Why did it matter?

Its importance is mostly about cost. Removing the critic substantially reduces RL training overhead, and that reduction is much of why reasoning training proliferated so fast across labs. GRPO became the de facto algorithm for RLVR, the machinery behind [DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1) and the scaled RL that the Sources credit with 2025's [quality gains](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training).

## What are its weak spots?

Scoring relative to the group has a structural hole: if every attempt at a hard problem is wrong, all rewards are equal, the group advantage is zero, and there is no gradient at all. That is [exploration collapse](#c/c-exploration-collapse), severe on hard problems and unfamiliar domains. Naive use also tends toward [length bias](#c/c-length-bias), chains that grow without improving. These gave rise to a flurry of [GRPO variants](#c/c-grpo-variants): DAPO, Dr. GRPO, REINFORCE++ (global rather than per-prompt advantage normalization), GSPO (sequence-level optimization to stabilize MoE models) and others. One study found current RLVR algorithms perform similarly to one another and remain far from optimal, so the differences between variants may matter less than the attention they get.

concepts.title: PPO
concepts.summary: Proximal Policy Optimization, the RLHF workhorse algorithm, which trains alongside a separate critic network.
concepts.overview: PPO is the reinforcement-learning algorithm classically used for [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf). Beside the model being trained it runs a separate critic, or value network, that estimates how good each step is, so updates can be judged against an expectation. The cost of that design is that the critic roughly doubles memory and compute. [GRPO](#c/c-grpo) was built as a cheaper alternative: it drops the critic and uses the average reward of a group of sampled attempts as the baseline instead. Understanding PPO's critic is what makes GRPO's saving, and its rapid adoption for [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr), make sense. Some later fixes, such as VC-PPO and VAPO, return to value-based ideas for long reasoning chains (see [GRPO variants](#c/c-grpo-variants)).

concepts.title: GRPO variants
concepts.summary: A wave of GRPO fixes (DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VAPO, REINFORCE++, GSPO) each targeting a specific RL failure mode.
concepts.overview: After [GRPO](#c/c-grpo) made RLVR affordable, a dense flurry of incremental fixes followed, the same breakthrough-then-refinements pattern seen in architecture. DAPO, Dr. GRPO, VC-PPO and VAPO address [length bias](#c/c-length-bias), difficulty imbalance, value-function management for long chains, and training stability. REINFORCE++ uses global advantage normalization to correct a bias from GRPO's per-prompt normalization. GSPO moves optimization from the token level to the sequence level to stabilize RL on [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) models, a sign that training reasoning into sparse routed models brings its own problems. The reasons the variants exist are the useful part: they map what breaks. One study cautions that current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and are far from optimal.

concepts.title: Length bias
concepts.summary: Naive RLVR stretches reasoning chains longer without necessarily making answers better.
concepts.overview: When a model is rewarded only for correct final answers, training tends to make its reasoning chains longer and longer, sometimes without any improvement in accuracy. Longer chains cost more at inference, since every reasoning token is generated sequentially, so wasted length is a real expense. It is one of the recurring failure modes of [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr). The responses are twofold: several [GRPO variants](#c/c-grpo-variants), including DAPO and Dr. GRPO, were designed partly to counter it, and reward engineering adds explicit penalties for inefficient or excessively long responses.

concepts.title: Exploration collapse
concepts.summary: When every sampled attempt is wrong, group-relative RL gets zero advantage and no learning signal.
concepts.overview: Exploration collapse is the sharpest structural problem in [GRPO](#c/c-grpo)-style [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr). Because each attempt is scored relative to its group's average, a problem where every sampled attempt fails gives every attempt the same reward, a group advantage of zero, and no gradient at all. The model cannot learn from problems it never solves even once. That makes the problem severe for hard problems and unfamiliar domains, exactly where learning matters most. Much recent work targets it, through entropy regularization, curiosity bonuses and curriculum design that raises difficulty gradually (see [RL data & curriculum](#c/c-rl-data-curriculum)).

concepts.title: Reward hacking
concepts.summary: A model satisfying its verifier or reward model without actually doing the intended reasoning.
concepts.overview: Reward hacking is when the model learns to score well without being right. It is the core weakness of [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf), whose learned [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) is a noisy proxy the model can learn to please, and a main reason [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) swapped that proxy for deterministic verifiers that check ground truth. Verifiers reduce the problem but do not remove it: a model can still find ways to satisfy the checker without genuine reasoning. The Sources' remedy is careful reward design, which is also why the quality of the reward signal is described as "the whole ballgame" in the move [from imitation to evaluation](#c/c-imitation-to-evaluation).

concepts.title: RL data & curriculum
concepts.summary: RLVR's data: verifiable problems plus their checkers, tuned for difficulty, cleaned of leaks, and ordered by curriculum.
concepts.overview: [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) needs a different kind of data from SFT or preference learning. Instead of responses or comparisons, the "dataset" is problems with checkable answers plus the verification machinery: math with known solutions, instructions with programmatically checkable constraints. [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) documents this, selecting tasks with verifiable outcomes and rewarding only verified-correct generations. Curation matters as much as in pre-training: datasets are balanced toward medium difficulty, cleaned of benchmark leakage ([decontamination](#c/c-decontamination)), and ordered by a curriculum that raises complexity gradually, which also helps against [exploration collapse](#c/c-exploration-collapse). The bottleneck is having a verifier at all, which is why RLVR stays confined mostly to math, code and format-following.

concepts.title: RLVR sharpens, doesn't expand
concepts.summary: A contested finding: RLVR makes correct answers more likely but narrows, rather than expands, what the model can solve.
concepts.overview: One careful study found a deflating result for [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr). Across PPO, GRPO and other algorithms, RL raised the likelihood of correct samples but decreased coverage of solvable problems: the model got better at producing high-reward answers it could already produce, without gaining reasoning beyond the base model's capacity. Distillation from a stronger teacher, by contrast, could transfer genuinely new reasoning patterns. The same work found current RLVR algorithms perform similarly and far from optimally. This cuts against the story that [reasoning emerges from RL](#c/c-reasoning-emerges). The Sources weigh it as a serious, credible critique but one research line, with others reporting broader gains; the truth likely depends on what counts as "new". It also prompted the overstated remark that [distillation drives reasoning gains](#c/c-hyp-distillation-reasoning).

concepts.title: Distillation drives reasoning gains
concepts.summary: The assistant's offhand claim that distillation explains a chunk of open-model reasoning gains, later judged overstated.
concepts.overview: While discussing [RLVR sharpens, doesn't expand](#c/c-rlvr-sharpens), the assistant said a chunk of apparent reasoning gains may be [distillation](#c/c-distillation) from stronger models doing the heavy lifting. The user asked for evidence, and the assistant retracted the confident version. The underlying paper showed distillation *can* transfer reasoning, not how much of any open model's reasoning came from it. The best-documented open case, [DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1), points the other way: RLVR produced the reasoning, then distillation spread it to smaller siblings ([RL, not copying, built R1](#c/c-rl-built-r1)). No reliable share can be measured because post-training data is undisclosed. Distillation from closed models is real and was pervasive for chat quality, as [Tülu 3's SFT answers](#c/c-open-sft-from-closed) show, but for headline reasoning gains it remains a plausible suspicion.

concepts.title: Agentic RL
concepts.summary: Using reinforcement learning to train models to use tools, browse and act over long multi-step tasks.
concepts.overview: Agentic RL extends [post-training](#c/c-post-training) from single answers to long-horizon behavior: training a model via reinforcement learning to use tools, browse and take actions across many steps. The Sources call it probably the biggest current frontier in training, and also the place where the assistant's January 2026 knowledge was least adequate. It inherits [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr)'s hard open problem: "be a helpful agent over 50 tool calls" has no clean verifier. The clearest documented example is [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5)'s [slime](#c/c-slime) infrastructure, which decouples generation from training so large-scale agent trajectories can be explored without GPUs sitting idle.

concepts.title: Pre-training
concepts.summary: The expensive first training phase: next-token prediction over trillions of tokens, producing a base model.
concepts.overview: Pre-training is where a model learns language and world knowledge, by predicting the next token over an internet-scale corpus: trillions of tokens, months of GPU time, the compute-heavy phase behind most [training compute](#c/c-training-compute). What comes out is a [base model](#c/c-base-model), a raw next-token predictor with enormous latent capability but no orientation toward helping. [Post-training](#c/c-post-training) then elicits and directs that capability. The boundary is fuzzy: a *mid-training* or continued pre-training phase, for example heavy math and code, often sits between them. Much of pre-training's quality now comes from the corpus itself, filtered web crawl in which [data is the main lever](#c/c-data-is-the-lever).
concepts.article:
## What happens in pre-training?

The model is trained to predict the next token over a vast corpus of internet-scale text. This is the expensive, compute-heavy phase: trillions of tokens and months of GPU time. Through that single objective it learns language, facts about the world and general capabilities. The phrase the Sources offer: pre-training builds the capabilities; [post-training](#c/c-post-training) elicits and directs them, and adds alignment.

## What does it produce?

A [base model](#c/c-base-model). It is not yet useful the way an assistant is: it continues text rather than answering. Ask it a question and it may produce more questions, because questions are often followed by similar questions in its training data. It is like someone who has read the entire internet but has never been told what to do with it.

## Where does it end?

Not cleanly. Between pre-training and post-training sits a fuzzy phase called mid-training or continued pre-training, for example training on a lot of math and code to build a foundation before formal post-training begins. Context extension also often happens after the main run: [DeepSeek-V3](#c/c-deepseek-v3) was trained on 4096-token sequences and stretched to about 160K with [YaRN](#c/c-yarn), because pre-training at long context is brutally costly.

## What is it trained on?

The backbone of open pre-training corpora is filtered web crawl from Common Crawl, layered with curated sources such as code, papers, books, Wikipedia, Q&A sites and math (see [corpus pipeline](#c/c-data-pipeline)). Modern corpus building is aggressive throwing-away: projects like DCLM and FineWeb-Edu [keep the best 10%](#c/c-keep-best-10) because quality per token beats quantity. Flagship labs keep their corpora secret, for legal as well as competitive reasons, so most of what is known comes from [open-data corpora](#c/c-open-data-corpora).

## How does it relate to post-training?

Training moves [from imitation to evaluation](#c/c-imitation-to-evaluation): pre-training imitates the corpus, SFT imitates curated demonstrations, and RL optimizes against a judgment of quality. Post-training datasets are tiny by comparison (thousands to millions of examples rather than trillions of tokens) and use a learning rate often an order of magnitude lower, so the pre-trained model stays recognizably the same model underneath.

concepts.title: Base model
concepts.summary: What pre-training produces: a raw next-token predictor with vast latent knowledge but no instinct to help.
concepts.overview: A base model is the output of [pre-training](#c/c-pre-training) and the starting point for [post-training](#c/c-post-training). It predicts the next token very well and carries enormous latent knowledge and capability, but it has no orientation toward being helpful, following instructions or holding a conversation. Ask it a question and it may continue with more questions, because that is what often follows a question in its training data. [Supervised fine-tuning](#c/c-sft) is the first step in turning it into an assistant. The base model's latent ability also matters for the RL debate: if [RLVR only sharpens](#c/c-rlvr-sharpens) what the base could already do, then how capable the base model was sets a ceiling on what RL delivers.

concepts.title: Supervised fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Supervised fine-tuning: continued next-token training on curated prompt and ideal-response pairs.
concepts.overview: SFT, also called instruction tuning, is Stage 1 of [post-training](#c/c-post-training). The mechanism is the same as [pre-training](#c/c-pre-training), predicting the next token, but the data is a curated set of demonstrations: prompts paired with ideal responses, thousands to millions of them. It teaches the assistant format (answer questions, follow instructions, take turns) and does most of the work of turning a [base model](#c/c-base-model) into something that behaves like an assistant at all. Its limit is that it can only imitate what it is shown, and demonstrations are expensive to write. That is why the pipeline moves on to a [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) and RL. Distillation from a stronger model is essentially SFT on that model's outputs, which is how open projects like [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) get their responses.
concepts.article:
## How does it work?

Take the [base model](#c/c-base-model) and continue training it with next-token prediction, but on a curated dataset of the behavior you want: prompts paired with good responses. The mechanism is unchanged from pre-training; only the data differs. Instead of raw internet text, the model imitates demonstrations, often written or curated by humans. SFT can be done by [full fine-tuning](#c/c-full-fine-tuning) or with adapters such as [LoRA](#c/c-lora), which is extremely common for SFT specifically.

## What does it teach?

The basic format of being an assistant: that a question should be followed by a helpful answer, that instructions should be followed, that a conversation takes turns. SFT does most of the heavy lifting in converting a base model into something assistant-like. The SFT data chosen also shapes safety behavior, honesty and tone, which is why post-training accounts for much of a model's personality.

## What are its limits?

SFT can only imitate the demonstrations it is shown, and writing demonstrations is expensive and cannot cover everything. It caps the model at the quality of its examples. That is the motivation for the next stages: it is often easier to compare two responses than to write the ideal one, which leads to the [reward model](#c/c-reward-model), and RL can then push beyond imitation. The Sources describe the progression as moving [from imitation to evaluation](#c/c-imitation-to-evaluation).

## Where do the demonstrations come from?

Demonstration data is one of the two main ingredients of [post-training data](#c/c-post-training-data). Prompts come from paid annotators, real user logs (such as WildChat) and model-generated synthesis. The responses, in open projects, increasingly come from other models: [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3)'s new synthetic SFT responses were all generated by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet (for code) ([open SFT answers come from closed models](#c/c-open-sft-from-closed)). This is output-based [distillation](#c/c-distillation), essentially a souped-up SFT. Closed frontier labs cannot distill from anything above themselves, so they rely more on human experts and their own models. Tülu 3 also found that regenerating completions for existing datasets through its synthetic pipeline improved downstream DPO results.

concepts.title: Reward model
concepts.summary: A model trained on comparisons between responses to score how good a response is.
concepts.overview: Stage 2 of [post-training](#c/c-post-training) rests on an observation: it is often easier to compare two responses and say which is better than to write the ideal one. So labs collect comparison data, with humans (or increasingly an AI) picking the preferred of two model outputs, and either train a separate reward model that scores responses or use the preferences directly, as [DPO](#c/c-dpo) does. The reward model supplies the signal that [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf) optimizes against; it is the "human feedback" in the acronym. Being learned, it is a noisy proxy that invites [reward hacking](#c/c-reward-hacking), which is why [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) replaces it with verifiers where it can. Its data is the preference half of [post-training data](#c/c-post-training-data), now often ranked by [LLM-as-a-judge](#c/c-llm-as-judge).

concepts.title: From imitation to evaluation
concepts.summary: Training moves from imitating a corpus, to imitating demonstrations, to optimizing against a judgment of quality.
concepts.overview: This is the conceptual throughline of how a model is trained. [Pre-training](#c/c-pre-training) imitates the corpus: predict what comes next. [Supervised fine-tuning](#c/c-sft) imitates curated good behavior. Reinforcement learning optimizes against a judgment of quality, which lets the model exceed its demonstrations. Each step relaxes a constraint: imitation caps you at the quality of your examples, while evaluation lets you climb past them, but only if the reward signal is good. The quality of the reward signal is "the whole ballgame," which is why swapping [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf)'s noisy learned reward for [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr)'s clean verifier was such a big deal, and why extending verifiable rewards to soft domains is the hard open problem.

concepts.title: DPO
concepts.summary: Direct Preference Optimization: train directly on preference pairs, skipping the separate reward model.
concepts.overview: DPO is a lighter-weight alternative to [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf). Instead of training a separate [reward model](#c/c-reward-model) and then running RL against it, DPO optimizes the language model directly on preference pairs, each a preferred and a dispreferred response to the same prompt. In effect it combines Stages 2 and 3 of [post-training](#c/c-post-training). It is simpler and popular in open models; [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3)'s recipe uses it, and found that regenerating SFT completions through its synthetic pipeline improved DPO results. Whether DPO matches full RL at scale is debated. Its input is the preference data built by the [preference data pipeline](#c/c-preference-pipeline).

concepts.title: Does post-training change all parameters?
concepts.summary: By default post-training updates every parameter, gently; LoRA-style methods update only small adapters.
concepts.overview: The question bundles two axes: how many parameters change, and how much. By default, [full fine-tuning](#c/c-full-fine-tuning): every parameter is eligible, just as in pre-training, but at a learning rate often an order of magnitude or more lower and over far fewer tokens, because post-training redirects a capable model rather than rebuilding it, and moving too hard causes [catastrophic forgetting](#c/c-catastrophic-forgetting). The alternative is parameter-efficient fine-tuning, dominated by [LoRA](#c/c-lora), which freezes the model and trains small adapters. Frontier labs are generally understood to use full fine-tuning for large-scale RL; everyone adapting open models overwhelmingly uses LoRA. MoE models add their own wrinkle, which [GRPO variants](#c/c-grpo-variants) like GSPO address. Exact lab recipes are proprietary, and the boundary of which is better where is fuzzy.

concepts.title: Full fine-tuning
concepts.summary: Updating every model parameter in post-training, at a much smaller learning rate than pre-training.
concepts.overview: Full fine-tuning is the default in the classic [post-training](#c/c-post-training) recipe: forward pass, loss, gradients to all weights, update, the same machinery as pre-training. The difference is magnitude. The learning rate is typically an order of magnitude or more lower, and the data is thousands to millions of examples rather than trillions of tokens, so the model stays recognizably itself with a thin behavioral layer on top. Move the weights too aggressively and you get [catastrophic forgetting](#c/c-catastrophic-forgetting). It is more expressive and more expensive than [LoRA](#c/c-lora), and it is generally understood to be what frontier labs use for large-scale RL, where constraining updates to a low-rank adapter would leave capability on the table; the exact internal recipes are not public.

concepts.title: Catastrophic forgetting
concepts.summary: Fine-tuning too aggressively erodes the knowledge and fluency a model learned in pre-training.
concepts.overview: Catastrophic forgetting is the main risk that shapes how [post-training](#c/c-post-training) is done. Post-training redirects an already capable model; if weights move too far, behavior shifts but the underlying knowledge and fluency degrade. That is why [full fine-tuning](#c/c-full-fine-tuning) uses a much lower learning rate than pre-training and far fewer tokens. [LoRA](#c/c-lora) avoids it by construction, because the original weights are frozen and only a small adapter is learned. The same concern appears in multi-task training, alongside [negative transfer](#c/c-negative-transfer): forgetting earlier tasks is guarded against with replay buffers, distillation and careful [data mixing](#c/c-data-mixing).

concepts.title: LoRA
concepts.summary: Low-Rank Adaptation: freeze the model and train two small matrices whose product approximates the needed update.
concepts.overview: LoRA is the dominant parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) method. It rests on an empirical observation that the change a model needs during fine-tuning is low-rank, so instead of training a full 7168×7168 update you train two skinny matrices, such as 7168×16 and 16×7168, whose product approximates it. The original model is frozen. That brings three payoffs: far less memory (optimizer state only for the adapter, so large models fit on one GPU), no [catastrophic forgetting](#c/c-catastrophic-forgetting) by construction, and modular megabyte-sized adapters that can be swapped or served together. QLoRA also quantizes the frozen base to 4-bit. It is the default for adapting open models, while [full fine-tuning](#c/c-full-fine-tuning) still tends to win for the deepest changes. Routing inputs to specialized LoRA adapters also keeps [specialists](#c/c-q-specialists) inside one model.

concepts.title: Do specialists beat a generalist?
concepts.summary: Both effects are real: specialists win on their own tasks, but diverse training transfers skills; labs blend.
concepts.overview: The user's intuition, that domain-specific post-training should beat one generalist, is an actively studied hypothesis, and the answer is a tension rather than a winner. [Negative transfer](#c/c-negative-transfer) is real: in controlled studies [specialists beat a generalist](#c/c-specialists-win) on their own tasks. But [positive transfer](#c/c-positive-transfer) is equally real: diverse training builds general skills and lets data-poor tasks free-ride on data-rich ones. And [transfer is asymmetric](#c/c-asymmetric-transfer), with some domains helping others and some intruding. What labs do is engineer for the good effect: [data mixing](#c/c-data-mixing) and staged training, specialize-then-[merge](#c/c-model-merging) as in [Apriel](#c/c-apriel), and modular adapters such as routed [LoRA](#c/c-lora) experts. Very large models seem to interfere less, so the case for specialists may be strongest at small scale; what frontier labs actually do is unknown.

concepts.title: Specialists beat a generalist
concepts.summary: The user's hypothesis that domain-specific post-training beats one generalist; supported in controlled, mostly small-scale studies.
concepts.overview: The user reasoned that a programmer and a business expert want different rewards, so separate post-training sets should beat one generalist, especially with small datasets. There is direct support. A vision-language study found that on 5 of 7 downstream tasks, a model instruction-tuned on all the data lost to a task expert fine-tuned on only the relevant subset. An expert-LM paper explains the mechanism as [negative transfer](#c/c-negative-transfer) and reports a +10.4% mean accuracy gain from selecting relevant experts at inference over a multi-task baseline. The caveats: most of this evidence is from SFT and smaller or vision-language settings, very large models appear to absorb diverse tasks with less interference, and [positive transfer](#c/c-positive-transfer) pulls the other way. [Asymmetric transfer](#c/c-asymmetric-transfer) refines rather than settles it.

concepts.title: Negative transfer
concepts.summary: When learning one task hurts performance on another, especially unrelated or conflicting tasks.
concepts.overview: Negative transfer, also called task interference, is the documented form of the user's intuition that specialists should win. Learning one task can hinder another, especially when the tasks are unrelated or conflicting, and progress on one task may oscillate or regress while another improves. Together with [catastrophic forgetting](#c/c-catastrophic-forgetting), it can make multi-task fine-tuning worse than single-task fine-tuning in data efficiency, stability and generalization. It is the reason [specialists beat a generalist](#c/c-specialists-win) in controlled studies. The counter-force is [positive transfer](#c/c-positive-transfer); the standard mitigations are [data mixing](#c/c-data-mixing), [model merging](#c/c-model-merging) and modular adapters such as routed [LoRA](#c/c-lora) experts.

concepts.title: Positive transfer
concepts.summary: Training on diverse tasks builds general skills, and data-rich tasks support data-poor ones.
concepts.overview: Positive transfer is why labs do not simply build specialists. Exposure to diverse tasks helps a model learn more fundamental capabilities and generalize better to unseen data, and tasks with abundant data implicitly regularize tasks with scarce data through shared knowledge. That last effect cuts against the user's small-dataset argument: a data-poor task can free-ride on a data-rich one in a joint model, which a standalone specialist cannot. It is observed directly in reasoning models: [Apriel](#c/c-apriel)'s report found that training on math improved coding. Whether two tasks help or hurt each other depends on whether they share underlying structure, and the effect is not symmetric ([transfer is asymmetric](#c/c-asymmetric-transfer)).

concepts.title: Transfer is asymmetric
concepts.summary: Some tasks help others and some hurt them: coding and math donate safely; factuality and fairness intrude.
concepts.overview: A late-2025 paper on cross-task transfer found that tasks play different roles rather than being simply compatible or conflicting. As donors, coding and math are "safe", with limited side effects, while factuality and fairness/bias are "intrusive": they improve their own scores but harm others.
