As recipients, coding is consistently receptive and math is brittle. The authors conclude that specializing on one task can create negative interference with other capabilities, a trade-off between peak performance on one metric and generalist competence. It refines the question of whether [specialists beat a generalist](#c/c-specialists-win): some skills transfer cleanly, some are one-way streets, some are destructive. The Sources treat it as one careful study's results, not established law.

concepts.title: Apriel
concepts.summary: An open reasoning model whose report found both task interference and math-to-code transfer, then merged specialists.
concepts.overview: Apriel is the open reasoning model whose report the Sources use to show both sides of the specialist question in practice. Its authors found negative interference from learning multiple tasks at once, and also beneficial cross-domain transfer: training on math improved coding ([positive transfer](#c/c-positive-transfer)). To balance the two, they trained specialized models that shared a common core of data but varied the domain-specific portions, then merged them by averaging their weights in specified proportions ([model merging](#c/c-model-merging)). Because open reports like this are readable, they are the main evidence that frontier labs likely grapple with the same tension, though closed recipes remain unknown.

concepts.title: Data mixing
concepts.summary: Controlling the proportions and order of tasks in training so they help rather than hurt each other.
concepts.overview: Rather than build separate models, most pipelines control what goes into one. Mixing means setting proportions: one documented three-stage pipeline filters tasks by output type to prevent interference, trains high-resource tasks to convergence first, then reintroduces all tasks with capped, temperature-scaled mixture weights so rare tasks do not dominate. Staging means setting order: sequential training allows task grouping and filtering that reduce conflicts, while replay buffers and distillation anchor earlier knowledge against [catastrophic forgetting](#c/c-catastrophic-forgetting). Getting the mix right is a large part of the craft of avoiding [negative transfer](#c/c-negative-transfer). The same problem appears in pre-training, where the art of a [corpus pipeline](#c/c-data-pipeline) is the proportions of web, code, papers and math.

concepts.title: Model merging
concepts.summary: Training specialist models separately and then averaging their weights into one generalist.
concepts.overview: Model merging is the hybrid that most directly vindicates the user's specialist intuition while still shipping a single model: specialize to avoid [negative transfer](#c/c-negative-transfer), then weight-merge to recover one generalist. [Apriel](#c/c-apriel) did exactly this, training specialists on a shared core of data with varying domain-specific portions and averaging their weights in specified proportions. It works surprisingly well; that averaging separately trained models works at all is non-obvious, and the Sources flag it as mechanically interesting without explaining why. It has become a real technique precisely because of the tension between specialists and generalists (see [do specialists beat a generalist?](#c/c-q-specialists)).

concepts.title: How much of open-model gains is distillation?
concepts.summary: Distillation built much 2023–24 open chat quality, but its share of reasoning gains is unmeasured.
concepts.overview: The user pressed the assistant on its remark that [distillation drives reasoning gains](#c/c-hyp-distillation-reasoning). The answer separates three claims. That [distilling closed models works](#c/c-distillation-works) is well established and even productized. That it is widespread in open models is strongly supported, especially for the 2023–24 wave ([early open models were distilled](#c/c-open-models-distilled)), and even Tülu 3's SFT responses come from closed models. That it explains a chunk of recent reasoning gains is where the assistant overreached: no reliable share exists, because labs do not disclose post-training data, using frontier outputs is often contractually prohibited, and evidence (models claiming to be ChatGPT, similar output distributions) is circumstantial. The best-documented case, [DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1), suggests [RL, not copying](#c/c-rl-built-r1), did the heavy lifting.

concepts.title: Distilling closed models works
concepts.summary: Training a smaller model on a stronger model's outputs is proven, productized and effective.
concepts.overview: With closed models you cannot see weights, hidden states or output distributions, so [distillation](#c/c-distillation) is output-based: generate a large set of the stronger model's responses and fine-tune a smaller model on them, essentially [SFT](#c/c-sft) on a better model's answers. It is not in doubt. OpenAI sells Model Distillation as a product, using outputs of GPT-4o and o1-preview to fine-tune GPT-4o mini for specific tasks. TinyGSM generated 12.3M synthetic math problems with GPT-3.5-turbo and got a 125M-parameter model to 63.1% pass@1 on grade-school math. Practitioners even report narrow-domain students beating GPT-4, a blog claim that holds only for specific tasks. It underpins much of open-model history ([early open models were distilled](#c/c-open-models-distilled)).

concepts.title: Early open models were distilled
concepts.summary: The 2023–24 open-model wave bootstrapped its chat quality on outputs from frontier closed models.
concepts.overview: For the instruction-following and chat behavior of the 2023–24 open models, much of the quality openly came from [distillation](#c/c-distillation). Alpaca was Llama fine-tuned on about 52K instructions generated by an OpenAI model. Open Orca contains GPT-4-distilled outputs, and ShareGPT consists of user-shared ChatGPT conversations, both standard fine-tuning sources. MagicCoder and CodeGemma also fine-tuned on data from larger models, and SPAN distilled GPT-4 agents' task-solving trajectories into specialized open models, extending the practice to tool use. This was the dominant bootstrapping method of that generation. It is solid evidence for the chat era but not a measurement of how much recent reasoning came from distillation (see [how much of open-model gains is distillation?](#c/c-q-distillation-share)).

concepts.title: RL, not copying, built R1
concepts.summary: The assistant's corrected view: in DeepSeek-R1, RL produced the reasoning and distillation then spread it downward.
concepts.overview: This is the retraction of the claim that [distillation drives reasoning gains](#c/c-hyp-distillation-reasoning). In the best-documented open reasoning case, [DeepSeek-R1](#c/c-deepseek-r1), the headline result was that [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) elicited reasoning largely without a distillation-from-frontier crutch: the "aha moment" emerged from RL on the base model. DeepSeek then distilled R1's reasoning into smaller models, but that is distilling its own model, not siphoning closed frontier intelligence. The restated position: distillation clearly can transfer reasoning and is heavily used to propagate it, but the idea that it secretly underlies headline open-model reasoning gains is a plausible suspicion that the evidence does not pin down. Accusations that specific labs distill competitors against terms of service surface periodically but rarely conclusively.

concepts.title: Training data
concepts.summary: What goes into pre-training and post-training datasets, how they are built, and how much work they are.
concepts.overview: Data is where much of the effort in building a model goes, and the part labs disclose least. Flagship corpora stay secret, for legal reasons (copyright and consent) as well as competitive ones, so what is known comes from deliberately open efforts. For pre-training, [open-data corpora](#c/c-open-data-corpora) such as [DCLM](#c/c-dclm) and FineWeb show a [corpus pipeline](#c/c-data-pipeline) of extraction, deduplication and [quality filtering](#c/c-quality-filtering) that [keeps the best 10%](#c/c-keep-best-10) of web text. For post-training, [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) documents [post-training data](#c/c-post-training-data): demonstrations, preferences and verifiable problems. The cross-cutting claims are that [data is the main lever](#c/c-data-is-the-lever) and that data work plausibly rivals or exceeds architecture work ([how much work is the data?](#c/c-q-corpus-effort)).

concepts.title: Beyond transformers
concepts.summary: Attempts to replace or simplify the transformer: state-space models, hybrids, byte-level, diffusion and latent-reasoning models.
concepts.overview: The standard LLM recipe (a [transformer](#c/c-transformer) with attention and FFN blocks, generating tokens left to right from a tokenizer) is still the frontier standard, but each of its assumptions is under attack. [Attention-free models](#c/c-attention-free) such as [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) replace attention with a fixed-size state; in practice [hybrids win](#c/c-hybrids-win), and they are [competitive at scale](#c/c-q-frontier-hybrids). The [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/c-blt) removes [tokenization](#c/c-tokenization). [Diffusion language models](#c/c-diffusion-lm) drop left-to-right generation. [Latent reasoning](#c/c-latent-reasoning) and concept models reason without emitting tokens. The recurring pattern is that alternatives are [absorbed, not replaced](#c/c-absorbed-not-replaced): the field keeps blends rather than switching wholesale. See [what other novel architectures are appearing?](#c/c-q-novel-architectures) for the ranking by maturity.

concepts.title: How much work is the data?
concepts.summary: No rigorous percentage exists, but data work plausibly rivals or exceeds architecture and training-code work.
concepts.overview: The user asked what share of research effort goes into managing the corpus. No rigorous figure exists: nobody has published a reliable cross-lab time-allocation study, and numbers like "80% of ML is data cleaning" are folklore repeated until they sound official. What the evidence does support, indirectly, is that the field reorganized around data ([data is the main lever](#c/c-data-is-the-lever)): DCLM is a whole benchmark in which only curation varies. For frontier pre-training, data work (sourcing, cleaning, dedup, filter design, mixing, decontamination, legal review) plausibly rivals or exceeds architecture and training-code work. The signal is stronger for post-training, where reports call dataset construction the hardest part and teams inherit canonical mixtures ([everyone reuses Tülu's mix](#c/c-data-reuse)). The direction is solid; the number, in the Sources' words, is vibes.

concepts.title: Open-data corpora
concepts.summary: Fully transparent pre-training corpora (Dolma, FineWeb, RefinedWeb, RedPajama, C4, DCLM) built from filtered web crawl.
concepts.overview: Flagship models, closed and open-weight alike, keep their training data secret; open-data corpora exist to reveal what a competitive corpus contains and how it is refined. Dolma was built under an open-data philosophy, with all sources public and an open license. The largest open corpora (C4, RefinedWeb, Dolma, RedPajama-V2, FineWeb, [DCLM](#c/c-dclm)) are all built from Common Crawl, a nonprofit public web archive, then refined through a [corpus pipeline](#c/c-data-pipeline). They do not say what any particular flagship was trained on, but they are benchmarked to rival closed corpora, so they are the main window into [training data](#c/c-training-data). Their headline lesson: [keep the best 10%](#c/c-keep-best-10).

concepts.title: DCLM
concepts.summary: A data-curation benchmark and corpus that holds the model fixed and varies only how data is filtered.
concepts.overview: DCLM (DataComp-LM) turns data curation into a competition: model architecture and training are fixed, and only the curation strategy varies, so the best dataset under equal compute wins. It provides a standardized 240-trillion-token pool extracted from Common Crawl. Its baseline recipe does paragraph-level deduplication and ranks documents with a fastText classifier trained on instruction-formatted samples and r/ExplainLikeImFive posts, keeping the top ~10% ([quality filtering](#c/c-quality-filtering)). DCLM-Baseline got a 7B model to 64% on MMLU with only 2.6T training tokens, and beat the prior open-data state of the art by about 6 MMLU points while using half the compute. That makes it the strongest evidence that [data is the main lever](#c/c-data-is-the-lever).

concepts.title: Keep the best 10%
concepts.summary: Modern corpus building throws away roughly 90% of web text because quality per token beats quantity.
concepts.overview: The dominant move in building a pre-training corpus is aggressive discarding. Projects like FineWeb-Edu and [DCLM](#c/c-dclm) drop the lowest-quality ~90% of their data to maximize average quality: start with hundreds of trillions of tokens and keep a small, high-quality slice. The reason is empirical. DCLM's central finding was that model-based [quality filtering](#c/c-quality-filtering) is key, and its filtered baseline let a 7B model reach 64% on MMLU with 2.6T tokens, competitive with runs using far more data. It is a concrete instance of [data is the main lever](#c/c-data-is-the-lever), and a reminder that the corpus is a heavily shaped artifact, not a neutral sample of the web.

concepts.title: Corpus pipeline
concepts.summary: The stages that turn raw web crawl into a training corpus: extraction, deduplication, filtering, mixing, decontamination.
concepts.overview: The open-data projects document a recognizable pipeline, each stage a research problem. Extraction and cleaning pull usable text from messy HTML, since much of Common Crawl is boilerplate, fragments and markup. Deduplication runs at several granularities (DCLM adds paragraph-level on top of document-level), because duplicates waste compute and can hurt quality. [Quality filtering](#c/c-quality-filtering), increasingly model-based, is where the real leverage is. Then comes mixing: filtered web crawl forms the backbone, layered with code, academic papers, books, Wikipedia, Q&A sites and math, and the art is in the proportions ([data mixing](#c/c-data-mixing)). [Decontamination](#c/c-decontamination) removes benchmark overlap. The Sources' estimate is that this whole pipeline plausibly rivals architecture work in effort ([how much work is the data?](#c/c-q-corpus-effort)).

concepts.title: Quality filtering
concepts.summary: Ranking documents with a small trained classifier and keeping only the top slice.
concepts.overview: Quality filtering is where most of the leverage in a [corpus pipeline](#c/c-data-pipeline) lies, and it is increasingly done by a model rather than by rules. [DCLM](#c/c-dclm) trains a small fastText classifier on examples of "good" text (instruction-formatted samples and r/ExplainLikeImFive posts), scores every document and keeps roughly the top 10% ([keep the best 10%](#c/c-keep-best-10)). That makes the choice of what counts as good a consequential design decision in its own right. It also leaves marks: web-filtered datasets carry measurable fingerprints that propagate through training, so curation choices imprint on the final model in identifiable ways.

concepts.title: Data is the main lever
concepts.summary: The field reorganized around data quality: better curation buys what would otherwise take much more compute.
concepts.overview: Data quality is now treated as a central axis of model performance. The strongest sign is [DCLM](#c/c-dclm) itself: a whole benchmark in which architecture and training are held fixed and only data curation varies. You do not build a competitive testbed around a variable unless that is where the action is. The results justify it: the same architecture on better-curated data gave multi-point benchmark gains, with DCLM-Baseline beating the prior open-data state of the art by about 6 MMLU points at half the compute. When curation buys what would otherwise take doubling compute, rational labs pour effort there, which is the basis for the Sources' estimate that data work plausibly rivals architecture work ([how much work is the data?](#c/c-q-corpus-effort)).

concepts.title: Tülu 3
concepts.summary: Ai2's fully open post-training recipe: weights, data, curation toolkit, training code and reproduction instructions.
concepts.overview: Tülu 3 is the main window into [post-training data](#c/c-post-training-data), because Ai2 open-sourced the entire recipe specifically to demystify what closed labs do. It is not a toy: the 405B version competes with GPT-4o-mini, Claude 3.5 Haiku and large open models like DeepSeek V3. Its documentation shows prompts drawn from annotators, real users and synthesis, with provenance analysis and [decontamination](#c/c-decontamination); SFT responses generated by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet ([open SFT answers come from closed models](#c/c-open-sft-from-closed)); a [preference data pipeline](#c/c-preference-pipeline) ranked by an LLM judge and used with [DPO](#c/c-dpo); and verifiable problems for RLVR. The 8B version used about 940K SFT samples and 250–300K preference pairs. Its mixture has become a common starting point ([everyone reuses Tülu's mix](#c/c-data-reuse)).

concepts.title: Post-training data
concepts.summary: Demonstrations for SFT, preference pairs for RLHF or DPO, and verifiable problems for RLVR.
concepts.overview: Far less is openly known about post-training data than about pre-training data; the best sources are a few deliberately open projects, above all [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3). The Qwen2 report states the core split: demonstration data (an instruction with a satisfactory response) for [SFT](#c/c-sft), and preference data (an instruction with a preferred and a dispreferred response) for [reward modeling](#c/c-reward-model), RLHF or DPO. A third, smaller kind is verifiable problems for RLVR ([RL data & curriculum](#c/c-rl-data-curriculum)). Prompts come from paid annotators, real user logs such as WildChat, and model synthesis, including persona-driven generation for diversity. The samples are few next to pre-training's trillions of tokens, but each is curated, generated or judged, so effort per example is far higher. Much of the documentation dates from late 2024 to early 2025, before the shift to heavier RL and agentic post-training.

concepts.title: Decontamination
concepts.summary: Removing training examples that overlap with benchmark test sets, so scores measure ability rather than memory.
concepts.overview: Decontamination means finding and removing training examples that overlap with the test sets of benchmarks the model will be evaluated on. Post-training data makes it a recurring obsession, because datasets assembled from public sources, user logs and synthesis can easily leak benchmark questions, which inflates scores without improving the model. [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) surveys available datasets, analyzes their provenance and decontaminates them; RLVR datasets are likewise curated with benchmark-leakage removal ([RL data & curriculum](#c/c-rl-data-curriculum)). It is the final stage of the [corpus pipeline](#c/c-data-pipeline), and the Sources describe contamination as the post-training analog of the pre-training quality problem.

concepts.title: Open SFT answers come from closed models
concepts.summary: Tülu 3's synthetic SFT responses were all written by GPT-4o or Claude 3.5 Sonnet.
concepts.overview: The [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) writeup states that all of its new synthetic SFT datasets contain responses created by GPT-4o or, for coding, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, because those gave the highest-quality responses. So even the flagship open post-training effort generates the answers its model imitates by calling closed frontier models: output-based [distillation](#c/c-distillation-works) baked into a documented recipe. It confirms the dependency behind the [distillation question](#c/c-hyp-distillation-reasoning) for chat and instruction quality. It also marks where open and frontier recipes diverge: closed labs cannot distill from anything above their own frontier, so their SFT responses come from human experts and their own models, and they rely more on paid expert annotation.

concepts.title: Preference data pipeline
concepts.summary: Tülu 3's three steps: pick prompts, generate responses from a pool of models, rank them with an LLM judge.
concepts.overview: Preference data is more mechanized than one might expect. [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) documents three stages. First, select prompts. Second, generate candidate responses from several models picked at random from a pool, including the model being trained, so some data is "on-policy". Third, rank the candidates with an [LLM-as-a-judge](#c/c-llm-as-judge) to form (preferred, rejected) pairs. These were tested rather than assumed: including on-policy data beat purely off-policy data, scaling the number of unique prompts helped, and using new prompts rather than reusing SFT prompts helped. The resulting pairs feed [DPO](#c/c-dpo) or a [reward model](#c/c-reward-model); the 8B Tülu used about 250–300K of them.

concepts.title: LLM-as-a-judge
concepts.summary: Using a language model instead of a human to decide which of two responses is better.
concepts.overview: Classic [RLHF](#c/c-rlhf) used human annotators to pick the better response; open pipelines now lean heavily on a model to do it, because that scales. In [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3)'s [preference data pipeline](#c/c-preference-pipeline), an LLM judge ranks candidate responses into preferred and rejected pairs. Humans have not vanished: Qwen2 describes a hybrid of collaborative human annotation and automated synthesis, with humans producing target responses and their positive and negative counterparts. The current reality is a blend sliding toward automation, with humans concentrated where judgment is hardest. How much human judgment remains in frontier preference data is not well disclosed, and how reliable LLM judges are is flagged as a thread worth pulling, since the whole pipeline now leans on it.

concepts.title: Everyone reuses Tülu's mix
concepts.summary: Building post-training data is the hard part, so teams inherit canonical mixtures like Tülu's rather than build their own.
concepts.overview: Post-training reports converge on dataset construction as the hard part. Motif's report calls building the training dataset one of the most challenging tasks of post-training. The revealing tell is that most projects do not build from scratch: Motif used existing curated mixtures from Tülu and Granite, and Moxin used the [Tülu 3](#c/c-tulu-3) SFT mixture of 939,344 samples drawn from datasets including CoCoNot, FLAN v2 and WildChat-GPT-4. When the field's standard move is to reuse a few canonical mixtures, assembling a good one is evidently expensive enough that capable teams would rather inherit it. That is strong indirect evidence that data work, not training code, is the bottleneck ([how much work is the data?](#c/c-q-corpus-effort)).

concepts.title: Can a simpler network match transformers?
concepts.summary: At small-to-mid scale simpler attention-free networks match transformers; at the frontier, hybrids that keep some attention win.
concepts.overview: The user asked whether anyone has simplified transformer wiring while keeping quality. There are three readings. The conservative one keeps the transformer but makes most attention cheap ([linear attention](#c/c-linear-attention)), which is cheaper wiring rather than simpler. The substantive one replaces attention entirely: [attention-free models](#c/c-attention-free), with [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) as the flagship, which drops both attention and MLP blocks for one repeated block and matched a strong Transformer++ recipe from about 125M to 1.3B parameters. At the frontier, though, no pure attention-free model has displaced transformers, because a [fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets). What is emerging instead is that [hybrids win](#c/c-hybrids-win): a minority of attention layers returns, trading some simplicity back for precise recall.

concepts.title: Attention-free models
concepts.summary: Models that replace attention with a fixed-size state updated per token, such as RWKV, RetNet, H3 and Mamba.
concepts.overview: Attention-free models avoid computing the quadratic [attention](#c/c-attention) matrix altogether. Instead of every token looking at every other token, they carry a fixed-size hidden state updated as they read, like a recurrent network. That gives O(1) memory per token, no [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) growing with sequence length, and inference as a single recurrent update. The family splits into recurrent designs (RWKV, RetNet) and state-space models (H3, [Mamba](#c/c-mamba), with Hyena in the broader family). They match transformers at small-to-mid scale, but the fixed state is a lossy summary ([fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets)), so frontier practice keeps some attention: [hybrids win](#c/c-hybrids-win).
concepts.article:
## What do they replace?

In a transformer, attention lets each token compare itself with every earlier token. That all-pairs interaction is what makes cost grow quadratically with sequence length, and it is why a [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) must store keys and values for every previous token. Attention-free models drop it. They maintain a fixed-size hidden state that is updated as the sequence is read, a return to the recurrent-network structure with new tricks. Memory per token is constant, and generating the next token is a single state update. For the user's question about simpler wiring, this is the real topological change: no all-pairs token interaction, just a state vector rolling forward.

## What kinds are there?

A survey sorts them into two groups: those that replace attention with recurrent computation, such as RWKV and RetNet, and those that use state-space representations, such as H3 and [Mamba](#c/c-mamba); Hyena belongs to the broader family. Mamba is the standout and the most aggressive simplifier, removing the MLP blocks as well as attention and stacking one homogeneous selective state-space block.

## How good are they?

At the scales tested, comparable to transformers. Mamba was the first attention-free model to match a strong standard Transformer recipe (Transformer++) across roughly 125M to 1.3B parameters, particularly as sequence length grows. These claims come largely from the architectures' own papers and efficiency surveys, which lean optimistic. The small-scale matching is well replicated, but frontier models are more than 100× larger, and no pure attention-free model has displaced transformers there.

## What is the catch?

The capability cost is structural. A fixed-size state is a lossy summary of everything seen so far, while attention keeps every token available to look back at. So attention-free models are characteristically weaker at precisely recalling an arbitrary earlier detail, and earlier SSMs struggled with discrete, content-rich data like text. Mamba's "selective" design, which makes the state-space parameters depend on the input so the model can choose what to keep or forget, was built to address this, but the bottleneck remains fundamental ([fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets)).

## Where did the idea end up?

In hybrids. The field has largely concluded it wants both: keep a minority of attention layers for precise recall and make most layers cheap state-space or linear layers ([hybrids win](#c/c-hybrids-win)). Jamba, Nemotron-H and Granite 4.0 ship this design at large scale ([are hybrids competitive at scale?](#c/c-q-frontier-hybrids)). The Sources read this as one more case of alternatives being [absorbed rather than replacing](#c/c-absorbed-not-replaced) the transformer.

concepts.title: Mamba
concepts.summary: A selective state-space model that stacks one simple block, with no attention or MLP, and scales linearly.
concepts.overview: Mamba is the standout [attention-free model](#c/c-attention-free) and the most aggressive simplifier of the transformer. A transformer block is attention plus an FFN; Mamba throws out both and stacks one homogeneous selective state-space block, carrying a fixed-size state instead of a growing [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache). Its authors report about 5× higher inference throughput than transformers and linear scaling in sequence length, and it was the first attention-free model to match a strong Transformer++ recipe, from about 125M to 1.3B parameters. The "selective" part, making the state-space parameters depend on the input, lets it choose what to keep or forget, fixing earlier SSMs' weakness with text. It still pays the cost that a [fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets), so at scale it lives inside [hybrids](#c/c-hybrids-win) such as [Jamba](#c/c-jamba), [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h) and [Granite 4.0](#c/c-granite-4).
concepts.article:
## How is it built?

Recall that a transformer [layer](#c/c-layers) is attention followed by a feed-forward (MLP) block. Mamba's authors integrate selective state-space layers into a simplified end-to-end architecture with neither attention nor MLP blocks. The network is one block type, a selective SSM, stacked repeatedly. Each block updates a fixed-size hidden state as it reads the sequence, so there are no attention heads, no separate feed-forward layers, and no KV cache that grows with context. That is exactly the "much simpler wiring" the user asked about.

## What does "selective" mean?

Earlier state-space models used fixed dynamics, which made them weak at content-based reasoning over discrete, content-rich data like text. Mamba makes the SSM's parameters functions of the input, so for each token the model can selectively propagate or forget information depending on what that token is. That is the innovation that made state-space models competitive on language.

## How good is it?

The authors report about 5× higher inference throughput than transformers and linear scaling in sequence length. On quality, Mamba was the first attention-free model to match a very strong standard Transformer recipe (Transformer++) across models from roughly 125M to 1.3B parameters, particularly as sequences get longer, and at those scales it matched or beat equal-sized transformers on downstream tasks. That is a real existence proof that a structurally simpler network can match transformer quality.

## What are its limits?

The clean comparisons are at 1.3B parameters or less; frontier models are more than 100× larger, and pure Mamba models have not clearly matched the best transformers there. The fixed-size state is a lossy summary, so precise recall of arbitrary earlier details is weaker than with attention ([fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets)). At scale these weaknesses show up in reasoning and code: [Jamba](#c/c-jamba) exhibits known SSM weaknesses there. And a 2026 paper found Mamba components bring a robustness vulnerability into hybrids ([hidden-state poisoning](#c/c-hidden-state-poisoning)).

## Where is it used?

Mostly as the cheap majority inside hybrids. [Jamba](#c/c-jamba) uses Mamba in 7/8 of its layers; [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h) swapped most attention layers for Mamba blocks; [Granite 4.0](#c/c-granite-4) is an enterprise Mamba hybrid. Jamba's ablations put the sweet spot at [about one attention layer in six](#c/c-attention-ratio) (see [hybrids win in practice](#c/c-hybrids-win)).

concepts.title: Fixed state forgets details
concepts.summary: A fixed-size state is a lossy summary, so attention-free models are weaker at recalling exact earlier details.
concepts.overview: This is the fundamental cost of the [attention-free](#c/c-attention-free) simplification. Attention keeps every earlier token available to look back at; a fixed-size state compresses everything seen so far into a vector of constant size, which cannot losslessly remember an arbitrarily long past. So these models are characteristically weaker at precise recall, questions like "what exactly did the token 4,000 positions back say." [Mamba](#c/c-mamba)'s selective mechanism mitigates this but cannot remove it. At scale it shows up as weaker reasoning and code generation, for example in [Jamba](#c/c-jamba). It is why the field reintroduces a minority of attention layers, and why [hybrids win](#c/c-hybrids-win).

concepts.title: Hybrids win in practice
concepts.summary: Keep a few attention layers, make the rest cheap SSM or linear layers: more efficiency at comparable quality.
concepts.overview: The field's answer to whether transformers can be simplified is a blend: keep a few attention layers for precise recall and make most layers cheap [state-space](#c/c-attention-free) or [linear-attention](#c/c-linear-attention) layers for efficiency. It is a Pareto win, with better throughput and memory at comparable quality, not a strict capability win. Jamba's ablations put the sweet spot at [about one attention layer in six](#c/c-attention-ratio), and [Jamba](#c/c-jamba), [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h), [Granite 4.0](#c/c-granite-4) and [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear) all follow the pattern. Deficits remain in reasoning and code, and [hidden-state poisoning](#c/c-hidden-state-poisoning) is a newly reported risk. The top closed models remain predominantly transformers as far as is public. Hybrids are the clearest case of alternatives being [absorbed, not replaced](#c/c-absorbed-not-replaced).
concepts.article:
## What is the claim?

Pure simplification gives up just enough capability that the frontier prefers a hybrid. Keep a minority of full-attention layers, which preserve the ability to look up any earlier token precisely, and make the majority cheap [state-space](#c/c-attention-free) or [linear](#c/c-linear-attention) layers, which run with fixed memory per token. The result is less topologically simple than either pure option, but it captures most of the efficiency with most of the quality. The last increment of quality seems to need some of the complex wiring back.

## Why not go all the way?

Because a [fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets). Attention-free models match transformers at small-to-mid scale, but their compressed state is weaker at precise recall of arbitrary earlier content. A few attention layers restore that ability at modest cost.

## How much attention is enough?

Jamba's ablations answered this quantitatively: moving toward more transformer layers (up to 1:1) generally improves benchmark quality but costs efficiency and throughput, while more Mamba layers improve efficiency. A ratio of 1 attention layer to 5–7 Mamba layers sat at the sweet spot of the Pareto frontier ([about one attention layer in six](#c/c-attention-ratio)). [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear), using linear attention instead of Mamba, keeps full attention in one layer in four.

## Who ships it?

Several well-resourced players: AI21's [Jamba](#c/c-jamba), up to 398B parameters with Mamba in 7/8 of layers; NVIDIA's [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h) at 8B and 56B; IBM's [Granite 4.0](#c/c-granite-4), whose small hybrid beat all open models except a 12× larger one on HELM IFEval; and Tencent's Hunyuan-TurboS. They publish open weights and competitive scores (see [are hybrids competitive at scale?](#c/c-q-frontier-hybrids)).

## What are the caveats?

Comparable quality is real on average but not uniform. Jamba shows known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code generation, the precise-recall tasks where compressed state struggles. A 2026 paper found hybrids inherit a robustness weakness from their Mamba components ([hidden-state poisoning](#c/c-hidden-state-poisoning)), though that is one paper. Several of the strongest comparisons are vendor-reported and favorably selected ([vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)). And none of these is the overall frontier leader; the very top models remain predominantly transformer-based as far as is publicly known.

concepts.title: Are hybrids competitive at scale?
concepts.summary: Yes: Jamba, Nemotron-H, Granite 4.0 and Hunyuan-TurboS ship large hybrids with competitive published scores.
concepts.overview: Hybrid models have moved past research demos into shipped, frontier-relevant families with open weights and published numbers. AI21's [Jamba](#c/c-jamba) scales to 398B parameters and roughly matched Mixtral and Llama-2 70B on common-sense tasks. NVIDIA's [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h) (8B, 56B) claims state-of-the-art capability with faster inference. IBM's [Granite 4.0](#c/c-granite-4) beat every open model but one on HELM IFEval while using much less GPU memory. Tencent's Hunyuan-TurboS rounds out the set. The design converged on [about one attention layer in six](#c/c-attention-ratio). The caveats: deficits in reasoning and code, a newly reported [hidden-state poisoning](#c/c-hidden-state-poisoning) weakness, vendor-selected benchmarks, and none of these leads the overall frontier. It is a Pareto win ([hybrids win in practice](#c/c-hybrids-win)), not a strict capability win.

concepts.title: Jamba
concepts.summary: AI21's Mamba–Transformer hybrid family, up to 398B parameters with Mamba in 7/8 of its layers.
concepts.overview: Jamba is the largest and longest-running Mamba-based hybrid family, scaling up to 398B parameters with [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) blocks making up 7/8 of the architecture. Its paper's scores put it among strong transformers of its era: on common-sense and reading tasks it roughly matched or beat Mixtral and Llama-2 70B (HellaSwag ~87, WinoGrande ~82.5, PIQA ~83), comparable quality demonstrated well beyond 1.3B. Its ablations supplied the field's rule of thumb, [about one attention layer in six](#c/c-attention-ratio). It also shows the limits: known SSM weaknesses in reasoning and code generation ([fixed state forgets details](#c/c-fixed-state-forgets)), and a 2026 paper found Jamba-1.7-Mini (52B) collapses under [hidden-state poisoning](#c/c-hidden-state-poisoning) triggers where pure transformers do not.

concepts.title: Nemotron-H
concepts.summary: NVIDIA's hybrid family (8B and 56B) that swapped most attention layers for Mamba blocks.
concepts.overview: Nemotron-H is NVIDIA's entry among [frontier-scale hybrids](#c/c-q-frontier-hybrids), and the one with the cleanest efficiency-at-quality claim. It replaced most attention layers with [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) blocks to boost throughput. NVIDIA's framing is that the family shows hybrid models can be state of the art in capabilities while offering faster inference, scaling to 56B (with an 8B sibling) and post-trainable to strong instruction-following and long-context results. That it went through real post-training, rather than only base-model benchmarks, is the notable part. The "state of the art" wording is NVIDIA's own ([vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)), and Mamba-2-based hybrids like Nemotron share the [hidden-state poisoning](#c/c-hidden-state-poisoning) weakness reported in 2026.

concepts.title: Granite 4.0
concepts.summary: IBM's late-2025 enterprise Mamba hybrid, competitive with far larger models at much lower memory use.
concepts.overview: Granite 4.0 is the most telling of the [hybrids](#c/c-q-frontier-hybrids) because it is recent, enterprise-shipped, and makes a size-efficiency claim. IBM reports that Granite-4.0-H-Small outperformed every open-weight model on Stanford HELM's IFEval instruction-following benchmark except Meta's [Llama 4](#c/c-llama-4) Maverick, a 402B-parameter model more than twelve times its size. On the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard v3 it keeps pace with much larger open and closed models at a low price point, and a defining feature is significantly reduced GPU memory use, the fixed-state benefit of [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) in a product. It is the strongest practical support for [hybrids win in practice](#c/c-hybrids-win), with the caveat that these are vendor-selected benchmarks where it looks especially good ([vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)).

concepts.title: About 1 attention layer in 6
concepts.summary: Jamba's ablations found about one attention layer per five to seven Mamba layers to be the sweet spot.
concepts.overview: How much attention does a hybrid actually need? [Jamba](#c/c-jamba)'s ablations gave a quantitative answer. Increasing the share of transformer layers, up to 1:1, generally improved benchmark quality but cost efficiency and throughput; more [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) layers improved efficiency. A ratio of 1:5 to 1:7 attention-to-Mamba layers was the sweet spot on the Pareto frontier, roughly one attention layer in six. The frontier hybrids cluster around keeping this small minority of attention, confirming that the precise-recall ability attention provides is worth a little of its cost ([hybrids win in practice](#c/c-hybrids-win)). [Kimi Linear](#c/c-kimi-linear), with linear rather than Mamba layers, keeps one full-attention layer in four.

concepts.title: Hidden-state poisoning
concepts.summary: A 2026 paper found Mamba-based hybrids collapse under hidden-state poisoning triggers where pure transformers do not.
concepts.overview: A 2026 security paper reported that hybrids inherit a novel robustness vulnerability from their [Mamba](#c/c-mamba) components. Under certain hidden-state-poisoning triggers, even the 52B Jamba-1.7-Mini hybrid collapsed on a robustness benchmark, whereas pure transformers did not, and the weakness extends to Mamba-2-based hybrids such as [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h). It suggests that the architectural simplification may carry security trade-offs that capability benchmarks do not reveal. The Sources hold it loosely: early research, one paper, one attack class. It is something to watch rather than a settled verdict against [hybrids](#c/c-hybrids-win).

concepts.title: What other novel architectures are appearing?
concepts.summary: Sorted by the assumption they attack: byte-level and SSM hybrids are validated; diffusion is credible; concept models are speculative.
concepts.overview: Beyond state-space hybrids, the useful way to organize new architectures is by which assumption of the standard LLM they attack. Tokenization: the [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/c-blt) learns from raw bytes and matched Llama 3 up to 8B. Left-to-right generation: [diffusion language models](#c/c-diffusion-lm) denoise whole sequences in parallel. The token output interface: Meta's Large Concept Model reasons over sentence-level concept embeddings, and [latent reasoning](#c/c-latent-reasoning) models think in internal space. The next-token objective: [multi-token prediction](#c/c-mtp) as the primary objective. By maturity, byte-level models and [SSM hybrids](#c/c-hybrids-win) are most validated; diffusion and MTP-as-primary are credible but unproven at the frontier; concept and latent-reasoning models are speculative. Many results are self-reported, and the assistant bets on [absorption over replacement](#c/c-absorbed-not-replaced).

concepts.title: Byte Latent Transformer
concepts.summary: Meta's tokenizer-free model: small byte encoder and decoder around a large transformer working on variable-length byte patches.
concepts.overview: The Byte Latent Transformer attacks an assumption taken for granted everywhere else in this Expedition: that text is chopped into tokens first ([tokenization](#c/c-tokenization)). It learns directly from raw bytes. To avoid the longer sequences bytes would create, it groups bytes into variable-length patches by entropy: easy, predictable stretches such as the ends of words get long patches, so compute is spent where prediction is hard, echoing MoE's dynamic compute allocation. Structurally, a small byte encoder bundles bytes into patches, a large latent transformer works on the patches, and a small decoder expands back to bytes. Meta reports parity with Llama 3 from 1B to 8B, and it decouples model size from sequence length. It is among the [most validated](#c/c-q-novel-architectures) alternatives, though its results are self-reported and at tested scales.

concepts.title: Tokenization
concepts.summary: Splitting text into subword tokens before the model sees it; a flawed tokenizer distorts the input.
concepts.overview: Standard LLMs never see characters: a tokenizer first chops text into subword tokens, and the model predicts tokens. That step can distort the input before any reasoning begins, so however capable the architecture, it works with a corrupted signal. The famous symptom is models failing to count the letters in a word, a tokenization artifact rather than a reasoning failure; byte-level models score near-perfectly on spelling tasks for this reason. The [Byte Latent Transformer](#c/c-blt) removes the tokenizer entirely, and newer work distills existing token-trained models into byte models, retaining over 90% of the teacher's performance with a roughly 2–3 point MMLU drop, or "byteifies" models to beat subword models on code and character tasks.

concepts.title: Diffusion language models
concepts.summary: Language models that generate a whole sequence in parallel by iteratively denoising it, instead of left to right.
concepts.overview: Standard LLMs are autoregressive: one token at a time, left to right. Diffusion language models borrow from image generation instead: start from noisy or masked text and refine the whole sequence over several steps, using bidirectional attention since each position refines a full draft. The appeal is parallelism, which breaks the one-token-at-a-time latency bottleneck and could make long reasoning chains cheap ([diffusion makes reasoning cheap](#c/c-diffusion-cheap-reasoning)). Text is discrete, which makes the math harder, and bidirectionality complicates [KV caching](#c/c-kv-cache). The assistant first called them unproven at scale, then corrected itself: by early 2026 [Mercury](#c/c-mercury) and [Gemini Diffusion](#c/c-gemini-diffusion) had shipped with coding parity at 5–10× speed. Most are [converted from autoregressive models](#c/c-ar-to-diffusion) and use [block diffusion](#c/c-block-diffusion); a ["no free lunch"](#c/c-no-free-lunch) critique contests the gains.
concepts.article:
## How do they generate text?

An autoregressive model extends a prefix one token at a time, each token waiting for the one before. A diffusion LM starts from noise or masked text covering the whole output and progressively denoises it toward coherent text over a number of refinement steps, the way image diffusion models work. Because the model refines a full draft rather than extending a prefix, it uses bidirectional attention: every position can see both directions. The whole block is filled in at once.

## Why is it hard for text?

Text is discrete, and diffusion was developed for continuous data like images, so the math is less natural. Research has tried several routes, such as Energy-Based Diffusion Language Models (ICLR 2025) and BitLM, which diffuses in a continuous or bitwise space. There are practical problems too: generating a fixed-size block makes variable-length output and exact stopping awkward, and bidirectional attention does not fit the [KV cache](#c/c-kv-cache) trick autoregressive serving relies on. Work such as Fast-dLLM and approximate KV caching retrofits caching onto diffusion.

## What changed in the assistant's view?

Two turns earlier the assistant described diffusion LMs as a real research area that had not matched top autoregressive models at frontier scale: promising, with intriguing speed. After searching, it revised that: as of early 2026, diffusion LMs had moved from research papers to deployed products. Inception Labs' [Mercury](#c/c-mercury) was the first commercial dLLM, and Google's [Gemini Diffusion](#c/c-gemini-diffusion) matched its autoregressive sibling on coding benchmarks at about 5× the speed. Much of this post-dates the assistant's January 2026 cutoff, so it reports vendor and secondary sources rather than settled knowledge (see [what's the latest on diffusion LMs?](#c/c-q-diffusion-latest)).

## How are they built?

Mostly by conversion. LLaDA showed dLLMs can be trained from scratch, DiffuLLaMA that autoregressive models can be converted, Dream 7B that AR initialization plus targeted training gives the strongest open models, and LLaDA 2.0 that 100B scale is feasible. The dominant approach now starts from a pre-trained autoregressive model and continues training with the diffusion objective ([converting AR models to diffusion](#c/c-ar-to-diffusion)). Production designs have converged on [block diffusion](#c/c-block-diffusion): autoregressive across blocks of about 32 tokens, diffusion within each, a blend rather than pure diffusion.

## Why could it matter for reasoning?

The dominant capability paradigm is long chains of thought ([test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute)), and those are exactly what hurts autoregressive latency, because every reasoning token is sequential. If diffusion can fill reasoning traces in parallel, it attacks the cost structure of reasoning specifically, a more strategically interesting claim than raw throughput ([diffusion makes reasoning cheap](#c/c-diffusion-cheap-reasoning)).

## How much should we believe?

The quality-parity evidence is narrow (coding and math, structured domains) and self-reported by vendors, and none of these models claims to be the best overall; they compete on speed at comparable quality, like the Mamba hybrids. A May 2026 survey pointedly titled "No Free Lunch" argues the speedups carry trade-offs that headline tokens-per-second figures hide ([no free lunch for diffusion](#c/c-no-free-lunch)). The Sources' verdict: real, accelerating and no longer dismissible, but not a confirmed transformer-killer.

concepts.title: What's the latest on diffusion LMs?
concepts.summary: Diffusion LMs shipped by early 2026 with coding parity at 5–10× speed; general parity remains thin and contested.
concepts.overview: The user asked for a deeper dig after the assistant's cautious first take on [diffusion LMs](#c/c-diffusion-lm), and the picture had changed. By early 2026 dLLMs had crossed into production: [Mercury](#c/c-mercury) was the first commercial one and [Gemini Diffusion](#c/c-gemini-diffusion) matched its autoregressive sibling on coding at about 5× the speed. The most interesting angle is that [diffusion makes reasoning cheap](#c/c-diffusion-cheap-reasoning). Building them matured into [conversion from AR models](#c/c-ar-to-diffusion), and production converged on [block diffusion](#c/c-block-diffusion), again a blend. The caveats are serious: parity evidence is narrow, in coding and math, and vendor-reported; a ["no free lunch"](#c/c-no-free-lunch) survey contests the speed story; and several key items postdate the assistant's cutoff, with some low-quality sources in the mix.

concepts.title: Mercury
concepts.summary: Inception Labs' diffusion LMs: Mercury Coder, the first commercial dLLM, and the reasoning-capable Mercury 2.
concepts.overview: Mercury was first to market with a commercial [diffusion LM](#c/c-diffusion-lm). Mercury Coder launched in February 2025; Mercury Coder Mini reached 1,109 tokens/s and Mercury Coder Small 737 tokens/s on H100s, 5–10× faster than comparable autoregressive models, and Mercury Coder Mini (1.3B) is released under Apache 2.0. Mercury 2 (February 2026) is reasoning-capable, reaching 1,009 tokens/s on a single Blackwell GPU, over 5× faster than Claude 4.5 Haiku Reasoning and GPT-5 Mini, with AIME 2025 91.1, LiveCodeBench 67.3, GPQA 73.6 and SciCode 38.4, solid but not frontier-leading. It is the showcase for [diffusion makes reasoning cheap](#c/c-diffusion-cheap-reasoning). All these figures are vendor-reported and postdate the assistant's cutoff ([vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)).

concepts.title: Gemini Diffusion
concepts.summary: Google's diffusion language model, announced May 2025, matching its autoregressive sibling on coding at about 5× the speed.
concepts.overview: Gemini Diffusion, announced at Google I/O in May 2025, is the sign that a frontier lab takes [diffusion LMs](#c/c-diffusion-lm) seriously. It generates at 1,479 tokens/s, about 5× faster than Gemini 2.0 Flash Lite, and on coding benchmarks it matches its autoregressive counterpart: HumanEval 89.6% vs 90.2%, MBPP 76.0% vs 75.8%. The Sources call that near-parity against its own AR sibling the single most important data point for whether diffusion can reach comparable quality: yes, at least in coding, for this model. The numbers are Google's own and cover a structured domain, so general parity is not established ([no free lunch for diffusion](#c/c-no-free-lunch), [vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)).

concepts.title: Diffusion makes reasoning cheap
concepts.summary: Diffusion can fill long chain-of-thought traces in parallel, attacking the main cost of today's reasoning models.
concepts.overview: This is the claim that makes [diffusion LMs](#c/c-diffusion-lm) more than a speed gimmick. The dominant capability paradigm is long reasoning chains, trained by [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) and spent as [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute), and those are exactly what hurts autoregressive latency, since every reasoning token is generated in sequence. If diffusion can generate those traces in parallel, it attacks the cost structure of reasoning itself. [Mercury](#c/c-mercury) is presented as demonstrating it, with Mercury 2 running a reasoning-capable model at over 1,000 tokens/s. The claim comes from vendor material, and the ["no free lunch"](#c/c-no-free-lunch) survey argues the speedups carry trade-offs that headline numbers hide.

concepts.title: Converting AR models to diffusion
concepts.summary: Building a diffusion LM by starting from a pre-trained autoregressive model and continuing with the diffusion objective.
concepts.overview: The training story for [diffusion LMs](#c/c-diffusion-lm) matured into mostly conversion rather than training from scratch. The lineage the Sources give: LLaDA proved dLLMs can be trained from scratch; DiffuLLaMA proved autoregressive models can be converted; Dream 7B showed AR initialization plus targeted training produces the strongest open models; LLaDA 2.0 demonstrated feasibility at 100B scale; Mercury and Gemini Diffusion proved production viability. The dominant approach now initializes from an existing autoregressive transformer and continues training with the diffusion objective, which is more compute-efficient and competitive. Because anyone can convert an existing transformer, the cost of entry dropped sharply, explaining the recent proliferation, including open-weight releases such as LLaDA 8B Instruct under MIT.

concepts.title: Block diffusion
concepts.summary: Autoregressive across blocks, diffusion within each block; the production standard for diffusion LMs.
concepts.overview: Block diffusion splits output into compact blocks, typically 32 tokens, generates the blocks left to right, and uses diffusion to fill each block in parallel. It has emerged as the standard for production [diffusion LMs](#c/c-diffusion-lm). That makes it a hybrid, autoregressive across blocks and diffusion within them, and the Sources draw the parallel to Mamba hybrids keeping some attention: the practical answer is again a blend rather than a pure alternative. It is one of the examples behind [absorbed, not replaced](#c/c-absorbed-not-replaced).

concepts.title: No free lunch for diffusion
concepts.summary: A May 2026 survey arguing diffusion LMs' speedups carry trade-offs that headline tokens-per-second figures hide.
concepts.overview: A May 2026 paper, "A Comparative Survey of Inference Acceleration for DLLMs against AR-LLMs: No Free Lunch," is the counterweight to the vendor case for [diffusion LMs](#c/c-diffusion-lm). Its title signals that the parallel-generation speedup is not free: the quality, speed and compute triangle has costs that careful comparison exposes. The assistant had not read it, so its contents are inferred from the title and context. It sits alongside other reasons for caution: parity evidence is narrow (coding and math), vendor-reported, and none of the models claims to be best overall. The Sources suggest it is the most intellectually honest next stop for checking [diffusion makes reasoning cheap](#c/c-diffusion-cheap-reasoning).

concepts.title: Latent reasoning
concepts.summary: Reasoning inside the model's internal representations instead of in emitted chain-of-thought tokens.
concepts.overview: Today's reasoning models think out loud: [RLVR](#c/c-rlvr) trains them to emit long chains of thought, spending [test-time compute](#c/c-test-time-compute) as generated tokens. Latent reasoning, or recurrent-depth models, moves the thinking inside: the model reasons in its internal latent space, sometimes by looping a block of layers a variable number of times to "think longer" without producing text. It connects to the [looped depth](#c/c-looped-depth) idea from the discussion of layers, and sits beside Meta's Large Concept Model, which reasons over sentence-level concept embeddings rather than tokens. The Sources class the whole category as promising but early and genuinely speculative: an interesting direction with no frontier-scale model yet shown to match transformers ([what other novel architectures are appearing?](#c/c-q-novel-architectures)).

concepts.title: Absorbed, not replaced
concepts.summary: Transformer alternatives tend to be partly absorbed into blends rather than replacing the transformer outright.
concepts.overview: Across the new-architecture threads a pattern recurs: challengers to the [transformer](#c/c-transformer) get partly absorbed rather than taking over. [Hybrids](#c/c-hybrids-win) keep a minority of attention layers among state-space layers; [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) became standard inside transformers; [block diffusion](#c/c-block-diffusion) mixes autoregressive generation across blocks with diffusion within them. So the assistant declined to name any alternative a transformer "successor" and bet on absorption over replacement. It labels this explicitly as a judgment call, not a fact, drawn from the historical pattern. It frames how to read [beyond transformers](#c/c-new-architectures): expect blends.

concepts.title: Zhipu (Z.ai)
concepts.summary: The Chinese AI lab, also known as Z.ai, behind the GLM family of open-weight models.
concepts.overview: Zhipu, branded Z.ai, is the Chinese lab behind the GLM models, from [GLM-4.5](#c/c-glm-45) through [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5), [GLM-5.1](#c/c-glm-51) and [GLM-5.2](#c/c-glm-52), which iterated extraordinarily fast through early 2026. It is on the US Entity List, which makes the reported training of GLM-5 on Huawei Ascend chips without NVIDIA hardware geopolitically notable. Its stock surged as much as 48% as GLM-5.2's open-source rollout coincided with a [US order suspending top American models abroad](#c/c-us-model-suspension). Nearly all its headline benchmark claims are self-reported, which is why its launches come with the caution that [vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks).

concepts.title: GLM-4.5
concepts.summary: Zhipu's 2025 mixture-of-experts model: 355B total parameters, 32B active, with a shared expert.
concepts.overview: GLM-4.5 is the predecessor that [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) scaled up from. It is a [mixture of experts](#c/c-moe) model with 355B total parameters and 32B active per token. It kept an always-on [shared expert](#c/c-shared-experts), like DeepSeek-V3 and Kimi K2, which put it on one side of an unsettled MoE design question after [Qwen3](#c/c-qwen3) dropped the shared expert. Its successors followed quickly: GLM-4.6 in September 2025, then 4.7, and GLM-5 in February 2026.

concepts.title: GLM-5
concepts.summary: Zhipu's February 2026 flagship: a 744B-parameter MoE with DeepSeek Sparse Attention and a published technical report.

attributes.signature: Imports DeepSeek's DSA (config 'glm_moe_dsa'); cut to 80 layers to reduce expert communication; slime async RL for agentic training. GLM-5.1 keeps this base; GLM-5.2 adds a 1M context and High/Max reasoning presets, with its architecture unpublished.

concepts.overview: GLM-5 is the substantive GLM flagship, the one with a real technical report. It scales [GLM-4.5](#c/c-glm-45)'s design to 744B total and about 40B active parameters, with 256 [experts](#c/c-experts) (8 active), trained on 28.5T tokens, 200K input context, MIT-licensed open weights. Three construction choices stand out: it imports [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/c-dsa) wholesale (config `glm_moe_dsa`), showing [techniques spread fast](#c/c-techniques-spread-fast); it cuts its layer count to 80 to reduce expert-parallel communication; and its headline engineering is [slime](#c/c-slime), asynchronous RL infrastructure for [agentic RL](#c/c-agentic-rl), which supports [quality moved to post-training](#c/c-quality-moved-to-post-training). It reportedly trained on 100,000 Huawei Ascend 910B chips, initially unconfirmed. Its 77.8% SWE-bench Verified is self-reported and trails Opus 4.6 by about 3 points: competitive, not dominant.

concepts.title: Techniques spread fast
concepts.summary: New techniques move between labs within months, as DeepSeek Sparse Attention did into GLM-5.
concepts.overview: The clearest illustration is [DeepSeek Sparse Attention](#c/c-dsa). It was one lab's late-2025 innovation, and within months it was the backbone of a second frontier-scale flagship: [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) imported it wholesale, and its architecture is even registered as `glm_moe_dsa`, making the import explicit. The Sources compare it with how models adopted [RoPE](#c/c-rope) after it was published. Rather than invent its own long-context mechanism, GLM reused the best available one. This is part of why the architectural backbone of [open frontier models](#c/c-open-models) is consolidating: good ideas diffuse quickly, so the differences between labs shift toward training recipes and data.

concepts.title: slime
concepts.summary: Zhipu's asynchronous RL infrastructure that decouples generation from training so GPUs stay busy.
concepts.overview: slime is the headline engineering of [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5), and the Sources' example of the post-training frontier. Standard RL for language models runs three serial phases (generate, score, update) that wait on each other; at 744B parameters GPUs sit idle during scoring because generation is not running, and vice versa. slime decouples generation from training asynchronously to maximize GPU utilization and allow massive-scale exploration of agent trajectories without synchronization bottlenecks. It is aimed squarely at [agentic RL](#c/c-agentic-rl): runs of 3,000–6,000 messages (about 60–100M output tokens) to hone long-range planning and tool use. GLM-5 builds on an earlier version of the framework.

concepts.title: GLM-5.1
concepts.summary: A March 2026 GLM update on the GLM-5 base, claiming 94.6% of Claude Opus 4.6's coding score.
concepts.overview: GLM-5.1 followed [GLM-5](#c/c-glm-5) in late March 2026 and inherits its base: a 744B MoE with 256 experts, 8 active, and 40B active parameters. Its reported claim is 94.6% of Claude Opus 4.6's coding score. The Sources hold that very loosely: it postdates the assistant's cutoff, the only source was a single SEO-oriented blog, and the numbers are explicitly unverified vendor claims ([vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks)). It is mainly the reference point for [what GLM-5.2 adds](#c/c-q-glm52-adds).

concepts.title: GLM-5.2
concepts.summary: Zhipu's June 13, 2026 release, headlined by a one-million-token context and High/Max reasoning presets.
concepts.overview: GLM-5.2 was released June 13, 2026, and at the time of the conversation was known only from launch coverage. Confirmed: a 1M-token context (identifier `glm-5.2[1m]`) with up to 131,072 output tokens, pitched at long-horizon agentic coding; two reasoning-effort presets, High and Max, with Max recommended for coding; and day-one availability on every GLM Coding Plan tier, with API, chatbot and MIT-licensed weights the following week. The newest coverage gives 753B parameters versus [GLM-5.1](#c/c-glm-51)'s 744B, which could be a change or loose reporting. There is no technical report, so how the long context was achieved is unknown. Coverage disagrees about benchmarks ([no benchmarks at launch](#c/c-glm52-no-benchmarks) versus [beats the frontier](#c/c-glm52-beats-frontier)), against a charged backdrop ([US suspends top models abroad](#c/c-us-model-suspension)).

concepts.title: What does GLM-5.2 add over 5.1?
concepts.summary: Confirmed: 1M context, High/Max reasoning presets, broad availability. Claimed: beating Western frontier models. Unknown: how.
concepts.overview: What [GLM-5.2](#c/c-glm-52) adds over [GLM-5.1](#c/c-glm-51) splits into three tiers. Confirmed: a one-million-token context, roughly 5× the GLM-5 line's 200K, with 131,072 output tokens; new High and Max reasoning-effort presets aimed at coding; and day-one availability on every Coding Plan tier, with MIT weights following. Claimed but unverified: that it beats GPT-5.5, Claude Opus 4.7 and even Fable 5 ([GLM-5.2 beats the frontier](#c/c-glm52-beats-frontier)), which contradicts earlier reports of [no benchmarks at launch](#c/c-glm52-no-benchmarks). Unknown: the architecture behind the longer context (extended DSA, a [YaRN](#c/c-yarn)-style RoPE scaling change, retraining?) and what the 753B-versus-744B difference represents, because no technical report had appeared.

concepts.title: GLM-5.2 beats the frontier
concepts.summary: Late launch coverage claimed GLM-5.2 beats GPT-5.5 and Claude models; the claims are vendor-originated and unverified.
concepts.overview: Coverage from June 16–17, 2026 carried strong claims about [GLM-5.2](#c/c-glm-52): that the 753B open-weights model beats GPT-5.5 on multiple long-horizon coding benchmarks at one-sixth the cost, scored higher than Claude Opus 4.7 on various benchmarks, and in some human blind tests even outperformed [Claude Fable 5](#c/c-fable-5). The assistant treats this with real skepticism. The claims appear only in the newest, partly aggregated coverage; they contradict reports two days earlier that there were [no benchmarks at launch](#c/c-glm52-no-benchmarks); "beats GPT-5.5 at 1/6th the cost" is classic launch framing; and they coincide with a charged moment ([US suspends top models abroad](#c/c-us-model-suspension)). It is a textbook case for [vendor benchmarks need checking](#c/c-vendor-benchmarks).

concepts.title: No benchmarks at launch
concepts.summary: The earliest GLM-5.2 coverage said Zhipu had published no official benchmark scores at all.
concepts.overview: The first reports on [GLM-5.2](#c/c-glm-52), from June 13–15, 2026, were emphatic that at release Zhipu published no official scores: no SWE-bench Verified, no LiveCodeBench, no HumanEval. One called the absence unusual for a release of this scale, and they advised treating any GLM-5.2 numbers as marketing promises until independent verification arrived. This directly contradicts the strong comparative claims that appeared two days later ([GLM-5.2 beats the frontier](#c/c-glm52-beats-frontier)). The likely explanation is that sources were written at different moments of a fast-moving launch, which is itself a reason to wait for a technical report and third-party evaluations.

concepts.title: US suspends top models abroad
concepts.summary: A June 2026 US order suspending top American models overseas, coinciding with GLM-5.2's open-source rollout.
concepts.overview: Several sources tied [GLM-5.2](#c/c-glm-52)'s launch timing to a US action restricting top American models abroad: Washington's order to suspend top US models overseas coincided with the open-source rollout, and [Zhipu](#c/c-zhipu)'s stock surged as much as 48%. The Sources report this from launch coverage rather than independent knowledge. Its relevance is as context: the louder "beats Western models" framing ([GLM-5.2 beats the frontier](#c/c-glm52-beats-frontier)) was made in a charged competitive moment, which is more reason to wait for independent benchmarks before believing head-to-head claims.

concepts.title: Vendor benchmarks need checking
concepts.summary: Headline model comparisons are usually self-reported and favorably selected; wait for independent evaluation.
concepts.overview: A caution that recurs across the Expedition. [DeepSeek-V3.2](#c/c-deepseek-v32)'s GPT-5 comparisons come from DeepSeek's own materials. [Granite 4.0](#c/c-granite-4) and [Nemotron-H](#c/c-nemotron-h) publish real numbers, but on benchmarks where they look especially good. [Mercury](#c/c-mercury) and [Gemini Diffusion](#c/c-gemini-diffusion)'s parity claims are vendor-reported and confined to coding and math. GLM's scores are self-reported by Z.ai, and [GLM-5.2's frontier claims](#c/c-glm52-beats-frontier) contradicted earlier reports of [no benchmarks at all](#c/c-glm52-no-benchmarks). The pattern is consistent: published numbers are real but selected, benchmark parity is exactly where independent replication matters, and results are often only "competitive, not dominant" once checked. Trust the claim after third-party evaluation across a broad suite.
